meta.title: Brain Circuit Atlas
meta.subtitle: An evidence-linked map of the cerebellum, motor and prefrontal cortex, basal ganglia, hippocampus, amygdala, visual cortex, insula, olfactory system, basal forebrain and their connections, from molecules to mind, and of two invertebrate brains, the octopus and the fruit fly
meta.disclaimer: Summaries, link statuses and map scores were drafted with AI assistance from PubMed abstracts and need review by domain experts. Diagrams are schematic.

statuses.label: Established
statuses.desc: Replicated across labs and methods; textbook level.

statuses.label: Supported
statuses.desc: Several consistent studies; details still open.

statuses.label: Emerging
statuses.desc: One or a few studies, or a single method or species.

statuses.label: Hypothesis
statuses.desc: Proposed and plausible, not directly tested.

statuses.label: Gap
statuses.desc: No curated link: a candidate for new research.

evidence.label: Causal manipulation
evidence.desc: Lesion, genetic, opto-/chemogenetic, pharmacological or stimulation experiments.

evidence.label: Patients & lesions
evidence.desc: Patient cohorts, lesion–symptom mapping, human genetics.

evidence.label: Recording & imaging
evidence.desc: Electrophysiology, calcium imaging, fMRI without manipulation.

intro.title: The cerebellum, wired into brain and body
intro.text: A map that joins motor, cognitive and social functions of the cerebellum, from molecules to behavior. Every connection is tied to the papers behind it and graded by how strong the evidence is.

speciesNote.human: Human: lobules and deep nuclei from the SUIT probabilistic atlas (Diedrichsen 2009, 2011), fitted to the Allen human brain. Brainstem nuclei not segmented in these atlases are approximate (≈).
speciesNote.mouse: Mouse: Allen CCFv3 lobules and nuclei. Most causal circuit evidence comes from mice.
speciesNote.macaque: Macaque: lobules, deep nuclei and brainstem nuclei from the SARM subcortical atlas (Hartig et al., 2021) and cortical areas from CHARM (Jung et al., 2021), on the NIMH Macaque Template. The substantia nigra is drawn whole; the tuberomammillary nucleus and brainstem serotonin neurons are approximate (≈).

intro.title: Motor cortex, from layers to the spinal cord
intro.text: Primary motor and premotor areas: their inputs, the layer 5 neurons that send commands to the brainstem and spinal cord, the plasticity behind skill learning, and what happens after stroke or paralysis. speciesNote.macaque: Macaque: CHARM primary motor (M1), premotor (PMd, PMv), supplementary motor (SMA, pre-SMA) and primary somatosensory areas; SARM motor thalamus (VA/VL) and basal nucleus (basal forebrain). Mouse ALM is shown at the premotor areas as a possible homologue.

intro.title: Prefrontal cortex, from receptors to decisions
intro.text: Dorsolateral, orbital, cingulate and (in rodents) medial prefrontal areas: the delay activity linked to working memory and the neuromodulators that tune it, their loops with the thalamus, hippocampus and amygdala, and what changes in schizophrenia, depression and after prefrontal damage. Every connection is tied to the papers behind it and graded by how strong the evidence is.

speciesNote.human: Human: Allen middle frontal gyrus (for the dorsolateral PFC), orbital gyri (OFC), gyrus rectus (ventromedial PFC), rostral cingulate gyrus (ACC) and subcallosal gyrus (for the subgenual cingulate, approximate). speciesNote.mouse: Mouse: Allen CCFv3 prelimbic, infralimbic, anterior cingulate and orbital areas, mediodorsal thalamus and dorsal raphe. Rodent prefrontal names and borders differ between atlases; the primate dorsolateral, ventromedial and subgenual areas are not drawn.
speciesNote.macaque: Macaque: CHARM dorsolateral PFC, orbitofrontal cortex, anterior cingulate areas 24 and 32 and subgenual area 25; SARM mediodorsal thalamus and dorsal raphe. Rodent prelimbic and infralimbic cortex are not drawn.

intro.title: Basal ganglia, from dopamine to action
intro.text: The striatum, pallidum, subthalamic nucleus and substantia nigra: the direct, indirect and hyperdirect pathways that link them with cortex and thalamus, the dopamine signals that shape learning and vigor, and what changes in Parkinson's and Huntington's diseases. Every connection is tied to the papers behind it and graded by how strong the evidence is.

intro.title: Hippocampus, from synapses to memory
intro.text: The dentate gyrus, CA fields, subiculum and entorhinal cortex: the trisynaptic pathway, place and grid cells, theta and sharp-wave ripples, adult neurogenesis, and what changes in amnesia, Alzheimer's disease, depression and PTSD. Every connection is tied to the papers behind it and graded by how strong the evidence is.

speciesNote.human: Human: Allen head, body and tail of the hippocampus (the head is the anterior hippocampus, the body and tail the posterior hippocampus) and the anterior parahippocampal gyrus, which contains the entorhinal cortex. The atlas does not separate the dentate gyrus, CA fields or subiculum, so they are shown in the hippocampus.
speciesNote.mouse: Mouse: Allen CCFv3 dentate gyrus, fields CA1, CA2 and CA3, subiculum, entorhinal area and medial septal nucleus. The dorsal and ventral hippocampus are approximate (≈): the upper and lower parts of the hippocampal fields. The pathways between the fields are drawn where they cross the dorsal hippocampus, as in a coronal section.
speciesNote.macaque: Macaque: SARM hippocampus and subicular complex, and CHARM entorhinal cortex. SARM labels the hippocampus as a whole, so the dentate gyrus and CA fields are shown in it, and the anterior (ventral) and posterior (dorsal) hippocampus are approximate (≈).

intro.title: Amygdala, from synapses to feelings
intro.text: The lateral, basal, central, medial and intercalated nuclei: how a tone comes to predict danger, the central amygdala cell types that choose between freezing and flight, how good and bad are coded, the amygdala's part in recognizing emotion and in valuing choices, and what changes in PTSD, anxiety disorders and autism. Every connection is tied to the papers behind it and graded by how strong the evidence is.

speciesNote.macaque: Macaque: SARM lateral, basolateral, basomedial, paralaminar, central and medial amygdaloid nuclei and the medial geniculate nucleus. SARM has no intercalated-cell label, so the intercalated cells are placed approximately (≈).

intro.title: Visual cortex, from receptive fields to recognition
intro.text: Primary visual cortex and the areas beyond it: how geniculate input builds orientation-tuned receptive fields, how inhibition and the extracellular matrix open and close the critical period for binocular vision, the areas and streams for motion, colour, objects, faces and action, how attention and running change visual responses, and what changes in amblyopia, cortical blindness, early blindness and migraine aura. Every connection is tied to the papers behind it and graded by how strong the evidence is.

speciesNote.human: Human: the Allen atlas does not mark visual areas, so V1 is drawn as the occipital pole, cuneus and lingual gyrus (which also hold V2 and V3), V4 as the occipital part of the fusiform gyrus, the fusiform face area as its temporal part and inferotemporal cortex as the inferior temporal gyrus; MT (V5) is placed approximately (≈). The lateral geniculate nucleus is shown in the thalamus, and the frontal eye field is not placed.
speciesNote.mouse: Mouse: Allen CCFv3 primary visual area (VISp), the higher visual areas LM, AL, AM, PM, LI and P (the anterior and rostrolateral areas are drawn with posterior parietal cortex) and the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus. speciesNote.macaque: Macaque: CHARM V1, V4, MT, inferior temporal cortex (TE and TEO) and area 8A (frontal eye field), and the SARM dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus. The fusiform face area and the mouse higher visual areas are not placed.

intro.title: Insula, the brain's map of the body
intro.text: The anterior and posterior insula and the taste cortex: how heartbeat, temperature, pain and taste are represented, how tastes gain pleasant or aversive value through the amygdala, how hunger and thirst change what insular neurons signal, the insula's part in empathy, disgust and the salience network, and what changes in smoking addiction, frontotemporal dementia, central pain and across psychiatric disorders. Every connection is tied to the papers behind it and graded by how strong the evidence is.

speciesNote.human: Human: the Allen short insular gyri stand for the anterior insula and the long insular gyri for the posterior insula. The atlas does not mark the taste cortex, which in humans lies in the insula and operculum, so it is shown in the anterior insula, as are the von Economo neurons.

intro.title: Olfaction, from receptor genes to memory
intro.text: The olfactory system: how a large family of receptor genes and a map of glomeruli in the olfactory bulb encode odours, how the bulb's map is scattered across piriform cortex but kept in the cortical amygdala, how odours gain learned or innate meaning, the vomeronasal system and social behaviour, how breathing paces olfactory and limbic activity, and why smell fails with age, in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's diseases and in COVID-19. Every connection is tied to the papers behind it and graded by how strong the evidence is.

speciesNote.macaque: Macaque: SARM piriform cortex and ventral cortical amygdaloid nucleus. The template does not include the olfactory bulb, so the bulb and the olfactory sensory neurons are placed approximately (≈) under the front of the orbital surface; the vomeronasal organ is not placed.

intro.title: Basal forebrain, from neuromodulation to attention and memory
intro.text: The medial septum, diagonal band, substantia innominata, nucleus basalis, lateral septum, and ventral pallidum: cholinergic, GABAergic, and glutamatergic projection systems, acetylcholine and GABA cotransmission, striatal disinhibition, the ascending arousal network, and what changes in Alzheimer's disease, attention disorders, and impaired consciousness. Every connection is evidence-graded and linked to primary literature.

speciesNote.human: Human: Allen substantia innominata (basal forebrain, Ch4); functional connectivity differentiates medial septal/diagonal band from nucleus basalis corticotopic profiles; ascending arousal network links brainstem and VTA through basal forebrain to the default mode network.
speciesNote.mouse: Mouse: Allen CCFv3 substantia innominata (SI), medial septal nucleus (MS), and ventral pallidum (VP); viral tracing distinguishes cholinergic, PV+, SOM+, and glutamatergic populations; ACh/GABA cotransmission in CA1; anterior BF (HDB/VDB) projection to prelimbic cortex; NAc D1/D2 regulation of amygdalar ACh.
speciesNote.macaque: Macaque: SARM basal nucleus (Ch4), medial septum (Ch1), and diagonal band (Ch2/Ch3); classical Ch1–Ch4 cholinergic mapping demonstrates topographical cortical and limbic projection organization; BF inactivation regulates global resting-state fMRI fluctuations.

intro.title: ADHD as a distributed, dimensional brain profile
intro.text: A clinical scope for evidence-linked ADHD phenotypes, control, reward, arousal and developmental circuits. Phenotypic dimensions come before core systems: the atlas separates associations, treatment perturbations and translational mechanisms rather than drawing a single ADHD lesion.

speciesNote.human: Human: ADHD records summarize group-level clinical, imaging, molecular and genetic findings; the 3D brain reuses existing anatomical meshes and does not diagnose individuals.
speciesNote.mouse: Mouse: translational receptor and circuit mechanisms are shown at approximate homologous structures; they are not direct models of every human ADHD phenotype.
speciesNote.macaque: Macaque: prefrontal catecholamine physiology is translational evidence, not proof of a human ADHD-specific lesion.

intro.title: Octopus brain, a large brain that evolved separately
intro.text: The cephalopod brain evolved independently of the vertebrate brain. Here: the vertical lobe’s learning and memory network and its long-term potentiation, the optic lobes’ visual maps, the basal lobes that command eight arms without a body map, the arms’ own nerve cords and suckers that taste by touch, two stages of sleep, and the optic gland that controls maturation and maternal death. Every connection is tied to the papers behind it and graded by how strong the evidence is.

speciesNote.octopus: Octopus: a schematic brain drawn for this site, because no octopus atlas volume is available to it. Lobe shapes, sizes and positions are approximate and for orientation only, so every label carries ≈. The vertical lobe’s amacrine and output neurons are shown in the vertical lobe. Findings come from several species (mainly Octopus vulgaris and O. bimaculoides).

intro.title: Fruit fly brain, wired synapse by synapse
intro.text: A brain of about 140,000 neurons whose wiring is known synapse by synapse, from electron microscopy connectomes of the whole brain and of the whole male central nervous system. Here: odours mapped from receptors to the antennal lobe, the mushroom body that learns which odours predict reward or punishment, the lateral horn’s innate responses, the central complex’s compass and sleep drive, motion vision from the lamina to looming detectors and escape, taste, descending control of walking, and the fruitless gene that wires courtship. Structural connectivity (electron microscopy wiring) and functional connectivity (correlated activity) are kept apart, and every connection is tied to the papers behind it and graded by how strong the evidence is.

speciesNote.fly: Fruit fly: neuropil meshes from the Janelia FlyEM male CNS connectome (CC-BY), simplified; paired neuropils are labelled on the fly’s left. Kenyon cells and the output, dopamine and APL neurons are shown in the mushroom body, projection neurons in the antennal lobe, T4/T5 cells in the lobula plate, LC neurons in the lobula, ring and E-PG neurons in the ellipsoid body, and descending neurons, with the giant fibre, at the neck connective. Photoreceptors and olfactory and gustatory receptor neurons lie outside the brain and are shown as approximate markers. Findings are from Drosophila melanogaster; the connectomes come from different flies, female and male.

entities.name: mGluR1
entities.summary: Metabotropic glutamate receptor on Purkinje-cell spines, recruited by strong parallel-fiber activity. It drives PLCβ, PKC and calcium signaling needed to induce LTD. Knockout mice lack LTD and have impaired eyeblink conditioning, but they are also ataxic.

entities.name: Protein kinase C
entities.summary: Kinase downstream of mGluR1 whose activity triggers AMPA-receptor internalization during LTD. Blocking it in Purkinje cells (L7-PKCI mice) disrupts PF–PC plasticity and impairs hippocampal place coding that relies on self-motion cues.

entities.name: AMPA receptors (GluA2)
entities.summary: Mediate fast parallel fiber–Purkinje transmission. LTD is expressed as clathrin-dependent endocytosis of GluA2-containing receptors. Mutant mice that cannot internalize them lack LTD under standard protocols yet learn normally; stronger induction protocols still evoke LTD in the same mutants.

entities.name: PLCβ3 / PLCβ4
entities.summary: Phospholipase C isoforms downstream of mGluR1, expressed in complementary stripes: PLCβ3 in zebrin-positive and PLCβ4 in zebrin-negative Purkinje cells. The same receptor therefore engages different signaling machinery in different modules.

entities.name: TRPC3 channel
entities.summary: Cation channel activated downstream of mGluR1. Blocking it reduces the higher simple-spike rate of zebrin-negative Purkinje cells, so modules operate at different intrinsic frequencies.

entities.name: GluD2–Cbln1 complex
entities.summary: Cbln1 secreted by granule cells binds the orphan receptor GluD2 on Purkinje spines. The complex organizes parallel fiber–Purkinje synapses from both sides and can induce new synapses. In the immature cerebellum, D-serine from Bergmann glia binds GluD2 to drive LTD.

entities.name: Zebrin II (aldolase C)
entities.summary: Expressed by subsets of Purkinje cells in parasagittal stripes conserved across vertebrates. Zebrin-positive and zebrin-negative modules differ in firing rate, signaling and plasticity.

entities.name: CACNA1A (Cav2.1)
entities.summary: α1A subunit of the P/Q-type calcium channel, abundant in Purkinje cells. Small polyglutamine expansions cause spinocerebellar ataxia type 6; mutations that disrupt the reading frame cause episodic ataxia type 2, and missense mutations cause familial hemiplegic migraine.

entities.name: ATXN1
entities.summary: Gene with an unstable CAG repeat. Expansion causes spinocerebellar ataxia type 1, and longer repeats are associated with earlier onset.

entities.name: TSC1 / mTOR pathway
entities.summary: Losing Tsc1 in Purkinje cells lowers their excitability and causes autistic-like behaviors in mice, which rapamycin prevents. PC-Tsc1 mice became a test bed for mapping cerebellar circuits relevant to autism.

entities.name: SHANK2
entities.summary: Postsynaptic scaffold gene linked to autism. Its loss impairs Purkinje intrinsic plasticity and PF–PC LTP, enhances inhibition and makes simple spikes irregular. Purkinje-specific knockouts show motor-learning and social deficits.

entities.name: FMR1 (FMRP)
entities.summary: Fragile X gene. Deleting it in Purkinje cells enhances LTD, elongates spines and impairs eyeblink conditioning, resembling the deficits of fragile X patients.

entities.name: Dopamine D1 receptor
entities.summary: Marks a distinct, mostly GABAergic population in the lateral cerebellar nucleus (also present in human dentate). Inhibiting these neurons impairs working memory, response inhibition, spatial memory and prepulse inhibition. Bergmann glia also express D1 receptors; activating them alters Purkinje-cell input (mouse).

entities.name: Atoh1 (Math1)
entities.summary: Transcription factor of the rhombic lip. Required for generating granule neurons.

entities.name: Ptf1a
entities.summary: Transcription factor of the cerebellar ventricular zone that specifies GABAergic neurons: Purkinje cells and interneurons.

entities.name: Sonic hedgehog
entities.summary: Secreted by Purkinje cells; drives proliferation of granule-cell precursors. Over-activation of the pathway underlies SHH-type medulloblastoma.

entities.name: SCN2A (NaV1.2)
entities.summary: Autism-risk sodium-channel gene. In granule cells, NaV1.2 supports high-frequency transmission and LTP at parallel fiber–Purkinje synapses. Its loss leaves the VOR hypersensitive in mice and children, and restoring expression rescues VOR plasticity.

entities.name: ZP2 (human granule cells)
entities.summary: A sperm-receptor gene co-opted in human granule cells. Pontine mossy fibers induce it, and it reduces synaptic proteins at mossy fiber–granule glomeruli and dampens activity: a human-specific synaptic regulator.

entities.name: Noradrenaline (adrenergic receptors)
entities.summary: Released in the cerebellar cortex by locus coeruleus fibers; activating this pathway inhibits Purkinje cells (rat). Through α2-adrenergic receptors it lowers climbing-fiber release probability and damps associative plasticity; through β2 receptors it excites basket cells; through α1 receptors on Bergmann glia it signals noxious stimuli; and through Purkinje-cell α1 receptors it triggers stress-induced attacks in a mouse model of episodic ataxia type 2. Blocking β-adrenergic receptors in lobule HVI and the interpositus impairs acquisition of eyeblink conditioning (rat). Theory proposes that noradrenaline gates unsupervised learning in the cerebellar cortex. In prefrontal cortex, stimulating α2A adrenoceptors strengthens working-memory delay firing by inhibiting cAMP and closing HCN channels (monkeys and rats). Locus coeruleus neurons projecting to prefrontal cortex differ biochemically and electrophysiologically from those projecting to motor cortex and release more noradrenaline (rat). In ADHD treatment models, alpha2A-related prefrontal signaling is a translational mechanism, while an ADHD-specific universal locus-coeruleus abnormality remains unresolved (human; review).

entities.name: Serotonin (5-HT receptors)
entities.summary: Serotonergic fibers reach all layers of the cerebellar cortex; in rats they arise almost exclusively from the gigantocellular, paragigantocellular and pontine (oralis) reticular nuclei, most of them outside the raphe nuclei. Serotonin selectively excites Lugaro cells, which inhibit Golgi cells, and depolarizes Golgi cells (likely via 5-HT2A receptors), which raises tonic inhibition of granule cells. During the first postnatal weeks, granule-cell 5-HT3 receptors modulate short-term plasticity at parallel-fiber synapses and regulate the timing of Purkinje-cell maturation (mouse). The 5-HT1A agonist buspirone gave a partial benefit in a small trial in cerebellar cortical atrophy. Theory proposes that serotonin sets the 'responsibility' of each microcomplex.

entities.name: Dopamine (D1–D3 receptors)
entities.summary: The cerebellum contains high dopamine levels, receives midbrain dopaminergic afferents and expresses all five dopamine receptor subtypes; in rats, dopaminergic VTA neurons project to the granular and Purkinje-cell layers, mainly of Crus I and the paraflocculus. Purkinje cells also make and release dopamine, which excites them in an autocrine way (a depolarization-induced slow current) and activates D1 receptors on Bergmann glia (mouse). Purkinje-cell D2 receptors regulate synaptic efficacy and sociability, and deleting glial D1 receptors reduces locomotion and social activity (mouse). A D1-receptor-positive population in the lateral nucleus supports working memory, response inhibition and spatial memory. Theory proposes that dopamine enhances goal-oriented learning. In rat primary motor cortex, dopaminergic terminals and D1/D2 receptors are needed for acquiring a motor skill and for LTP, but not for executing a learned skill. In monkey prefrontal cortex, blocking D1 receptors impairs memory-guided saccades, and D1 stimulation shapes delay activity along an inverted U: low levels sharpen spatial tuning, high levels reduce delay firing in all directions, through cAMP signaling (monkeys and rats). In mice, a fast-firing population of midbrain dopamine neurons that lacks functional somatodendritic D2 autoreceptors projects to prefrontal cortex, and the authors of an optogenetic study conclude that phasic dopamine release in medial PFC tunes its neurons to behaviorally relevant events during learning. In the striatum, its differential effects on striatonigral and striatopallidal neurons are mediated by their D1 and D2 receptors, respectively (rat), and its complementary actions in the two cell types keep corticostriatal plasticity bidirectional and Hebbian (mouse). The output of primate dopamine neurons apparently signals reward prediction errors, and in rats, activating dopamine neurons at reward delivery is sufficient for long-lasting increases in cue-elicited reward seeking. In ADHD, molecular-imaging and pharmacodynamic reviews support dopamine-related reward and treatment mechanisms without establishing a uniform untreated dopamine deficit (human).

entities.name: Acetylcholine (nicotinic & muscarinic)
entities.summary: Cholinergic markers in the cerebellum are sparse and vary between species and lobules. The predominant fiber system that may use acetylcholine is mossy fibers from the vestibular nuclei to the nodulus and ventral uvula; beaded cholinergic fibers from the pedunculopontine and lateral paragigantocellular nuclei (and, to a lesser extent, raphe nuclei) reach the cortex and nuclei (rat). Acetylcholine release hyperpolarizes Golgi cells, and presynaptic muscarinic receptors reduce mossy-fiber glutamate release; α7 nicotinic receptors let weak mossy-fiber bursts induce LTP at granule-cell synapses; muscarinic receptors transiently excite interpositus neurons. Most, if not all, cerebellar nicotinic receptors are on intrinsic cells (rat). The α4β2 partial agonist varenicline improved axial measures in a trial in SCA3. Theory proposes that acetylcholine sets the speed of supervised learning. Lesions of the basal forebrain cholinergic system disrupt the cortical map reorganization that accompanies motor skill learning (rat).

entities.name: Histamine (H1/H2 receptors)
entities.summary: Histaminergic neurons of the hypothalamic tuberomammillary nucleus send fine varicose fibers throughout the cerebellar cortex and nuclei, part of direct, bidirectional hypothalamo-cerebellar connections. Histamine directly excites Purkinje cells, granule cells and nuclear neurons. In the cerebellar nuclei it depolarizes projection neurons, but not interneurons, through H2 receptors coupled to HCN channels, and histamine acting on H2 receptors in the interpositus nucleus improves motor balance and coordination (rat).

entities.name: Orexin (hypocretin)
entities.summary: Orexin-A fibers from perifornical and lateral hypothalamic neurons reach the vestibular nuclei and the cerebellar nuclei (densest in the fastigial nucleus), with a few in paraflocculus cortex (rat). Orexins excite interpositus neurons through OX2 receptors (rat), and orexinergic fibers excite Purkinje cells in a floccular microzone implicated in blood-flow redistribution during defense reactions (rabbit). On an accelerating rotarod, orexinergic input to the dentate adds to exercise-induced anxiety relief (mouse). A review lists orexin among candidate therapeutic targets in ataxias and psychiatric disorders.

entities.name: CRF (corticotropin-releasing factor)
entities.summary: Very highly expressed throughout the inferior olive and found in climbing fibers. CRF raises Purkinje-cell firing, enhances climbing fiber–Purkinje transmission through presynaptic CRF2 receptors, and is permissive for parallel-fiber LTD (via PKC). CRF-expressing olivary neurons also excite glutamatergic interpositus neurons through CRF1 and CRF2 receptors (rat). Reducing olivary CRF impairs motor performance under challenging conditions, and chronic social defeat stress lowers it (mouse); CRF given into the cerebellum improves rotarod performance (rat). Bilateral central amygdala lesions lower cerebrospinal fluid CRF (monkey), and CRF+ central amygdala neurons mediate conditioned flight (mouse).

entities.name: CGRP (calcitonin gene-related peptide)
entities.summary: Transiently present in developing climbing fibers. Its receptor is mainly astrocytic, and CGRP triggers Ca²⁺ release from stores in Bergmann glia (mouse). In culture, CGRP stimulates Purkinje-cell dendrite growth, most likely through astrocytes; the CGRP-receptor antagonist CGRP8-37 does not block this (rat).

entities.name: Opioid peptides (μ/δ receptors)
entities.summary: Enkephalin immunoreactivity occurs in Golgi cells and mossy fibers of the cerebellum in mammals, birds, amphibians and fish. μ- and δ- (but not κ-) opioid receptors on parallel-fiber terminals reduce glutamate release onto Purkinje cells, and endogenous opioid peptides at these synapses do the same (mouse). Pontine neurons that receive a rostral anterior cingulate input mediating placebo analgesia are rich in opioid receptors (mouse).

entities.name: Oxytocin and its receptor
entities.summary: Where the oxytocin receptor is expressed in the cerebellum has been controversial: expression patterns vary widely between knock-in reporter lines. In Oxtr-Cre reporter mice, expression in Bergmann glia was more variable than in Purkinje cells, and physical damage with inflammation selectively upregulated it in Bergmann glia; the authors suggest that the receptor may affect neural processing in pathological conditions. A review lists oxytocin among candidate therapeutic targets. Axons of hypothalamic oxytocin neurons reach most forebrain regions, including the central amygdala, where stimulating these axons activates a local GABAergic circuit (in vitro) and evoked oxytocin release decreases freezing in fear-conditioned rats; oxytocin decreases freezing without affecting the cardiovascular response (rat). In healthy men, intranasal oxytocin reduces amygdala activation by fear-inducing visual stimuli and the amygdala's coupling to brainstem regions implicated in fear (human).

entities.name: Cholecystokinin (CCK1 receptor)
entities.summary: In ATXN1[30Q]D776 mice, an SCA1 model that is ataxic without progressive Purkinje-cell pathology, cerebellar Cck is upregulated; removing Cck1 receptors makes the disease progressive, with Purkinje-cell death. The Cck1R agonist A71623 dampened Purkinje-cell pathology and motor deficits in SCA1 mice, improved motor performance in SCA2 mice and corrected mTORC1 signaling.

entities.name: Neuropeptide Y
entities.summary: Intranasal neuropeptide Y alleviated motor deficits and neuropathology in a mouse model of Machado–Joseph disease (SCA3). A review lists NPY among eight cerebellar neuropeptides that are candidate therapeutic targets.

entities.name: PACAP
entities.summary: Pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide acts as a transient, layer-specific brake on granule-cell migration: exogenous PACAP slows migration in the external granular and molecular layers, and blocking endogenous PACAP speeds migration in the Purkinje-cell layer (early postnatal mice).

entities.name: Endocannabinoids (2-AG, CB1)
entities.summary: Purkinje cells release endocannabinoids when depolarized or when mGluR1 is activated; acting retrogradely on presynaptic CB1 receptors, they suppress parallel- and climbing-fiber transmission. Parallel-fiber LTD requires the endocannabinoid 2-AG and CB1 receptors, including CB1 on granule cells. CB1-knockout mice are impaired in delay eyeblink conditioning, but the deficit stems from their reduced locomotor activity: treadmill walking rescues it, and granule-cell-specific knockouts learn normally. Activating cerebellar CB1 signaling causes ataxia-like deficits, and CB1 deficits can cause progressive ataxia.

entities.name: Nitric oxide
entities.summary: Climbing-fiber stimulation releases nitric oxide, and NO or cGMP can substitute for climbing-fiber activity in inducing LTD; LTD requires NO coinciding with a depolarization-induced postsynaptic Ca²⁺ rise (rat). NMDA receptors on molecular-layer interneurons, not on granule or Purkinje cells, are required for LTD and OKR adaptation, and an NO donor restores LTD (mouse). A 1 Hz parallel-fiber LTP also depends on NO (rat).

entities.name: Adenosine & ATP (purines)
entities.summary: Short trains of molecular-layer activity release adenosine, probably from parallel fibers, which feeds back to inhibit parallel fiber–Purkinje transmission (rat). ATP, most likely from molecular-layer interneurons, acts on P2 receptors to release Ca²⁺ from stores in Bergmann glia (rat).

entities.name: D-serine
entities.summary: Released by Bergmann glia in the immature cerebellum. It binds GluD2 to drive AMPA-receptor endocytosis and LTD; mice whose GluD2 lacks the D-serine binding site have impaired LTD and motor dyscoordination during development.

entities.name: Estrogen (estradiol)
entities.summary: Estradiol enhances parallel fiber–Purkinje LTP (not LTD), increases parallel-fiber synapse density and, acting on Purkinje-cell estrogen receptor β, improves gain-decrease adaptation of the VOR (mouse). Estrogen-receptor activation of mGluR1a strongly enhances parallel fiber–Purkinje transmission; blocking local (aromatase-dependent) estrogen synthesis weakens it, lowering estrogen impairs locomotor performance, and the facilitation occurs in both sexes (mouse).

entities.name: Thyroid hormone (TR)
entities.summary: Developmental thyroid-hormone-receptor signaling in Purkinje cells is needed for motor coordination and learning. With a dominant-negative receptor, LTD-inducing stimulation produces LTP, dendritic Ca²⁺ signals are smaller, and SERCA2 and IP3R1 are reduced; adult-onset thyroid-hormone deficiency does not do this (mouse).

entities.name: Glycine (co-transmitter)
entities.summary: A fast inhibitory co-transmitter in parts of the circuit. Lugaro cell → Golgi cell synapses are mixed GABA/glycinergic, whereas basket- and stellate-cell inputs to Golgi cells are purely GABAergic (rat), and GABA-glycinergic nuclear neurons inhibit a subset of Golgi cells (mouse). Nuclear interneurons contact principal neurons through glycine-receptor-rich synapses, whereas Purkinje-cell inhibition of the nuclei is almost purely GABAergic. Many fastigial premotor neurons are glycinergic and project ipsilaterally. Inferior-olive input from the vestibular nuclei is mixed GABA/glycine; input from the cerebellar nuclei is purely GABAergic (mouse).

entities.name: Purkinje cell
entities.summary: The sole output neuron of the cerebellar cortex (GABAergic). Each receives more than 100,000 parallel-fiber synapses but usually a single climbing fiber (some multi-dendritic cells keep more), and fires simple spikes and complex spikes. Population simple-spike activity predicts movement kinematics. Molecular identity (zebrin) varies by module.

entities.name: Granule cell
entities.summary: The most numerous neurons in the brain (~60 billion in humans). Each receives about four mossy-fiber inputs, which theory says maximizes coding dimension. Population activity is high-dimensional but often denser than classic theory assumed, and it carries predictive, reward-expectation and seconds-long timing signals.

entities.name: Golgi cell
entities.summary: Inhibitory interneuron of the granular layer that provides feedforward and feedback inhibition to granule cells, shaping the timing and sparseness of the input layer. Serotonin depolarizes them and acetylcholine hyperpolarizes them. They receive mixed GABA/glycinergic inhibition from Lugaro cells, and GABA-glycinergic nuclear neurons inhibit a subset of them.

entities.name: Molecular-layer interneurons
entities.summary: Stellate and basket cells, now split into two molecularly distinct types (MLI1, MLI2). They inhibit Purkinje cells and grade climbing-fiber calcium signals, which can flip the sign of plasticity and learning. Noradrenaline excites basket cells through β2 receptors, and MLI NMDA receptors are required for parallel-fiber LTD.

entities.name: Unipolar brush cell
entities.summary: Glutamatergic interneuron of the granular layer that receives mossy-fiber input. In the nodulus and ventral uvula, putatively cholinergic mossy fibers from the vestibular nuclei contact unipolar brush cells as well as granule cells. Gene expression and electrophysiological properties vary continuously rather than falling into discrete types. Human rhombic-lip UBC progenitors are linked to Group 3/4 medulloblastoma.

entities.name: Cerebellar nuclear neurons
entities.summary: Excitatory projection neurons plus inhibitory (including olive-projecting) neurons. Each nucleus repeats a conserved set of two excitatory and three inhibitory classes; the fastigial nucleus has five output-specific excitatory classes. Glycine is a co-transmitter: interneurons inhibit principal neurons through glycine-receptor-rich synapses, GABA-glycinergic neurons project to the cortex and inhibit a subset of Golgi cells, and many fastigial premotor neurons are glycinergic.

entities.name: Inferior olive neurons
entities.summary: Electrically coupled neurons with subthreshold oscillations that give rise to climbing fibers. Their activity is sculpted by GABAergic feedback from the cerebellar nuclei. They express very high levels of CRF. Input from the cerebellar nuclei is asynchronous and purely GABAergic, whereas vestibular input is synchronous and mixed GABA/glycine.

entities.name: PF–Purkinje LTD
entities.summary: Depression of parallel fiber–Purkinje synapses after conjunctive PF and CF activity (high calcium). Predicted by Albus and demonstrated by Ito. It needs mGluR1/PKC signaling and AMPA-receptor endocytosis. Whether it is necessary for learning is debated. Induction also needs endocannabinoid (2-AG/CB1) and nitric-oxide signaling, and CRF from climbing fibers is permissive.

entities.name: PF–Purkinje LTP & intrinsic plasticity
entities.summary: Potentiation induced by parallel-fiber activity without a climbing-fiber signal (lower calcium), the counterpart of LTD in an inverse BCM rule. Intrinsic excitability also changes. Both are lost in Shank2 mutants. Estradiol enhances it, and a 1 Hz form depends on nitric oxide.

entities.name: Rhombic lip & ventricular zone
entities.summary: Two germinal zones: the Atoh1-positive rhombic lip makes glutamatergic neurons (granule cells, unipolar brush cells, nuclear projection neurons) and the Ptf1a-positive ventricular zone makes GABAergic neurons. In humans the rhombic lip is uniquely expanded and long-lived.

entities.name: Bergmann glia
entities.summary: Astroglia of the cerebellar cortex that respond to several modulators: locus coeruleus noradrenaline through α1-adrenergic receptors (Ca²⁺ 'flares' after noxious stimuli), Purkinje-cell dopamine through D1 receptors, ATP through P2 receptors, and CGRP. In the immature cerebellum they release D-serine, which drives LTD through GluD2. Their oxytocin-receptor expression is variable and rises after inflammatory damage. Activating Bergmann glia lowers Purkinje-cell firing, and their α1 and D1 signaling affects pain-related behavior, locomotion and social activity (mouse).

entities.name: Lugaro cell
entities.summary: Inhibitory interneuron beneath the Purkinje-cell layer; about two-thirds of genetically labeled Lugaro cells are GABA/glycinergic. Serotonin selectively excites Lugaro cells, and they receive serotonergic fibers. They innervate Golgi cells and molecular-layer interneurons but not Purkinje cells; one Lugaro cell's long transverse axon contacts more than 100 Golgi cells. Their dendrites and ascending axons stay within aldolase C (zebrin) compartments, whereas the transverse axons cross several.

entities.name: Mossy fiber → granule → parallel fiber
entities.summary: The main input stream. Mossy fibers from pontine, spinal, vestibular and reticular nuclei excite granule cells, whose parallel fibers run along the folium and contact many Purkinje cells. Mossy fibers from the vestibular nuclei are the predominant putative cholinergic input, and some mossy fibers contain enkephalin.

entities.name: Climbing fiber pathway
entities.summary: One climbing fiber from the inferior olive per Purkinje cell, producing complex spikes. Classically viewed as a motor-error teaching signal, it also carries reward, reward-prediction and learned predictive signals. Climbing fibers contain CRF, which is permissive for LTD, and transiently CGRP during development.

entities.name: Expansion recoding
entities.summary: Marr–Albus idea that the vast granule layer recodes mossy-fiber patterns into high-dimensional, separable codes for Purkinje-cell learning. The few inputs per granule cell maximize coding dimension in theory, granule-cell axon populations are high-dimensional, and Golgi inhibition decorrelates them. How sparse the code is remains debated.

entities.name: Feedforward inhibition
entities.summary: Parallel fibers excite molecular-layer interneurons that then inhibit Purkinje cells, sharpening timing and gating climbing-fiber calcium. Purkinje-cell collaterals add feedback within zones.

entities.name: Microzones & modules
entities.summary: Strips of Purkinje cells that share climbing-fiber input from one olive subregion and project to one nuclear group. This olivo-cortico-nuclear module is the putative unit of computation.

entities.name: Zebrin± modules (upbound / downbound)
entities.summary: Zebrin-negative Purkinje cells fire simple and complex spikes at higher rates than zebrin-positive cells, a difference that depends on TRPC3. Zebrin-negative modules support eyeblink conditioning, in which the learned eyelid closure relies on suppressed Purkinje firing; zebrin-positive modules are linked to VOR adaptation. De Zeeuw proposes that each microzone is bound either to increase ('upbound') or to decrease ('downbound') its activity early in learning.

entities.name: Internal (forward) models
entities.summary: Theory that cerebellar circuits learn to predict the sensory consequences of commands (forward models) or to generate commands (inverse models). The idea has been extended to thought and to social prediction.

entities.name: Reward & prediction signals
entities.summary: Climbing fibers and granule cells carry reward expectation, delivery and omission signals in specific microzones, in mice and monkeys. Granule cells can ramp toward a reward over seconds. This suggests cerebellar learning also uses reinforcement-like teaching signals.

entities.name: Distributed synergistic plasticity
entities.summary: Learning spread across many plasticity sites (PF–PC LTD and LTP, interneuron synapses, intrinsic excitability, cerebellar and vestibular nuclei) that act together. This can explain learning when one mechanism is removed.

entities.name: Crus I / vermis → thalamus → mPFC circuit
entities.summary: Right Crus I and posterior vermis connect through the cerebellar nuclei and ventromedial thalamus to medial prefrontal cortex. In mice these circuits regulate social and flexible behavior, and they are disrupted in autism models.

entities.name: Anterior lobe (I–V)
entities.summary: Primary sensorimotor cerebellum with an inverted somatotopic body map. Lesions here cause ataxia rather than cognitive deficits.

entities.name: Lobule VI
entities.summary: Transition zone: hand and face sensorimotor representation plus language, spatial and executive activations. In mice, juvenile perturbation of lobule VI alters reversal learning.

entities.name: Crus I
entities.summary: Large association territory coupled to frontoparietal and default-mode networks. Right Crus I is engaged in language and mentalizing, and its dysfunction is implicated in autism.

entities.name: Crus II
entities.summary: Association territory in a closed loop with prefrontal area 46 in monkeys. In humans it is active in mentalizing, executive and language tasks.

entities.name: Lobule VIIB
entities.summary: Linked with executive and working-memory activations and frontoparietal control networks.

entities.name: Lobule VIII
entities.summary: Second, upright sensorimotor map; also attention networks. Right lobule VIII lesions are associated with spatial deficits.

entities.name: Lobule IX
entities.summary: Hemispheric IX joins the third nonmotor (default-mode) representation; vermal IX (uvula) contributes to oculomotor and vestibular control.

entities.name: Lobule X & flocculus
entities.summary: Vestibulo-cerebellum for gaze and balance, with direct projections to the vestibular nuclei. The flocculus is the classic site of VOR-adaptation studies.

entities.name: Posterior vermis (VI–IX)
entities.summary: Midline posterior lobe: oculomotor control (VI–VII) and affective and autonomic functions. Vermis injury is associated with affective symptoms and with worse outcomes after preterm cerebellar injury.

entities.name: Vermis (midline zone)
entities.summary: Midline cortex projecting to the fastigial nucleus: axial posture, gait and eye movements, plus autonomic and affective functions.

entities.name: Paravermis (intermediate zone)
entities.summary: Intermediate cortex projecting to the interposed nuclei: limb control and associative motor learning such as eyeblink conditioning.

entities.name: Lateral hemispheres
entities.summary: Lateral cortex projecting to the dentate nucleus. It supports movement planning and sequencing and, through loops with association cortex, cognitive, language and social functions. Expanded in apes and especially humans.

entities.name: Fastigial nucleus
entities.summary: Medial nucleus and output of the vermis. Five glutamatergic classes target posturomotor, oromotor, autonomic, orienting and vigilance circuits. Outputs to thalamus and PAG support motor planning and fear memory. Many of its premotor neurons are glycinergic and project ipsilaterally, and it receives the densest orexin fibers among the cerebellar nuclei (rat).

entities.name: Interposed nucleus
entities.summary: Output of the paravermis to the red nucleus and thalamus. Essential for conditioned eyeblink responses. Histamine acting on its H2 receptors improves balance and coordination, and orexins (OX2), CRF from olivary neurons and muscarinic agonists excite its neurons (rat).

entities.name: Dentate (lateral) nucleus
entities.summary: Output of the lateral hemispheres. It projects via thalamus to motor and prefrontal cortex (area 46) and to striatum. Greatly expanded in humans, where a frontal-projecting excitatory class predominates.

entities.name: Cerebellar cortex
entities.summary: A tightly folded sheet with ~78% of the neocortex's surface area in humans. Across 19 mammalian species including humans, the cerebellum has on average 3.6 neurons for every neuron in the cerebral cortex, and only 19% of the human brain's ~86 billion neurons are in the cerebral cortex. The same three-layer microcircuit repeats across functionally distinct modules.

entities.name: Deep cerebellar nuclei
entities.summary: The main output of the cerebellum (fastigial, interposed, dentate). Targets include thalamus, brainstem motor nuclei, VTA, PAG and inferior olive. The nuclei evolved by duplicating a conserved cell-type set.

entities.name: Vestibular nuclei
entities.summary: Brainstem nuclei that receive direct Purkinje input from the vestibulo-cerebellum. They drive the VOR and are a site of motor memory. Their mossy fibers to the nodulus and ventral uvula are the predominant putative cholinergic input to the cerebellum.

entities.name: Pontine nuclei
entities.summary: Relay from much of the neocortex to the cerebellar cortex as mossy fibers, mostly to the opposite side. Also relays subthalamic input to the cerebellum. Pontine neurons that receive a rostral anterior cingulate input mediating placebo analgesia are rich in opioid receptors (mouse). Extrastriate areas concerned mainly with spatial vision, visual motion and the peripheral visual field project to the pontine nuclei, but ventral V4, area TEO and the inferior temporal gyrus do not, and primary visual cortex sends only a few corticopontine cells, from its representation of the lower peripheral field (monkey).

entities.name: Inferior olive
entities.summary: Sole source of climbing fibers, which cross to the opposite cerebellum. Inhibitory feedback from the cerebellar nuclei closes the olivo-cortico-nuclear loop.

entities.name: Thalamus
entities.summary: Relays cerebellar output to cortex: motor thalamus to motor and prefrontal areas, ventromedial thalamus to mPFC, intralaminar nuclei to striatum, and parafascicular nucleus in anxiety. Motor thalamus (VA/VL) innervates layers 2/3–5B of mouse M1, and inactivating the thalamus disrupts dexterous reaching at any stage. In rats, motor-thalamic neurons of a zone dominated by inhibitory afferents send many axon varicosities to cortical layer I and also reach the striatum, whereas those of a zone dominated by excitatory afferents target the middle layers. In mice, thalamic neurons show selective persistent activity that predicts movement direction during planning, and photoinhibiting the thalamus collapses ALM activity; the thalamus also relays a Go-cue signal from the midbrain that switches motor cortex from planning to a motor command. The mediodorsal nucleus connects with prefrontal cortex in a nucleus-to-field pattern (monkey), and its neurons change their firing during the delay of a delayed-response test (monkey). In mice, its input sustains medial prefrontal delay activity during working memory and amplifies prefrontal connectivity to maintain rule representations, while the prefrontal projection back to it supports the subsequent choice. It is part of the basal ganglia–thalamocortical 'motor' circuit (primate models); in a proposed center–surround model, a 'hyperdirect' signal first inhibits large areas of the thalamus and cortex before the direct pathway disinhibits the targets of the selected motor program. Its taste area, the parvicellular ventral posteromedial nucleus, projects to insular-opercular cortex (review).

entities.name: Motor & premotor cortex
entities.summary: Frontal motor areas: primary motor cortex (M1) and the premotor areas, all of which send corticospinal axons to the spinal cord (monkey). Forms closed loops with the cerebellum (cortico-pontine input; nuclear output via thalamus). In mice, a frontal–fastigial loop maintains motor-planning activity, and dentate activity is needed for it.

entities.name: Prefrontal cortex
entities.summary: Frontal association cortex. Here it covers the dorsolateral and orbitofrontal cortex and anterior cingulate of primates and the medial prefrontal areas of rodents, whose names and borders differ between rodent atlases. Theory proposes that cognitive control stems from actively maintained prefrontal activity patterns that represent goals and the means to achieve them, biasing processing in other brain structures. A review argues that even mild acute uncontrollable stress can rapidly impair prefrontal cognitive abilities, and that prolonged stress changes prefrontal dendrites. Cerebellar output reaches it through the thalamus: transneuronal tracing from area 46 labels neurons in restricted parts of the dentate nucleus, separate from those that project to motor areas (monkey), and in mice cerebellar-recipient neurons are denser in associative areas, including orbital, anterior cingulate, prelimbic and infralimbic cortex, than in sensorimotor cortex, which holds the most. In turn, dorsolateral and, less so, medial prefrontal cortex project to the basilar pons, whereas orbitofrontal cortex does not (monkey). Functional connectivity separates dorsolateral, medial and anterior prefrontal circuits with the opposite cerebellar hemisphere, and in schizophrenia weaker cerebellum–right DLPFC connectivity goes with more severe negative symptoms (human).

entities.name: Posterior parietal cortex
entities.summary: Association cortex in loops with the cerebellum. Connectivity between right Crus I and inferior parietal lobule is altered in autism. During top-down attention, prefrontal neurons signal the target location before parietal neurons, and during bottom-up attention parietal neurons signal it first (monkey). The dorsal visual stream from striate to posterior parietal cortex is proposed to mediate the sensorimotor transformations for visually guided action (review), and a spatial location task activates lateral superior parietal cortex (human).

entities.name: Striatum
entities.summary: The major component of the basal ganglia. Its two output systems, striatonigral and striatopallidal neurons, express D1 and D2 dopamine receptors respectively (rat). Dopaminergic input to the dorsal striatum is indispensable for the emergence of striatal activity that mediates adaptive changes in movement vigor (mouse), and lesions of the dorsolateral striatum disrupt habit formation (rat). Receives disynaptic cerebellar input via intralaminar thalamus. This short-latency path can shape corticostriatal plasticity and, when aberrant, causes dystonia. Cerebellar nuclei also raise striatal dopamine during satiation. Receives corticostriatal input from neurons in lower layer 5A of mouse motor cortex. In mice performing a flexible lick-timing task, it ramps with frontal cortex before licks, and briefly inhibiting it rewinds this timer.

entities.name: Subthalamic nucleus
entities.summary: Basal ganglia nucleus that receives the 'hyperdirect' excitation of motor-related cortical areas, bypassing the striatum, and relays it to the globus pallidus; it is also a station of the 'indirect' pathway from the external to the internal pallidum. It projects disynaptically, via the pontine nuclei, to the cerebellar cortex. Excessive activity in it is implicated in Parkinson's disease: lesioning it reduced akinesia, rigidity and tremor in MPTP-treated monkeys, and stimulating it improves motor symptoms in patients.

entities.name: VTA (dopamine)
entities.summary: Receives monosynaptic excitatory input from the cerebellar nuclei. Activating this input is rewarding, and it is required for social preference in mice. In rats, its dopaminergic neurons project to the cerebellar cortex and its non-dopaminergic neurons to the lateral and interpositus nuclei; its dopaminergic neurons also project to primary motor cortex, where they are needed for learning, but not performing, a reaching skill. Optogenetically released dopamine from its projections in medial PFC is neither rewarding nor aversive, but pairing that release with a sound speeds later learning to discriminate the sound (mouse).

entities.name: Periaqueductal gray
entities.summary: Ventrolateral PAG receives fastigial input that bidirectionally controls fear-memory strength and modulates extinction. An inhibitory pathway from the central amygdala to the ventrolateral PAG produces freezing by disinhibiting excitatory outputs to premotor targets in the medulla (mouse), and lesions of the caudal midbrain central gray disrupt conditioned freezing but not the conditioned arterial pressure response (rat).

entities.name: Hippocampus
entities.summary: Essential, with the adjacent entorhinal, perirhinal and parahippocampal cortices, for establishing long-term memory for facts and events, a role that is temporary as memory gradually becomes independent of it (review). Loss of recent memory follows bilateral hippocampal lesions, and a lesion limited to field CA1 caused enduring anterograde amnesia (human). It also maps space: unit activity in freely moving rats gave preliminary evidence that it acts as a spatial map, cells that respond at specific locations are found mainly in the human hippocampus, and hippocampal lesions impair place navigation (rat). In the classic trisynaptic pathway, information proceeds from the entorhinal cortex to the dentate gyrus, to CA3 and then to CA1, the main hippocampal output. Receives multisynaptic input from restricted cerebellar regions and synchronizes with them at 6–12 Hz. Cerebellar plasticity shapes place cells that rely on self-motion cues. In monkeys, most hippocampal-formation neurons that project to prefrontal cortex target medial areas, then orbital areas, and few reach lateral areas. In rats, correlated firing and theta (4–12 Hz) coupling between CA1 and medial PFC strengthen during spatial working memory; and in mice, direct hippocampal-prefrontal input is needed to encode spatial cues.

entities.name: Amygdala
entities.summary: Long associated with emotion and motivation, it processes both fearful and rewarding stimuli (review). Work on fear conditioning pinpoints it as an important component of the system for acquiring, storing and expressing fear memory, and the findings from experimental animals apply to the human brain (review). A patient with focal bilateral amygdala lesions showed no fear when exposed to snakes, spiders or a haunted house, although she exhibited other basic emotions (human). Its neurons encode the positive and negative value of images rapidly enough to account for learning (monkey), and excitotoxic lesions impair choices after a food is devalued but not reversal learning (monkey). Single neurons in the right amygdala of neurosurgical patients show a categorical selectivity for pictures of animals that appears independent of emotional valence or arousal (human). Its connections with prefrontal cortex are densest in posterior orbitofrontal and posterior medial areas (monkey). In mice, basolateral amygdala firing becomes entrained to medial prefrontal theta input when animals recognize safety. Amygdala damage abolishes the larger response of fusiform and occipital cortex to fearful than to neutral faces, although the visual areas are intact (human).

entities.name: Red nucleus & brainstem motor nuclei
entities.summary: Targets of interposed and fastigial outputs (rubrospinal, reticulospinal and vestibulospinal systems) for limb and axial control. Also receives pyramidal-tract axons from motor cortex: in mice, one type projects to medullary motor centres and carries late preparatory activity and motor commands.

entities.name: Spinal cord
entities.summary: Spinocerebellar pathways carry limb and trunk proprioception as mossy fibers; descending brainstem pathways carry cerebellar influence to motor neurons. Receives corticospinal axons from M1 and six premotor areas (monkey); in mice, motor-cortex corticospinal axons contact spinal premotor interneurons directly.

entities.name: Body (muscles & proprioceptors)
entities.summary: Movement and proprioceptive feedback. Body maps appear twice in the cerebellum (anterior lobe and lobule VIII).

entities.name: Vestibular labyrinth
entities.summary: Head-motion signals reach the vestibular nuclei and, as primary vestibular mossy fibers, the flocculonodular lobe directly.

entities.name: Eyes & visual input
entities.summary: Image motion on the retina (retinal slip) reaches the flocculus through the inferior olive as an error signal; the oculomotor vermis controls saccades.

entities.name: Gut nutrient signals
entities.summary: Nutrients infused into the gut activate anterior deep cerebellar nuclei neurons in mice. The afferent route is not yet known.

entities.name: Closed cerebro-cerebellar loops
entities.summary: Cortical areas that send input to a cerebellar region receive output from the same region. Parallel motor, prefrontal and parietal loops are the anatomical basis for nonmotor functions.

entities.name: Cerebellum–basal ganglia network
entities.summary: Disynaptic links in both directions (dentate → thalamus → striatum; subthalamic nucleus → pons → cerebellar cortex) make the two subcortical systems one network.

entities.name: Developmental sensitive periods
entities.summary: The cerebellum may instruct maturation of remote cortical circuits during sensitive periods ('developmental diaschisis'). Early disruption could then produce lasting nonmotor deficits such as autism.

entities.name: Evolutionary expansion
entities.summary: The cerebellum expanded faster than predicted in apes, and its neuron numbers scale with the neocortex's across mammals. Human Crus I/II and the frontal-projecting dentate class are enlarged, and the human cerebellar surface is ~78% of the neocortex's. Human-specific changes appear in Purkinje subtypes, granule-cell synapse genes (ZP2) and progenitor gene regulation.

entities.name: Substantia nigra pars compacta
entities.summary: Dopamine neurons that project to the dorsal striatum. Cerebellar nuclei excite them monosynaptically, raising striatal dopamine; the input is active before movement and for reward. Their loss in Parkinson's disease causes deficits in movement initiation and slowness of movement. In mice, a large proportion of them transiently increase their activity before self-paced movement, and inhibiting or briefly activating them while the animal is immobile lowers or raises the probability and vigour of its future movements; midbrain dopaminergic axons in the striatum that carry rapid locomotion signals are largely distinct from those that respond to unexpected rewards. Stimulating the substantia nigra potentiates corticostriatal synapses through dopamine receptors (rat). In monkeys, the dorsolateral striatum receives input from a broad expanse of midbrain dopamine cells, which also relay an ascending spiral from the ventromedial striatum.

entities.name: Locus coeruleus
entities.summary: Noradrenaline nucleus that integrates input from, and broadcasts to, many brain regions; its inputs include cerebellar Purkinje cells (mouse). Its fibers reach the cerebellar cortex, where activating the pathway inhibits Purkinje cells (rat) and noxious stimuli release noradrenaline onto Bergmann glia (mouse). Its neurons projecting to prefrontal cortex differ from those projecting to motor cortex and release more noradrenaline there (rat). Phasic activation of it reshapes taste coding in the gustatory cortex along a palatability axis (mouse), but its activity is not driven by taste novelty: it is suppressed while mice lick and rises briefly when licking stops (mouse).

entities.name: Brainstem serotonin neurons
entities.summary: Source of the cerebellum's serotonergic fibers, which reach all cortical layers and form a plexus around Purkinje-cell somata. Several raphe and reticular nuclei project to the cerebellum, but in rats double labeling placed the serotonergic neurons almost exclusively in the gigantocellular, paragigantocellular and pontine (oralis) reticular nuclei; most are not in the raphe nuclei.

entities.name: Tuberomammillary nucleus
entities.summary: Hypothalamic source of the cerebellum's histaminergic afferents, a third type of cerebellar afferent besides mossy and climbing fibers. Its fine varicose fibers reach the cerebellar cortex and nuclei, part of direct, bidirectional hypothalamo-cerebellar connections.

entities.name: Lateral hypothalamus (orexin)
entities.summary: Orexin (hypocretin) neurons in the perifornical and lateral hypothalamus send fibers to the vestibular and cerebellar nuclei (densest in the fastigial nucleus) and a few to paraflocculus cortex (rat). Orexinergic input excites interpositus neurons (rat) and floccular Purkinje cells (rabbit), and its input to the dentate adds to exercise-induced anxiety relief (mouse). Ventral CA1 neurons projecting to the lateral hypothalamic area are enriched in anxiety cells, and activating their terminals there increases anxiety and avoidance (mouse). Lesions of the lateral hypothalamic area, a target of the central amygdala, interfere with the conditioned arterial pressure response but not conditioned freezing (rat).

entities.name: Pedunculopontine nucleus (ACh)
entities.summary: Brainstem cholinergic nucleus. With the lateral paragigantocellular nucleus (and, to a lesser extent, raphe nuclei), it sends beaded cholinergic fibers to the cerebellar cortex and nuclei; in the nuclei they form a moderately dense network (rat). In mice, its ascending glutamatergic neurons, with those of the midbrain reticular nucleus, respond to an auditory Go cue; the signal reaches motor cortex via the thalamus.

entities.name: Midbrain reticular nucleus (MRN)
entities.summary: In mice, ascending glutamatergic neurons of the midbrain reticular and pedunculopontine nuclei respond to an auditory Go cue with short-latency, phasic, cue-selective changes in firing. The signal reaches motor cortex via the thalamus and switches it from planning-related activity to a motor command that drives the movement.

entities.name: Motor coordination
entities.summary: Coordination, posture, balance and eye movements. Body maps lie in the anterior lobe and lobule VIII. In flies, descending neurons link sensory neuropils of the brain with motor neuropils of the nerve cord (fly), and MDN descending neurons trigger backward walking (fly).

entities.name: Motor learning & adaptation
entities.summary: VOR adaptation, eyeblink conditioning, prism adaptation and locomotor learning: the classic cerebellum-dependent forms of learning.

entities.name: Timing & prediction
entities.summary: Sub-second timing of movement and perception, and predictive signals about upcoming events. In mice performing a flexible lick-timing task, frontal cortex and striatum ramp before licks: silencing frontal cortex pauses this timer and inhibiting striatum rewinds it, consistent with the striatum integrating frontal-cortex input. Learning a motor timing task needs CaMKII-dependent plasticity in two pyramidal-tract subtypes of mouse premotor cortex.

entities.name: Executive function
entities.summary: Planning, set-shifting, working memory and response inhibition; impaired after posterior cerebellar lesions. Theory proposes that cognitive control stems from actively maintained prefrontal representations of goals; in the Stroop task, anterior cingulate conflict-related activity predicts greater prefrontal activity and behavioral adjustments (human). In rats performing a Stop task, arkypallidal neurons of the globus pallidus respond early and selectively to Stop cues, supporting a model in which their projections to striatum cancel actions in preparation.

entities.name: Language
entities.summary: Verbal fluency, grammar, reading and verbal working memory, lateralized to the right cerebellum (crossed connections with left-hemisphere language cortex).

entities.name: Social cognition
entities.summary: Mentalizing and social preference. Human imaging points to Crus I/II; mouse circuit studies implicate Crus I, vermis, VTA and mPFC pathways. In mice, the strength of excitatory input onto layer V pyramidal neurons of medial PFC tracks dominance rank, and raising or lowering synaptic efficacy in dorsal mPFC moves animals up or down the hierarchy. Patients with bilateral ventromedial prefrontal damage make abnormally utilitarian judgments on emotionally aversive moral dilemmas. A patient with selective bilateral amygdala damage was impaired at recognizing fear in facial expressions (human). In patient SM, impaired recognition of fear stems from not making normal use of the eye region of faces, which the authors trace to a lack of spontaneous fixations on the eyes, and her recognition of fearful faces became normal when she was told to look at the eyes (human). In the medial amygdala, a GABAergic subpopulation promotes aggression and two other social behaviors, whereas neighboring glutamatergic neurons promote repetitive self-grooming and inhibit social interactions (mouse). Empathy for pain engages a core network of anterior insula and medial/anterior cingulate cortex that overlaps with responses to one's own pain (human). In male mice, loss of vomeronasal signalling abolishes male-male aggression and leads to courtship of both sexes (mouse). In the predominantly asocial octopus, MDMA enhances prosocial behaviour and the serotonin transporter keeps its MDMA binding site (octopus), and untrained octopuses learn a visual discrimination by watching trained ones (octopus). In flies, male courtship is specified by male-specific splicing of the fruitless gene (fly), and a single class of olfactory neurons mediates behavioural responses to the sex pheromone cVA (fly).

entities.name: Emotion & fear
entities.summary: Emotion perception and regulation, fear learning and extinction, and anxiety. A patient with selective bilateral amygdala damage was impaired at recognizing fear in facial expressions (human), and the amygdala responds more to fearful than to happy faces, even when the faces are masked so that most viewers report seeing only neutral ones (human). A patient with focal bilateral amygdala lesions showed no fear in frightening situations and an impoverished experience of fear in daily life, although she exhibited other basic emotions (human). Feeling disgust and seeing it on others' faces activate the same anterior insula sites (human), and a patient with insula and putamen damage showed impaired recognition of disgust (human).

entities.name: Reward & motivation
entities.summary: Reward expectation and reinforcement. The cerebellum both carries reward signals and drives dopamine circuits. The output of dopamine neurons apparently signals reward prediction errors (primate), and activating them at reward delivery is sufficient for long-lasting increases in cue-elicited reward seeking (rat). The amygdala processes positive as well as negative emotions, and its role in stimulus–reward learning might be as important as its role in fear conditioning (review); excitotoxic amygdala lesions impair choices after a food is devalued (monkey), and mice work to earn optical stimulation of basolateral amygdala inputs to the nucleus accumbens. In flies, dopamine neurons of the PAM cluster signal sugar reward to the mushroom body (fly), and octopamine reinforces short-term appetitive memory through dopamine neurons (fly).

entities.name: Feeding & drinking
entities.summary: Meal termination and thirst. Anterior deep-nuclei neurons reduce meal size through striatal dopamine, and Purkinje cells activated by the hormone asprosin increase water intake. PKC-δ+ neurons of the lateral central amygdala are activated by diverse anorexigenic signals, are required for those signals to inhibit feeding, and suppress food intake when activated (mouse). Mouse insular neurons respond preferentially to food cues only when the animal is hungry, a bias that hypothalamic AgRP neurons restore through the paraventricular thalamus and basolateral amygdala (mouse). Orbitofrontal responses to the odour of a food decline after that food is eaten to satiety (human). In flies, a single pair of brain neurons commands the entire feeding motor program and responds to food only when the fly is starved (fly).

entities.name: Spatial navigation
entities.summary: Path integration and spatial memory, through interactions with the hippocampus. Hippocampal place cells fire at particular locations, preliminary evidence that the hippocampus acts as a spatial map, and medial entorhinal grid cells form a neural map of the spatial environment (rat; cells with similar firing are found in humans); hippocampal lesions impair place navigation (rat), and deleting NMDA receptors from CA1 pyramidal cells impairs spatial memory (mouse). In flies, neurons tiling the ellipsoid body represent heading by combining visual landmarks with self-motion (fly), a heading representation in the central brain behaves as a ring attractor (fly), and ellipsoid body neurons are needed for visual place learning (fly).

entities.name: Pain & nociception
entities.summary: Pain is among the emotional functions the cerebellum contributes to. In mice, noxious stimuli release locus coeruleus noradrenaline onto Bergmann glia, and this α1-adrenergic glial signaling promotes nocifensive behavior and neuropathic pain. A rostral anterior cingulate → pontine pathway mediates placebo analgesia, and Purkinje cells show similar activity during expectation of pain relief (mouse). Stimulating the upper posterior insula evokes painful sensations (human), and the anterior insula and rostral anterior cingulate respond to a loved one's pain as well as one's own (human). Octopuses avoid a place where they experienced pain and prefer one where it was relieved, suggesting that an invertebrate experiences the affective component of pain (octopus).

entities.name: Cerebellar motor syndrome
entities.summary: Ataxia of gait and limbs, dysmetria and dysarthria, mainly after anterior-lobe (III–VI) damage.

entities.name: Cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome
entities.summary: Executive, linguistic, visuospatial and affective impairments after posterior-lobe and vermis damage, screened with the CCAS scale.

entities.name: Autism spectrum disorder
entities.summary: Perinatal cerebellar injury raises autism risk, and Purkinje-specific loss of ASD genes (Tsc1, Shank2) causes autism-like behavior in mice. Eyeblink conditioning is altered across autism mouse models. Crus I–prefrontal/parietal circuits are implicated.

entities.name: Schizophrenia
entities.summary: Framed as 'cognitive dysmetria'. Cerebellar grey matter is smaller in patients, already in the youngest. Cerebellum–DLPFC connectivity tracks negative symptoms, and TMS that restores it reduces them. In the prefrontal cortex, dorsolateral blood flow fails to rise during the Wisconsin Card Sort, deep layer 3 pyramidal neurons of area 46 have a lower dendritic spine density, and a review concludes that parvalbumin interneurons make less GABA, which contributes to a diminished capacity for the gamma synchrony that working memory requires. The Val allele of a common COMT polymorphism is transmitted more often to offspring with schizophrenia and goes with worse prefrontal cognition; the authors suggest it slightly raises risk by increasing prefrontal dopamine catabolism (human).

entities.name: Spinocerebellar ataxias
entities.summary: Inherited ataxias, many caused by CAG/polyglutamine expansions (SCA1: ATXN1; SCA6: CACNA1A) that affect Purkinje cells.

entities.name: Fragile X syndrome
entities.summary: FMR1 loss. Patients and Purkinje-specific knockout mice show impaired eyeblink conditioning.

entities.name: Dystonia
entities.summary: In mice, aberrant cerebellar output causes dystonia: torsinA knockdown in the adult cerebellum (not the basal ganglia) and activation of glutamatergic nuclear neurons both suffice, and the signal can reach the striatum. In humans the cerebellum contributes, but whether it is the primary site is unresolved.

entities.name: Preterm cerebellar injury
entities.summary: Cerebellar hemorrhage in preterm infants is followed by high rates of motor, language, cognitive and autism-screen problems. Even without injury, prematurity displaces cerebellar maturation, with incomplete granule-cell maturation and Purkinje refinement.

entities.name: Hyperphagia (Prader–Willi syndrome)
entities.summary: Insatiable appetite; altered cerebellar food responses in patients led to the discovery of a cerebellar satiation circuit.

entities.name: Dandy–Walker malformation
entities.summary: Malformation with posterior vermis hypoplasia, associated with disrupted development of the human rhombic lip. Exome sequencing finds a genetic cause in a minority of families and implicates vascular development.

entities.name: Medulloblastoma
entities.summary: The most common malignant childhood brain tumor. The SHH group arises in the granule-cell lineage of the upper rhombic lip when Sonic hedgehog signaling is activated. Groups 3 and 4 carry signatures of human rhombic-lip lineages (photoreceptor and unipolar-brush-cell programs), and Group 4 tumors resemble rhombic-lip progenitors stalled in development.

entities.name: Essential tremor
entities.summary: The most common tremor disorder. Postmortem cerebellum shows Purkinje-cell degeneration and climbing-fiber rewiring. In mice, surplus climbing-fiber synapses left by a pruning deficit drive tremor-generating cerebellar oscillations.

entities.name: General psychopathology (p factor)
entities.summary: A liability shared across common mental disorders. Higher p-factor scores go with lower pontine white-matter integrity and a smaller left lobule VIIb.

entities.name: Cognitive aging & Alzheimer's disease
entities.summary: Cerebellar regions age at different rates. Larger cerebellar volume predicts better cognition in later life and, in Alzheimer's disease, while amyloid burden is low, suggesting a reserve role.

entities.name: Episodic ataxia type 2
entities.summary: Physical or emotional stress triggers episodes of severe motor dysfunction that manifest as ataxia and dystonia. Caused by CACNA1A mutations, such as ones that disrupt the reading frame, and allelic with familial hemiplegic migraine. In tottering mice, a model of EA2, stress-released noradrenaline acts on Purkinje-cell α1-adrenergic receptors and, through casein kinase 2, disrupts pacemaking and triggers attacks; blocking the cascade prevents them.

entities.name: Primary motor cortex (M1)
entities.summary: Sends corticospinal output and holds effector-specific foot, hand and mouth zones; in humans these alternate with inter-effector regions of the somato-cognitive action network (SCAN). The human hand area lies in a knob-shaped segment of the precentral gyrus. In monkeys, the populations of neurons active for different fingers overlap extensively, and M1 has a rostral 'old' part without cortico-motoneuronal cells and a caudal 'new' part with them. Its cell types are broadly conserved across mouse, marmoset and human.

entities.name: Premotor areas
entities.summary: Six premotor areas of the monkey frontal lobe, in area 6 on the lateral and medial surfaces and in the cingulate sulcus (areas 23 and 24), project to the arm area of M1 and directly to the spinal cord; together, their arm representations hold as many corticospinal neurons as M1's arm area, or more. Some supplementary motor area cells fire only for a sequence of movements in a particular order, which M1 cells do not. Output-null patterns of preparatory activity in dorsal premotor cortex largely account for its attenuation in M1 (monkey). Rodent secondary motor cortex (M2) is grouped here, as its input reaches pyramidal-tract neurons of mouse M1 directly; mouse anterior lateral motor cortex (ALM), a possible homologue of primate premotor cortex, has its own entry.

entities.name: Anterior lateral motor cortex (ALM)
entities.summary: An anterior lateral region of mouse motor cortex, possibly homologous to primate premotor cortex. Unilateral inactivation during movement planning disrupts contralateral movements, and in a whisker-based decision task, inhibiting it during the memory period biases licking to the same side. Neurons predicting ipsi- and contralateral movements are intermingled in equal proportions; a contralateral population bias appears only in brainstem-projecting layer 5 neurons, late in planning. Its preparatory activity depends on activity of the dentate nucleus, and preparatory activity in frontal cortex depends on a loop through the fastigial nucleus and thalamus. Its preparatory activity is similar in auditory and tactile tasks: most neurons are direction-selective, and delay activity is monotonic and low-dimensional. During the delay it moves toward discrete end points for each movement direction that resist transient perturbations, evidence of discrete attractor dynamics. It forms a loop with the thalamus: photoinhibiting the thalamus collapses ALM activity, and photoinhibiting ALM diminishes thalamic activity. In brain-wide recordings, choice coding is concentrated in ALM and the subcortical areas receiving its input, in an ALM-dependent manner.

entities.name: Motor maps (somatotopy)
entities.summary: Ordered representations of stimulation-evoked movements, long central to ideas about motor cortex. They change with use: training expands the representations of the movements practised and shrinks others (monkey), and practice enlarges the M1 area activated by a finger sequence (human). Long stimulation trains evoke whole postures, arranged as a map of hand positions around the body across primary motor and premotor cortex (monkey). Finger territories are not segregated: neurons for different fingers overlap throughout the hand area (monkey).

entities.name: Somato-cognitive action network (SCAN)
entities.summary: Inter-effector regions that interrupt the classic homunculus of human M1, alternating with foot, hand and mouth areas. They have thinner cortex and strong functional connectivity with each other and with the cingulo-opercular network, lack movement specificity, and co-activate during action planning and axial body movements; macaque and infant data suggest homologues and developmental precursors. Proposed to integrate goals, physiology and body movement.

entities.name: Pyramidal-tract neurons (L5B)
entities.summary: Output neurons of layer 5B that project to the brainstem and spinal cord. In mouse motor cortex two types reach basal ganglia and brainstem targets: one also projects to thalamus that feeds back to motor cortex and carries early preparatory activity, the other projects to the medulla and carries late preparatory activity and motor commands. Mouse corticospinal neurons form topographically ordered ensembles for reaching or grasping and contact spinal premotor interneurons.
