In the cat, geniculate neurons connect to simple cells according to their on or off signature, which implies that simple receptive fields and their orientation selectivity are laid down at the first thalamocortical synapse, and the orientation tuning of geniculate input survives inactivation of the cortex. Cells sharing an orientation preference are grouped in columns (monkey), and the centres of orientation pinwheels are highly ordered at single-cell resolution (cat). Mouse V1 neurons are nearly as orientation selective as those of other species (mouse); activating PV+ interneurons sharpens their tuning and improves orientation discrimination (mouse), and layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons sharing an orientation preference connect at twice the rate of those with orthogonal preferences (mouse).

entities.name: V1 layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons
entities.summary: They connect at twice the rate when they share an orientation preference as when their preferences are orthogonal, and at much higher rates when their responses to natural stimuli are similar, pointing to fine-scale subnetworks (mouse). During locomotion in a virtual environment they are strongly driven by running and by mismatch between actual and expected visual flow, suggesting predictive coding (mouse). Somatostatin interneurons contribute to their surround suppression (mouse).

entities.name: V1 PV+ interneurons
entities.summary: Parvalbumin-positive interneurons. Optogenetically activating them sharpens the orientation tuning and direction selectivity of nearby neurons and improves orientation discrimination, whereas activating somatostatin or VIP interneurons does not (mouse).

entities.name: V1 SOM+ interneurons
entities.summary: Somatostatin-expressing interneurons of the superficial layers. Unlike pyramidal cells, they respond more as a stimulus extends into the receptive-field surround, because horizontal cortical axons preferentially excite them, and they contribute to the surround suppression of pyramidal cells (mouse).

entities.name: V1 VIP+ interneurons
entities.summary: Locomotion activates them independently of visual stimulation, largely through nicotinic input from the basal forebrain; activating them increases V1 visual responses in stationary mice, and damaging them abolishes the enhancement of V1 responses by locomotion (mouse).

entities.name: Ocular dominance plasticity
entities.summary: Experience-dependent plasticity of binocular responses in V1. In mice, 4 days of monocular deprivation at postnatal day 28 maximally reduce responses to the deprived eye, during a critical period between P19 and P32, through a competitive, correlation-based plasticity of geniculocortical and intracortical connections (mouse). Disrupting one isoform of glutamic acid decarboxylase prevents it and benzodiazepines restore it (mouse), and studies of mice lacking GAD65 suggest that a threshold level of inhibition may trigger the critical period, once in life (mouse). Degrading the chondroitin sulphate proteoglycans of perineuronal nets lets monocular deprivation shift ocular dominance in adult rats (rat). Early experimental strabismus or anisometropia often causes amblyopia, with reduced cortical binocularity (monkey).

entities.name: GAD65
entities.summary: An isoform of glutamic acid decarboxylase, the GABA-synthesizing enzyme. In mice lacking it, benzodiazepines unmask plasticity to monocular deprivation at any age, and enhancing GABA transmission early in life makes them insensitive to deprivation as adults (mouse).

entities.name: Perineuronal nets
entities.summary: Extracellular-matrix structures formed by chondroitin sulphate proteoglycans. In rat visual cortex they form as the critical period ends, later after dark rearing, and degrading the proteoglycans with chondroitinase-ABC reactivates ocular dominance plasticity in adults (rat).

entities.name: Amblyopia
entities.summary: A developmental disorder of pattern vision. Macaques often develop it after early experimental strabismus or anisometropia; cortical binocularity is reduced, and in severe cases neurons driven by the amblyopic eye have lower spatial resolution, although these changes do not explain all of the visual deficit (monkey).

entities.name: Cortical blindness and blindsight
entities.summary: Blindness in part of the visual field after damage to visual cortex. Some visual capacity remains in the hemianopic field after a restricted occipital ablation (human), and some patients with extensive damage to primary visual cortex can point or make saccades toward stimuli in the blind field (human). Koniocellular geniculate neurons that innervate extrastriate cortex are likely to sustain some visual behaviours without V1 (review).

entities.name: Early blindness
entities.summary: In people blind from early life, tactile discrimination such as Braille reading activates primary and secondary visual cortex, which it deactivates in sighted people (human), and disrupting occipital cortex with magnetic stimulation causes errors in reading Braille and distorts tactile perception (human).

entities.name: Migraine with aura
entities.summary: During visual aura in three people, fMRI showed changes with the characteristics of cortical spreading depression, starting in extrastriate area V3A and spreading slowly over occipital cortex in register with the retinotopy of the percept (human).

entities.name: Posterior cortical atrophy
entities.summary: In five patients, a progressive dementia was heralded by disorders of higher visual function, followed by alexia, agraphia, visual agnosia and components of Balint's and Gerstmann's syndromes, with memory relatively spared until late; imaging showed predominant parieto-occipital atrophy in two of five patients (human).

entities.name: Akinetopsia (motion blindness)
entities.summary: A patient with bilateral posterior brain damage, attributed to the lateral temporo-occipital cortex, showed a disturbance of movement vision with no impression of movement in depth and impaired visually guided eye and finger movements, while movement perception through hearing and touch was intact (human).

entities.name: Visual perception
entities.summary: Seeing form, colour, motion and depth. These attributes are thought to be analysed in parallel subdivisions of the visual system (review), and colour and motion activate different prestriate areas, V4 and V5 (human). Fly motion vision splits photoreceptor signals into ON and OFF channels in the lamina (fly) and computes motion along the four cardinal directions separately in each, in T4 and T5 cells (fly).

entities.name: Face perception
entities.summary: In humans and macaques, fMRI shows cortical regions that respond more to faces than to objects; in macaques almost all visually responsive neurons in the largest such region are strongly face selective (monkey), and inferotemporal cortex holds a population of face-selective neurons whose responses depend on the configuration of facial features (monkey). In humans a region of the fusiform gyrus is selectively involved in face perception (human).

entities.name: Frontal eye field
entities.summary: A frontal area where stimulation can evoke saccades. Brief stimulation of an FEF site, below the current that evokes saccades, enhances the visual responses of V4 neurons at the corresponding location and can suppress those at non-corresponding locations (monkey).

entities.name: Insular cortex
entities.summary: Cortex hidden in the depth of the hemisphere by the frontal and temporal opercula (human). In the rhesus monkey it has agranular, dysgranular and granular sectors and forms with lateral orbital and temporopolar cortex a paralimbic belt, and the human insula has a virtually identical plan (monkey). It receives input from prefrontal, orbital, opercular, cingulate, olfactory, temporopolar, superior temporal, rhinal and posterior parietal cortex and projects back to the areas that project to it; through its connections with the amygdala it gives somatosensory, auditory, gustatory, olfactory and visceral sensations a route to the limbic system (monkey). Imaging meta-analysis divides the human insula into sensorimotor (mid-posterior), social-emotional (anterior-ventral), olfacto-gustatory (central) and cognitive (anterior-dorsal) regions (human). Smokers whose brain damage involved the insula were more likely to have their addiction disrupted (human). In mice its neurons respond preferentially to food cues when the animal is hungry (mouse), and its ongoing activity tracks the return to homeostasis during hunger and thirst (mouse).

entities.name: Anterior insula
entities.summary: The anterior insula, with agranular and dysgranular cortex in front of the granular posterior part (human). Activity in the right anterior insula predicts the accuracy of heartbeat detection, and its gray matter volume correlates with interoceptive accuracy and visceral awareness (human); its re-representation of interoception is proposed as a basis for subjective feelings and awareness (review). It responds both to one's own pain and to a signal that a loved one is in pain, with responses that correlate with empathy scores (human), and to feeling disgust as well as seeing it on others' faces (human). With the dorsal anterior cingulate it anchors a salience network (human), and gray matter loss across psychiatric diagnoses converges in both insulae and the dorsal anterior cingulate (human). Perceived thermal intensity correlates with right anterior insula activity (human).

entities.name: Posterior insula
entities.summary: The posterior insula, mostly granular cortex (monkey). Graded cooling activates the dorsal margin of the middle/posterior insula, which corresponds to the lamina I spinothalamocortical pathway of monkeys (human), and stimulating the upper posterior insula evokes painful sensations, while posterior sites also evoke non-painful somatic sensations (human). Posterior insula/secondary somatosensory responses are specific to one's own pain, not a loved one's (human). In mice the posterior insula processes aversive stimuli and bodily states; its projection to the central amygdala mediates anxiety-related behaviours, and a separate accumbens-projecting pathway regulates feeding (mouse).

entities.name: Gustatory cortex
entities.summary: The primary taste cortex, which in humans consists of the insula and operculum (human). In mice each taste quality (sweet, bitter, umami, salty) has its own cortical field (mouse), and manipulating the sweet and bitter fields controls taste perception and behaviour even without taste input (mouse). Its sweet- and bitter-responsive fields project to distinct parts of the amygdala, and these inputs assign taste valence (mouse), and its projection to the lateral central amygdala is needed to learn taste-guided avoidance (mouse). Expecting a milder taste reduces its response to an aversive bitter taste (human). In primates the thalamic taste area projects to insular-opercular cortex (review). Phasic locus coeruleus activation strengthens the link between its responses and palatability, shifting the representations of all tastants except sucrose in the aversive direction (mouse).

entities.name: Von Economo neurons
entities.summary: Large bipolar projection neurons found only in great apes and humans, and only in anterior cingulate and frontoinsular cortex (human). Frontotemporal dementia causes an early, severe and selective loss of them, which Alzheimer's disease does not (human), and they are proposed to contribute to awareness (review).

entities.name: Addiction to smoking
entities.summary: Smokers with brain damage involving the insula were more likely than smokers with damage elsewhere to quit easily and immediately, without relapse or a persisting urge to smoke (human).

entities.name: Frontotemporal dementia
entities.summary: A neurodegenerative disease that erodes social behaviour and emotion and injures anterior cingulate and frontoinsular cortex early; it causes a selective loss of von Economo neurons, unlike Alzheimer's disease (human).

entities.name: Central post-stroke pain
entities.summary: Lesions of the dorsal posterior insula, where cooling is represented, can produce central post-stroke pain, which the authors take to support the proposal that central pain results from loss of the normal inhibition of pain by cold (human).

entities.name: Mental illness across diagnoses
entities.summary: In 193 morphometry studies of schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, depression, addiction, obsessive-compulsive disorder and anxiety, gray matter loss converged in the dorsal anterior cingulate and both insulae, with few diagnosis-specific effects (human).

entities.name: Salience network
entities.summary: An intrinsic connectivity network anchored by the dorsal anterior cingulate and orbital frontoinsular cortices, with robust subcortical and limbic connectivity; connectivity of its cingulate node correlates with anxiety (human). The right fronto-insular cortex appears to drive switches between the central-executive and default-mode networks (human), and the network is proposed to mark salient events for further processing (review).

entities.name: Interoception
entities.summary: Sensing the physiological condition of the body. Right anterior insula activity and gray matter volume relate to the accuracy of heartbeat detection and to visceral awareness (human), graded cooling activates the dorsal posterior insula (human), and mouse insular cortex tracks the return to homeostasis during hunger and thirst (mouse).

entities.name: Taste
entities.summary: Detecting sweet, bitter, umami, salty and sour tastes. In mice each quality is represented in its own field of gustatory cortex (mouse), and amygdala inputs from those fields assign taste valence separately from taste identity (mouse). Fly taste cells are tuned by category, Gr5a cells to sugars and Gr66a cells to bitter compounds, and their activity is sufficient to drive acceptance or avoidance (fly).

entities.name: Olfactory system
entities.summary: Distributed activity of sensory neurons in the nose is converted into a segregated map in the olfactory bulb and passed on to higher olfactory centres, including the piriform cortex and the cortical amygdala (mouse); a separate vomeronasal organ is thought to mediate pheromone-driven social behaviour (mouse). In humans, odours activate piriform and right orbitofrontal cortex (human), and smell identification declines markedly after the seventh decade (human). Smell is severely impaired in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases (human), and impaired smell can precede clinical Parkinson's disease by at least 4 years (human).

entities.name: Odorant receptor genes
entities.summary: An extremely large multigene family of seven-transmembrane-domain proteins expressed only in the olfactory epithelium, likely to encode odorant receptors (rat). About 1000 receptor types are expressed in the mouse nose (mouse); one receptor recognizes several odorants and one odorant several receptors, but different odorants activate different combinations, so odours are encoded combinatorially (mouse).

entities.name: Olfactory sensory neurons
entities.summary: Sensory neurons of the nasal epithelium. Neurons expressing different receptors are scattered within four zones (mouse), and those expressing a given receptor converge on one or a few glomeruli (rat), two fixed loci among about 1800 in the mouse bulb (mouse). Ablating the dorsal-zone neurons abolishes innate responses to aversive odorants, although the mice still detect them (mouse). The SARS-CoV-2 entry protein ACE2 is expressed in nasal support, stem and perivascular cells rather than in these neurons (mouse, monkey, human).

entities.name: Olfactory bulb
entities.summary: Where the distributed input from the nose converges on glomeruli to form a highly organized, perhaps stereotyped, spatial map (mouse); glomerular positions are bilaterally symmetric and constant across individuals (rat). Its dorsal domain carries innate aversive information (mouse). Mitral and granule cells interact through reciprocal dendrodendritic synapses (rat), and adult neurogenesis replaces most of its granule neurons (mouse). Rats discriminate odours at maximal accuracy within a single sniff (rat).

entities.name: Mitral cells
entities.summary: Projection neurons of the olfactory bulb. Their dendrites release glutamate onto granule cell dendrites and receive GABAergic dendrodendritic inhibition back, which can mediate lateral inhibition between mitral cells without axonal action potentials (rat). Individual olfactory cortex neurons receive input from multiple mitral cells representing broadly distributed glomeruli (mouse).

entities.name: Bulb granule cells
entities.summary: Inhibitory interneurons of the olfactory bulb that provide NMDA receptor-dependent dendrodendritic inhibition to mitral cells (rat). They are replaced throughout adult life: subventricular zone cells migrate long distances and become olfactory bulb neurons (mouse), continuous neurogenesis replaces the majority of bulb granule neurons, and ablating new neurons gradually depletes them (mouse).

entities.name: Piriform cortex
entities.summary: The primary olfactory cortex. Axons from individual glomeruli project diffusely across it, and its neurons sample the whole bulb without obvious spatial bias (mouse); odours evoke sparse spiking there, shaped by broadly tuned inhibition and fast oscillations (rat). Activating arbitrary ensembles of its neurons paired with reward or shock elicits learned behaviour (mouse). In humans, posterior piriform ensemble patterns track perceived odour quality (human), sniffing alone activates it (human), and odours activate it bilaterally (human); the identification and categorization of odours are thought to rely on odour objects formed there (review). Nasal breathing synchronizes its oscillations with those of the amygdala and hippocampus (human).

entities.name: Cortical amygdala
entities.summary: The cortical amygdaloid nuclei. Projections from individual glomeruli form spatially stereotyped patches there, and it preferentially receives dorsal bulb input (mouse); its circuit from the bulb is necessary for innate aversive and appetitive odour responses, and activating its odour-responsive neurons recapitulates them (mouse).

entities.name: Vomeronasal organ
entities.summary: A sensory organ thought to mediate social behaviours and neuroendocrine changes elicited by pheromones; activation of its sensory neurons requires the ion channel TRP2 (mouse).

entities.name: Smell loss (anosmia)
entities.summary: More than half of people aged 65 to 80 and more than three-quarters of those over 80 have major impairment of smell identification (human). In COVID-19, infection of non-neuronal cells of the olfactory epithelium is suggested to cause anosmia (mouse, monkey, human).

entities.name: Smell
entities.summary: Detecting and discriminating odours. Odours are encoded by combinations of receptors (mouse), rats discriminate them at maximal accuracy within a single sniff (rat), and the cerebellum is activated by odours and by sniffing (human). In flies each olfactory neuron likely expresses one of 57 odorant receptor genes, and neurons expressing the same gene converge on one or two antennal lobe glomeruli, a map of receptor activation (fly).

entities.name: Octopus brain
entities.summary: The central brain of the octopus. Only about one third of octopus neurons are central; the rest lie in the peripheral nervous system, including the eight arms (octopus). A histological atlas of the adult Octopus minor brain delineates more than 70 subregions (octopus), and diffusion MRI tractography of 25 lobes found 92 connections between them, largely matching earlier studies (octopus). Its genome shows massive expansions of protocadherins and C2H2 zinc-finger transcription factors and extensive mRNA editing (octopus). In embryos, neural progenitors outside the brain cords, in the lateral lips next to the eyes, generate neurons that migrate long distances into the lobes (octopus). Cephalopod neural systems have been compared with the vertebrate cortex, thalamus, basal ganglia, cerebellum and other structures, but how far a vertebrate equivalence exists is unanswered (review). Inhibiting nitric oxide synthesis blocks touch learning (octopus), and the muscarinic antagonist scopolamine impairs memory recall without affecting predation (octopus).

entities.name: Vertical lobe
entities.summary: A learning and memory centre of the octopus brain. Its synapses show glutamatergic long-term potentiation similar to that in vertebrates (octopus); enhancing its pathway speeds and cutting it slows short-term avoidance learning, but both impair recall the next day, so it acquires long-term memory through LTP and also modulates short-term learning (octopus). Removing about half of it impairs short-term recall of a visual discrimination learned by watching another octopus, but not its acquisition or long-term retention (octopus). About 1.8 million input axons sparsely innervate its amacrine interneurons, which make up most of its roughly 25 million cells (octopus); serotonin-immunoreactive terminals innervate its neuropil, and applied 5-HT facilitates transmission and LTP induction (octopus). Its cells are enriched for learning- and memory-related genes and resemble Drosophila Kenyon cells molecularly (octopus), and JZ Young likened its organization to the hippocampus, the cerebellum and the insect mushroom body (review). Differences between social and solitary species include multiple compartments (gyri) in it (octopus). Its activity can be recorded in untethered, behaving animals, with episodes of 2 Hz large-amplitude oscillations (octopus), and during active sleep its activity, with that of the superior frontal lobe, is the strongest of the brain regions recorded (octopus).

entities.name: Superior frontal lobe
entities.summary: A lobe of the supra-oesophageal brain. Its median part, the median superior frontal lobe (MSFL), sends the glutamatergic input axons of the vertical lobe, which innervate millions of amacrine interneurons en passant (octopus). It receives fibres from the optic lobe (octopus), and during active sleep its activity, with that of the vertical lobe, is the strongest of the brain regions recorded, while in quiet sleep both generate oscillations resembling sleep spindles (octopus).

entities.name: Vertical lobe amacrine interneurons
entities.summary: The small interneurons of the vertical lobe: input axons from the median superior frontal lobe innervate them en passant, and they converge sharply onto the large output neurons (octopus). Simple amacrine cells (89.3% of the lobe's roughly 25 million cells) each receive one input axon at a synapse endowed with LTP, while the newly described complex amacrine cells integrate many inputs and appear to provide balancing inhibition (octopus). They are cholinergic, with a GABAergic subpopulation, and their neurites show intense nitric oxide synthase activity (octopus).

entities.name: Vertical lobe large output neurons
entities.summary: The output neurons of the vertical lobe, onto which amacrine interneurons converge through cholinergic synapses (octopus). Their cell bodies label for GABA, suggesting an inhibitory output, and they co-express FMRFamide-like neuropeptides, suggesting a neuromodulatory role as well; a group of them is glutamatergic (octopus). In the cuttlefish, unlike the octopus, synaptic plasticity lies at this cholinergic fan-in layer (cuttlefish).

entities.name: Subvertical lobe
entities.summary: A supra-oesophageal lobe whose cells project to the optic lobe; fibres partly from its posterior part reach the neuropil of the vertical lobules (octopus).

entities.name: Basal lobes
entities.summary: The higher motor centres of the central brain. Microstimulating them in freely behaving octopuses evokes discrete and complex movements, but no site moves a single arm or body part, so they lack a central topographical map (octopus), and they coordinate the arms without body-part maps of sensory and motor information (review). The anterior, median and dorsal basal lobes send input to the optic lobe, and the optic lobe sends fibres to the lateral basal lobe (octopus).

entities.name: Brachial lobe
entities.summary: A lobe of the sub-oesophageal brain whose cells send input to the optic lobe (octopus).

entities.name: Eye (octopus)
entities.summary: Cephalopods have camera-type eyes and rely heavily on vision (octopus). Photoreceptors of its retina project to the optic lobe on the same side (octopus), and octopuses use vision to guide a single arm to a goal (octopus).

entities.name: Optic lobe
entities.summary: The paired primary visual processing centres. Two-photon imaging shows retinotopically organized ON and OFF receptive fields, with the OFF pathway and greater size selectivity emerging across its layers (octopus), and single-cell sequencing finds six major neuronal classes with distinct laminar positions and immature neurons in this continuously growing tissue (octopus). It receives input from the retina, the contralateral optic lobe and many higher motor and associative centres, which makes its medulla an exceptionally complex integrative area (octopus). Its enlargement and division differ with habit and habitat across octopus species (octopus).

entities.name: Peduncle lobe
entities.summary: Part of the peduncle complex, which rests on the optic tract between the optic lobe and the central brain; described as a visuo-motor centre that regulates visuomotor behaviour (octopus).

entities.name: Olfactory lobe
entities.summary: Part of the peduncle complex, thought to receive input from the olfactory organ. It is heterogeneous and includes steroidogenic territories that overlap cells expressing molluscan neuropeptides and dopamine beta-hydroxylase (octopus).

entities.name: Optic gland
entities.summary: The principal neuroendocrine centre of the octopus, an analogue of the vertebrate pituitary, in the peduncle complex (octopus). It controls sexual maturation, lifespan and reproduction: removing it abolishes maternal brooding and reverses the post-mating decline toward death (octopus). Across reproductive stages it up- and downregulates catecholamine, steroid, insulin and feeding-peptide pathways (octopus), after reproduction it raises synthesis of pregnane steroids, 7-dehydrocholesterol and bile acid intermediates (octopus), and its neurochemistry extends into neighbouring lobular territories (octopus).

entities.name: Arm nervous system
entities.summary: Most octopus neurons lie outside the brain, in the peripheral nervous system including the eight arms (octopus). Each arm's axial nerve cord is segmented, with nerves leaving between segments and a topographic map of the suckers ('suckerotopy') (octopus, squid). Severed arms still produce near-normal extensions, so the basic motor program lies in the arm itself (octopus), and fetching food uses three dynamic joints, the middle one set where two waves of muscle activation collide (octopus). Motor command axons run along the cerebrobrachial tracts and recruit many motor neurons en passant (octopus). Nerve cords link each arm with the arms two away on either side, outside the brain (octopus), and when crawling the octopus recruits arms moment to moment without rhythmic patterns (octopus). Arm injury causes neural hyperexcitability in injured and uninjured arms for at least 24 h (octopus). The arms' flexibility is argued to have shaped unique brain-body-behaviour relationships, in which intelligent behaviour emerges from the octopus's embodied organization (review).

entities.name: Suckers
entities.summary: Hundreds of suckers line each arm. A ganglion in each sucker's stalk has cells expressing sensory and motor neuron markers and sends fibres to the sucker muscles and to the oral roots that extend to the axial nerve cord, suggesting local reflexes for each sucker (octopus). Suckers 'taste by touch' with cephalopod-specific chemotactile receptors, which diverged from nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and detect poorly soluble, greasy molecules (octopus). A chemical in octopus skin inhibits their attachment reflex, so that the arms do not interfere with each other (octopus).

entities.name: Octopus GnRH (oct-GnRH)
entities.summary: A gonadotropin-releasing-hormone-like neuropeptide expressed in cell bodies of many octopus brain lobes and, densely, in the olfactory lobe. Through the optic-gland nerve it reaches the optic gland, where it is thought to excite gonadotropin release; the subpedunculate lobe exerts the opposing FMRFamide inhibition, so the two form a neuroendocrine axis analogous to the vertebrate hypothalamo-hypophysial-gonadal axis (Octopus vulgaris).

entities.name: Sleep
entities.summary: Sleep and its stages. Octopuses alternate long 'quiet' sleep with short 'active' sleep bouts with dynamic skin patterns and rapid eye movements, suggesting an ultradian cycle analogous to that of amniotes (octopus); active sleep is homeostatically regulated, and its skin patterns and brain activity resemble waking (octopus). Fly rest is sleep-like, with a raised arousal threshold and homeostatic regulation independent of the circadian clock (fly); in flies, a subset of ellipsoid body neurons generates sleep drive (fly) and the mushroom bodies regulate sleep (fly).

entities.name: Reproduction and maternal care
entities.summary: Sexual maturation, reproduction and care of offspring. In the octopus the optic glands control maturation, reproduction and lifespan; after mating, brooding females fast and decline toward death, a course that removing the glands reverses (octopus).

entities.name: Fruit fly brain
entities.summary: The brain of the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster. An electron microscopy wiring diagram of a whole adult female brain contains 139,255 neurons and about 5 × 10^7 chemical synapses (fly), and a connectome of the entire male central nervous system, brain and nerve cord, contains 166,700 neurons of 11,710 types, with sex-specific and dimorphic neurons concentrated in higher brain centres (fly). Network analysis of the whole-brain connectome finds rich-club organization, with about 30% of neurons highly connected (fly). The right optic lobe alone holds about 53,000 neurons of 732 types (fly).

entities.name: Structural connectome (EM wiring diagram)
entities.summary: Structural connectivity: synaptic wiring diagrams reconstructed from electron microscopy, as distinct from functional connectivity measured from activity. Connectomes now cover most of the central brain, with cell types and computational compartments (fly), the whole brain of an adult female with annotated cell types and predicted neurotransmitters (fly), the entire male central nervous system, brain and nerve cord (fly), and the right optic lobe (fly). A medulla connectome identified the cell types of a motion detection circuit whose connections fit their direction selectivity (fly), and connectomes of the mushroom body and central complex revealed new inputs, outputs and network motifs (fly). The whole-brain network has a rich club of highly connected neurons, and its data are shared in the FlyWire Codex (fly). A whole-brain spiking model built only from connectivity and predicted transmitters predicted the neurons that respond to tastes and are required for feeding initiation, and neurons that elicit motor neuron firing, which optogenetic activation and behaviour then confirmed (fly).

entities.name: Resting-state functional connectivity
entities.summary: Functional connectivity: correlations between the activity of brain regions, here measured by calcium imaging, as distinct from synaptic wiring. Correlating spontaneous (“resting-state”) calcium signals between atlas regions of the adult central brain reveals an intrinsic functional network (fly). Relating published connectome data to published whole-brain imaging, these correlations track direct region-to-region structural connectivity strongly, but the fit varies across the brain, and some regions, including the mushroom body, depend more on indirect connections (fly). Imaging all cells in a large volume of the brain during spontaneous behaviour shows that the activity of most neurons correlates or anticorrelates with running and flailing, alongside high-dimensional activity of small, spatially organized clusters (fly).

entities.name: Antennal lobe
entities.summary: The olfactory neuropil that receives the olfactory receptor neurons, organized into glomeruli. Neurons expressing a given receptor gene project to one or two spatially invariant glomeruli, so it holds a two-dimensional map of receptor activation (fly); about 50 receptor neuron classes send axons to 50 corresponding glomeruli (fly). Its second-order neurons are more broadly tuned than their afferents in the same glomerulus, implicating lateral interactions within it (fly).

entities.name: Mushroom body
entities.summary: An associative centre of the insect brain (fly). Its 2,000–2,500 intrinsic Kenyon cells run as parallel fibres (fly) and integrate input from olfactory glomeruli (fly). Ablating it abolishes associative odour learning without other gross deficits (fly); output from its α/β neurons is needed to retrieve olfactory memory but not to acquire or consolidate it (fly), and long-term memory requires its vertical lobes (fly). The dendrites of its output neurons form 15 compartments that tile its lobes, and each dopaminergic neuron type sends its axons to one or at most two of them (fly), and its connectome shows extensive visual input, connections with the central complex and output neurons that contact descending neurons directly (fly). It also regulates sleep: changing PKA activity in it, or silencing, exciting or ablating it, alters sleep (fly), and blocking synaptic output in lines that share expression in it, or ablating it, reduces sleep (fly). In a comparison of connectome and resting-state imaging data, it was among the regions whose functional connectivity depends more strongly on indirect connections (fly).

entities.name: Lateral horn
entities.summary: A higher olfactory centre implicated in innate behaviour (fly). Projection neurons relay olfactory information to it as well as to the mushroom body; fruit odours are represented mostly in its posterior-dorsal part and candidate pheromone channels in its anterior-ventral part, suggesting that it is organized by the biological value of odours (fly). About 30% of its projections converge with mushroom body outputs, and activating some of its cell types changes valence behaviour or drives specific locomotor programs (fly).

entities.name: Central complex
entities.summary: A collection of neuropil compartments, including the ellipsoid body, important for visually guided behaviours (fly). In insects its recurrent circuits enable directed locomotion, sleep and context- and experience-dependent spatial navigation; its complete electron microscopy connectome shows network motifs likely to extract the fly’s head direction, maintain it with attractor dynamics and combine it with other sensorimotor information for vector-based navigation, and pathways by which context and internal state may select its behaviours (fly). Behavioural genetics implicated it in innate responses to vertical visual features and in memory for visual patterns (fly).

entities.name: Ellipsoid body
entities.summary: A toroidal neuropil at the centre of the fly brain (fly), formed largely by the axons of ring neurons (fly). Neurons whose dendrites tile it encode the fly’s heading relative to landmarks, update it from self-motion in darkness and hold it by persistent activity; their dynamics and circular layout suggest a ring attractor (fly). Its neurons are needed for visual place learning, whereas the mushroom bodies are not (fly), and its GABAergic ring neurons for a spatial orientation memory lasting seconds (fly). A subset of its neurons generates sleep drive through plasticity that tracks sleep need (fly).

entities.name: Fan-shaped body
entities.summary: The central-most part of the fly brain (fly). Two groups of neurons forming parallel horizontal strata in it hold short-term memory traces for the elevation and contour orientation of visual patterns (fly). Its PFNd and PFNv neurons multiply velocity signals with compass heading signals, and their convergence onto hΔB neurons turns body-centred velocity into a world-centred representation; perturbing PFNd neurons disrupts path integration (fly). Activating neurons that include dorsal fan-shaped body projections induces sleep, and sleep induced after massed training lets flies form a long-term memory (fly).

entities.name: Anterior optic tubercle
entities.summary: A central-brain visual centre on the anterior visual pathway. Neurons of two lineages receive input from visual projection neurons of the medulla and connect the tubercle with the ring neurons of the ellipsoid body, forming two parallel channels, one with small retinotopic receptive fields and one with a large contralateral field, that may encode the position of a bright feature such as a celestial body; the pathway resembles the sky-compass pathway of other insects (fly).

entities.name: Optic lobe
entities.summary: The visual neuropils beside the central brain, including the lamina (fly), medulla (fly), lobula (fly) and lobula plate (fly). The right optic lobe of a male fly holds about 53,000 neurons classified into 732 types, about half newly named (fly).

entities.name: Lamina
entities.summary: The first optic neuropil, where photoreceptor signals split into five parallel pathways, L1–L5. L1 output is needed for responses to moving ON edges and L2 output for OFF edges, so the lamina splits vision into ON and OFF channels, much as bipolar cells do in the vertebrate retina (fly).

entities.name: Medulla
entities.summary: An optic neuropil built of a repeating module. An electron microscopy connectome of the module identified the cell types of a motion detection circuit whose connections onto individual motion-sensitive neurons fit their direction selectivity (fly). Its visual projection neurons feed the anterior visual pathway to the central complex (fly).

entities.name: Lobula
entities.summary: An optic neuropil whose lobula columnar (LC) visual projection neurons carry visual features to distinct optic glomeruli in the central brain; 22 LC types have been described (fly).

entities.name: Lobula plate
entities.summary: An optic neuropil with four retinotopic layers: T4 and T5 cells tuned to the same cardinal direction terminate in the same layer, so ON and OFF motion detectors with the same tuning converge there (fly). The dendrites of LPLC2 looming detectors ramify across these layers (fly).

entities.name: Subesophageal zone (gnathal ganglia)
entities.summary: The region of the brain below the oesophagus, the subesophageal ganglion or zone. A pair of motor neurons there controls a subprogram of a simple taste behaviour; they are activated by sugar stimulation of gustatory neurons and inhibited by bitter compounds, though no direct connections from the sensory neurons were detected (fly).

entities.name: Ventral nerve cord
entities.summary: The fly’s nerve cord, which descending neurons connect to the brain through the neck (fly). It is a layered system of neuropils reflecting the fly’s two largely independent means of locomotion, walking and flight (fly). The male connectome covers it together with the brain (fly).

entities.name: Photoreceptors
entities.summary: The light-sensing cells of the compound eye. Their signals split in the lamina into five parallel pathways, L1–L5 (fly), and the whole-brain connectome traces pathways from a subset of photoreceptors to descending motor pathways (fly).

entities.name: Olfactory receptor neurons
entities.summary: Sensory neurons that detect odours. Each is likely to express a single one of 57 odorant receptor genes (fly), and about 50 classes project to 50 corresponding glomeruli in the antennal lobe (fly). A pheromone can act through a single class: Or67d neurons are necessary and sufficient for behavioural responses to the male pheromone cVA (fly).

entities.name: Projection neurons (olfactory)
entities.summary: Second-order olfactory neurons that carry odour information from the antennal lobe’s glomeruli to the mushroom body and the lateral horn (fly). Second-order neurons are more broadly tuned than their afferents in the same glomerulus (fly), and the glomerular inputs to individual Kenyon cells combine apparently at random (fly). Blocking most projection neurons impairs odour detection and male courtship (fly).

entities.name: Kenyon cells
entities.summary: The intrinsic neurons of the mushroom body, about 2,000 with parallel axons (fly). Each integrates input from a different, apparently random combination of olfactory glomeruli, and together they encode odours as sparse patterns of activity (fly); feedback inhibition from the APL neuron keeps this code sparse and decorrelated, which flies need to discriminate similar odours (fly). The rutabaga adenylyl cyclase is needed only in Kenyon cells for a component of olfactory short-term memory (fly), and cAMP signalling in one subpopulation of them is necessary and sufficient for both appetitive and aversive memories (fly).

entities.name: Mushroom body output neurons
entities.summary: The output neurons of the mushroom body: 21 types whose dendrites occupy 15 compartments along the Kenyon cell axons and whose axons reach five neuropils outside it (fly). Activating them causes attraction or repulsion depending on cell type, and the ensemble is suggested to represent valence collectively (fly). Pairing an odour with activation of specific dopamine neurons depresses the odour’s synapses at the mushroom body output site (fly). MB-V2 output neurons, which project to the lateral horn among other targets, are needed to retrieve aversive memory but not to form it (fly), and some output neurons contact descending neurons directly (fly).

entities.name: Dopamine neurons (mushroom body)
entities.summary: Dopaminergic neurons that innervate the mushroom body: 20 types, each projecting to one or at most two output-neuron compartments (fly). Dopamine is required for aversive odour conditioning (fly), while a group in the PAM cluster signals sugar reward, is activated by sugar ingestion and has its outputs mainly in the medial lobes (fly). Pairing an odour with activation of specific dopamine neurons induces learning and plasticity confined to their compartments (fly), and octopamine reinforces short-term appetitive memory through a subset of them (fly). They receive feedback from the output neurons (fly).

entities.name: APL neuron
entities.summary: A GABAergic neuron that forms a negative feedback loop with the Kenyon cells: they activate it and it inhibits them, keeping odour responses sparse and decorrelated; disrupting the loop stops flies learning to discriminate similar, but not dissimilar, odours (fly).

entities.name: Ring neurons
entities.summary: Central complex neurons whose axons largely form the ellipsoid body, all generated by a single lineage (fly). Their dendrites are visually responsive and retinotopic, with excitatory and inhibitory subfields like those of simple cells in mammalian primary visual cortex and a preference for vertical features (fly). They receive the anterior visual pathway from the anterior optic tubercle (fly), and GABAergic ring neurons are needed for a spatial orientation memory lasting seconds (fly).

entities.name: E-PG compass neurons
entities.summary: Central complex neurons that function as an internal compass, similar to mammalian head-direction cells. They track a simulated sun in flight, and silencing them abolishes menotaxis, flying at an arbitrary heading to the sun, leaving only frontal phototaxis (fly).

entities.name: Heading-shifting neurons
entities.summary: Clockwise- and anticlockwise-shifting neurons of the central complex whose wiring and physiology let them rotate the heading estimate according to the fly’s angular velocity; they are needed for the heading system to track heading in the dark, and stimulating them shifts the heading signal predictably (fly).

entities.name: T4 and T5 motion detectors
entities.summary: Direction-selective neurons, the elementary motion detectors: T4 cells respond to moving ON edges and T5 cells to OFF edges, each subpopulation is tuned to one of the four cardinal directions, and each terminates in the matching lobula plate layer; blocking T4 or T5 selectively impairs downstream responses and turning to ON or OFF motion (fly). The same design, parallel ON and OFF pathways converging onto direction-selective neurons, is found in mammalian motion vision (review).

entities.name: Lobula columnar neurons (LC, LPLC)
entities.summary: Visual projection neurons that carry lobula output to distinct optic glomeruli in the central brain. Of 22 types described, several drive specific behaviours when activated, two respond to looming and resemble natural avoidance, and another responds to small moving objects (fly). LPLC2, a lobula plate/lobula columnar type, detects looming with high selectivity by radial motion opponency and terminates on the giant fibre (fly).

entities.name: Giant fibre
entities.summary: A descending neuron that receives the LPLC2 looming detectors and drives the jump-muscle motor neuron to trigger escape take-off (fly). Facing a looming stimulus, a fly makes a long escape that initiates stable flight or a short, fast take-off, and the giant fibre’s spike timing relative to parallel escape circuits decides which (fly).

entities.name: Gustatory receptor neurons
entities.summary: Taste neurons on many parts of the body, including the legs and the proboscis. Their projections in the first relay of the brain are segregated by taste category, sugars versus noxious substances, and by their location in the periphery (fly). Gr5a cells respond to sugars and Gr66a cells to bitter compounds, and activating them is enough to drive acceptance or avoidance (fly). A connectome of the male gustatory system traces complete sensory-to-motor pathways from them to feeding, foraging, endocrine and social behaviour circuits (fly).

entities.name: Descending neurons
entities.summary: Neurons that carry the brain’s output through the neck to the nerve cord. About half of all fly descending neurons have been identified and mapped from sensory neuropils in the brain to motor neuropils in the nerve cord (fly). MDN descending neurons are required for backward walking at a barrier and can trigger it (fly), and some mushroom body output neurons contact descending neurons directly (fly).

entities.name: Feeding (Fdg) neurons
entities.summary: A single pair of brain neurons whose activation induces the entire feeding sequence and whose suppression or ablation eliminates sugar-induced feeding; they respond to food only in starved flies and sit at the top of the feeding motor hierarchy (fly).

entities.name: Odorant receptors (Or genes)
entities.summary: A family of 57 genes encoding the fly’s odorant receptors, of which a sensory neuron likely expresses only one (fly). Most olfactory neurons also express Or83b, a broadly expressed and conserved atypical receptor that the others need to reach the dendrites and that is essential for responses to many odorants (fly). The pheromone cVA acts through Or67d (fly).

entities.name: cAMP/PKA signalling (rutabaga)
entities.summary: Signalling through cyclic AMP and protein kinase A. The rutabaga adenylyl cyclase is needed only in Kenyon cells for a component of olfactory short-term memory (fly), cAMP signalling in one Kenyon cell subpopulation is necessary and sufficient for appetitive and aversive memories (fly), and enhancing PKA activity in the adult mushroom bodies changes sleep greatly (fly).

entities.name: fruitless (FruM)
entities.summary: A gene spliced differently in males and females, whose male-specific transcription factors, FruM, specify the neural substrates of courtship (fly). Male splicing is essential for male courtship and sufficient to make females court other females (fly); FruM is expressed in about 2% of central neurons, inactivating them abolishes courtship and masculinizing them in females largely confers it (fly). By regulating dendrite position it connects one cluster of third-order olfactory neurons to pheromone input and disconnects another, rerouting the pheromone signal by sex (fly).

entities.name: Octopamine
entities.summary: A neuromodulator presumed to be the arthropod homologue of noradrenaline. It is required for appetitive but not aversive olfactory conditioning (fly), and it reinforces only short-term appetitive memory, through dopamine neurons, partly via the OAMB receptor in a subset of mushroom-body-targeted dopamine neurons (fly).

entities.name: Dopamine receptors DopR1 and DopR2
entities.summary: D1-like dopamine receptors of the Kenyon cells. The D1 receptor dDA1 (DopR1) is enriched in the mushroom body; mutants with abnormal dDA1 expression learn very poorly with shock and less well with sugar, and restoring it in mushroom body neurons rescues both (fly). DopR1 and DopR2 couple to different second messengers and direct opposite synaptic plasticity, so that the timing of odour and dopamine decides whether an association is written or reversed (fly).

entities.name: dunce (cAMP phosphodiesterase)
entities.summary: The first fly learning mutant: dunce flies fail to learn to avoid a shock-paired odour although they sense odour and shock (fly), and with classical conditioning they learn appreciably but forget within the first 30 minutes (fly). Searches for mutants of learning, of cyclic AMP metabolism and of fertility led to the same gene, which appears to encode a cAMP phosphodiesterase (fly).

entities.name: CREB (dCREB2)
entities.summary: A family of transcription factors needed for long-term memory. Consolidated odour memory has two components, anaesthesia-resistant memory and long-term memory, which alone needs protein synthesis (fly), and inducing a dominant-negative CREB transgene blocks long-term memory completely while sparing learning and anaesthesia-resistant memory (fly).

entities.name: Amnesiac neuropeptide
entities.summary: The product of the amnesiac gene, an apparent neuropeptide precursor. amnesiac flies learn but forget within 30 minutes (fly). It is expressed strongly in the two DPM neurons, which project over all the mushroom body lobes; blocking their vesicle recycling shortens memory, and restoring amn in them rescues it (fly).

entities.name: Neuropeptide F (dNPF)
entities.summary: The fly orthologue of mammalian neuropeptide Y. Stimulating dNPF neurons mimics hunger and promotes appetitive memory performance in fed flies, which needs the dNPF receptor in six dopamine neurons of one mushroom body region (fly).

entities.name: Shaker (potassium channel)
entities.summary: A voltage-dependent potassium channel that controls membrane repolarization and transmitter release. A screen of 9,000 mutant lines found a short sleeper, minisleep, with a point mutation in Shaker; other Shaker alleles also sleep little, and short-sleeping Shaker flies live shorter lives (fly).

entities.name: DPM neurons
entities.summary: A pair of large neurons that project over all the lobes of the mushroom body. They express the Amnesiac neuropeptide, needed for normal olfactory memory (fly), and release serotonin onto α/β Kenyon cells, needed for anaesthesia-resistant memory (fly).

entities.name: Mushroom body neuroblasts
entities.summary: The four neural stem cells that build each mushroom body. Each gives rise to the whole repertoire of mushroom body neurons and glia (fly), producing γ neurons first, then α′/β′ neurons, and α/β neurons last (fly).

entities.name: Fly models of Parkinson’s disease
entities.summary: Expressing human α-synuclein in flies causes adult-onset loss of dopaminergic neurons, filamentous inclusions and locomotor dysfunction (fly), and flies lacking parkin, mutated in a familial juvenile parkinsonism, have locomotor defects from muscle degeneration, with mitochondrial pathology first (fly).

entities.name: Fly model of Alzheimer’s disease (Aβ42)
entities.summary: Expressing human Aβ42 in the fly brain causes diffuse amyloid deposits, age-dependent learning defects and extensive neurodegeneration, whereas Aβ40 causes only learning defects (fly).

entities.name: Fly model of fragile X syndrome (dfmr1)
entities.summary: Flies lacking dfmr1 activity have courtship, courtship-memory and mushroom body defects that metabotropic glutamate receptor antagonists or lithium rescue, implicating enhanced mGluR signalling (fly).

entities.name: Fly model of polyglutamine disease (SCA3)
entities.summary: An expanded-polyglutamine fragment of the spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 protein causes nuclear inclusions and late-onset degeneration in flies, to which neurons are especially susceptible; the anti-apoptotic gene P35 mitigates it (fly).

entities.name: Associative learning
entities.summary: Learning that one stimulus predicts another, as in classical conditioning. Flies learn to avoid an odour paired with electric shock, a memory that lasts a day (fly); this requires the mushroom bodies (fly), and flies also learn odours paired with sugar reward, which dopamine neurons of the PAM cluster signal (fly).

entities.name: Lateral septum
entities.summary: Topographically divided into dorsal (LSd), intermediate (LSi), and ventral (LSv) subregions; receives major CA3/CA1 hippocampal inputs and projects to the medial septum, hypothalamus (MPO, LHA), mammillary body, and VTA (rat).
entities.desc: The major relay station connecting the hippocampus to the rest of the brain. Receives dense topographic glutamatergic projections from CA3, CA1, and subiculum, and sends GABAergic inhibitory projections back to the medial septum (providing negative feedback to the theta generator) and forward to the lateral hypothalamus and VTA to link contextual memory with motivation and reward.

entities.name: Diagonal band of Broca
entities.summary: Comprises the vertical limb (VDB, Ch2) and horizontal limb (HDB, Ch3); anterior-medial cholinergic neurons project to prelimbic cortex (PrL) to improve attentional sequencing (mouse) and innervate the olfactory bulb and hippocampus.

entities.name: Substantia innominata & nucleus basalis
entities.summary: Houses the Ch4 magnocellular cholinergic group providing topographically organized projections to neocortex and amygdala; modulated by striatal D1 and D2 medium spiny neurons to control salience-associated acetylcholine dynamics (mouse, monkey, human).
entities.desc: Substantia innominata and nucleus basalis of Meynert (Ch4). Contains large magnocellular cholinergic neurons broadcasting subsecond acetylcholine transients to prefrontal and sensory-motor cortices during cue detection and attentional effort, alongside parvalbumin+ GABAergic projection neurons that synchronize cortical gamma oscillations (30–80 Hz).

entities.name: Ventral pallidum
entities.summary: Ventral striatopallidal relay containing bursting cholinergic neurons alongside GABAergic and glutamatergic populations; projects to BLA, mPFC, lateral habenula, and parasubthalamic nucleus and signals rewards and punishments (mouse).

entities.name: Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons (ChAT+)
entities.summary: Broadly projecting modulatory population releasing acetylcholine across the cortical mantle, hippocampus, and amygdala; exhibits bursting dynamics, regulates cortical state transitions and attentional selection, and can co-release GABA.
entities.desc: ChAT-positive projection neurons of the basal forebrain and medial septum. Broadcast acetylcholine and co-release GABA to regulate cortical and hippocampal state transitions, cue salience, and synaptic plasticity.

entities.name: Basal forebrain GABAergic projection neurons (PV+ & SOM+)
entities.summary: Parvalbumin-positive (fast-firing) and somatostatin-positive GABAergic projection neurons targeting cortical interneurons and subcortical arousal hubs; SOM+ neurons exhibit highly reciprocal connections with upstream regions (mouse).
entities.desc: Parvalbumin-positive (PV+) and somatostatin-positive (SOM+) projection neurons of the basal forebrain. Project to prefrontal cortex to entrain gamma oscillations and from the medial septum to hippocampal interneurons to drive theta pacing.

entities.name: ACh and GABA co-transmission
entities.summary: Septohippocampal cholinergic axon terminals contain distinct GABAergic vesicle pools that release both acetylcholine and GABA, exerting dual excitatory and fast inhibitory control to suppress sharp-wave ripples and pace theta rhythms.

entities.name: Ascending reticular arousal network
entities.summary: Multimodal subcortical-to-cortical network linking brainstem tegmental nuclei, VTA, hypothalamus, thalamus, and basal forebrain with the default mode and awareness networks to sustain wakefulness and conscious state (human).

entities.name: Tyramine
entities.summary: Synthesized from tyrosine by tyrosine decarboxylase (Tdc2). Tdc2-positive neurons label both tyramine and octopamine populations, but tyramine acts as an independent signaling molecule via distinct G-protein-coupled receptors (TyrR, TyrRII, Oct/TyrR). Tyramine regulates motor switching, walking and flight initiation, and courtship, often exerting physiological actions antagonistic to octopamine (fly).

entities.name: Histamine
entities.summary: Synthesized by histidine decarboxylase (Hdc) in photoreceptors and mechanosensory neurons. Rather than slow neuromodulation, histamine mediates fast inhibitory synaptic transmission to lamina monopolar neurons (L1–L3) via histamine-gated chloride channels encoded by ort (hclA/HisCl2) and HisCl1 (fly).

entities.name: Nitric oxide
entities.summary: A noncanonical gaseous cotransmitter synthesized on demand by nitric oxide synthase (NOS) in a specific subset of mushroom body dopaminergic neurons (PPL1-γ1pedc and PAM-γ5). NO diffuses to activate soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC/Gyc88E) in Kenyon cells, driving slow cGMP accumulation that regulates memory decay and updating, operating in opposition to classical dopamine-mediated reinforcement (fly).

entities.name: Carbon monoxide
entities.summary: A gaseous messenger synthesized in mushroom body Kenyon cells by heme oxygenase (HO). CO acts retrogradely on presynaptic dopaminergic terminals to regulate on-demand dopamine release during associative conditioning, necessary for olfactory memory consolidation (fly).

entities.name: Adenosine receptor (AdoR)
entities.summary: Purinergic G-protein-coupled receptor encoded by AdoR, expressed in central neurons and surface/cortex glia. Responds to extracellular adenosine to modulate sleep homeostasis, metabolic stress resistance, and neural resilience (fly).

entities.name: Short neuropeptide F
entities.summary: A local peptidergic neuromodulator encoded by sNPF, signaling through sNPFR1. Functionally and genetically distinct from NPF, sNPF is upregulated during starvation to facilitate presynaptic transmitter release at Or42b olfactory receptor neuron terminals, boosting odor sensitivity and food search (fly).

entities.name: Tachykinin (Tk)
entities.summary: Local and central neuropeptide acting via G-protein-coupled receptors TkR86C (DTKR) and TkR99D. Provides presynaptic gain control at antennal lobe olfactory glomeruli, regulates sleep/arousal, and modulates male-male aggressive action selection (fly). Genetic manipulation of Tk neurons produces distinct phenotypes from deleting the Tk ligand itself (fly).

entities.name: Leucokinin (Lk)
entities.summary: Pleiotropic neuropeptide acting through the leucokinin receptor (LkR). Released by lateral horn and subesophageal/abdominal neurons to coordinate post-feeding sleep, meal size, water and ion excretion (diuresis), and metabolic balance (fly).

entities.name: SIFamide
entities.summary: Potent behavioral coordinator produced by four widely arborizing hub neurons in the pars intercerebralis. Released via volume transmission to act through SIFaR across multiple neuropils, translating internal starvation state into behavioral prioritization by suppressing courtship and promoting food intake (fly).

entities.name: Allatostatin A (AstA)
entities.summary: Inhibitory neuropeptide signaling through AstA-R1 and AstA-R2. Coordinates context-specific switches between foraging and feeding, inhibiting sugar-sensitive dopamine neurons and feeding initiation while stimulating locomotion (fly).

entities.name: Drosulfakinin (DSK)
entities.summary: Cholecystokinin (CCK) homolog encoded by Dsk, acting via DskR1 and DskR2. Released by central neurons to stimulate insulin-producing cells, signal satiety, suppress meal size, and regulate male aggression (fly). Distinct from sex peptide (fly).

entities.name: Drosophila insulin-like peptides (DILPs)
entities.summary: Family of peptide hormones (DILP1–DILP8) signaling through a single tyrosine kinase insulin receptor (InR). Produced by median neurosecretory insulin-producing cells (IPCs) and peripheral fat body to coordinate nutrient storage, lifespan, metabolic sleep, and hunger-dependent behavior (fly).

entities.name: Adipokinetic hormone (AKH)
entities.summary: Insect glucagon homolog produced by neuroendocrine cells of the corpora cardiaca. Signals through the G-protein-coupled AKH receptor (AKHR) to mobilize trehalose and lipids and trigger starvation-induced hyperactivity and food-seeking behavior (fly).

entities.name: Pigment-dispersing factor (PDF)
entities.summary: Principal circadian transmitter synthesized by ventrolateral clock pacemaker neurons (s-LNvs and l-LNvs). Signals through the PDF receptor (PDFR) to dorsal clock neurons, central complex ring neurons, and sleep centers to drive morning locomotor anticipation and circadian synchronization (fly).

entities.name: Ventrolateral clock neurons (LNvs)
entities.summary: Circadian clock pacemaker neurons consisting of four small (s-LNv) and four to five large (l-LNv) ventrolateral neurons per hemisphere. They express PER, TIM, CRY and PDF, synchronizing central circadian oscillation and driving morning arousal (fly).

entities.name: Insulin-producing cells (IPCs)
entities.summary: Fourteen median neurosecretory cells in the pars intercerebralis that synthesize and secrete DILP2, DILP3, and DILP5. They receive octopaminergic, serotonergic, and peptidergic (DSK, sNPF) inputs to regulate systemic energy metabolism, growth, and starvation-induced feeding (fly).

entities.name: SIFamide hub neurons
entities.summary: Four large interneurons in the pars intercerebralis with extensive brain-wide arborizations reaching the antennal lobes, mushroom bodies, central complex, and subesophageal zone. They act as a central hub arbitrating competing drives, suppressing courtship to favor food search during hunger (fly).

entities.name: Inferior frontal lobe
entities.summary: The chemotactile learning and memory matrix of the octopus supraesophageal brain. Analogous to the visual vertical lobe system, the inferior frontal lobe receives ascending tactile and chemical inputs from the brachial lobe and suckers (Sepela et al., 2025; van Giesen et al., 2020), contains small interneurons for sensory discrimination, and projects to the subvertical and basal motor lobes to guide sucker grasping, exploration, or rejection (Young, 1971; Jung et al., 2018; Jacobs et al., 2022).

entities.name: Superior buccal lobe
entities.summary: Anterior-most lobe of the supraesophageal mass situated directly above the esophagus and radular apparatus. Coordinates mouthparts, beak biting, radula rasping, salivary venom injection, and swallowing in response to tactile feeding inputs from the inferior frontal lobe (Young, 1971; Jung et al., 2018; Jacobs et al., 2022).

entities.name: Pedal lobe
entities.summary: Major subesophageal motor center coordinating somatic locomotion, the funnel, jet propulsion, head steering, and eye stabilization. Receives descending commands from anterior and median basal lobes and reciprocal connections from the palliovisceral lobe, sending motor efferents to the funnel and mantle musculature (Young, 1971; Jung et al., 2018; Jacobs et al., 2022).

entities.name: Palliovisceral lobe
entities.summary: Posterior subesophageal motor center controlling the mantle, visceral organs, respiratory pumping, circulation, ink sac ejection, and chromatophore skin patterning. Integrates motor commands from the subvertical and basal lobes and coordinates dynamic camouflage during active sleep and predatory concealment (Young, 1971; Jung et al., 2018; Pophale et al., 2023; Jacobs et al., 2022).

entities.name: Optic tract
entities.summary: The massive bilateral tract connecting the optic lobes with the central brain. Carries retinotopic visual output from the optic lobe medulla into the superior frontal lobe for visual memory and into the lateral and anterior basal lobes for immediate motor orienting and camouflage (Pungor et al., 2023; Jacobs et al., 2022; Jung et al., 2018).

entities.name: Cephalopod FMRFamide
entities.summary: Inhibitory cardioactive and neuroendocrine neuropeptide in cephalopods. Synthesized in the subpedunculate and peduncle lobes, FMRFamide fibers innervate the optic gland to exert tonic inhibition over gonadotropic secretion, controlling sexual maturation, post-reproductive brooding, and programmed senescence (Di Cosmo et al., 1998; Iwakoshi-Ukena et al., 2004).

entities.name: Glutamate
entities.summary: Primary excitatory and plastogenic neurotransmitter at the median superior frontal lobe (MSFL) to vertical lobe amacrine synapse. Mediates fast depolarization that activates voltage-dependent calcium influx and triggers retrograde nitric oxide synthesis required for long-term potentiation and visual learning (Hochner et al., 2003; Shomrat et al., 2008; Bidel et al., 2023).

entities.name: ADHD profile
entities.summary: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition whose symptoms and impairment vary across people and across development. Group-level findings in cognition, brain structure, networks and treatment response do not identify a single lesion or a universal neurotransmitter deficit (human; review).

entities.name: Response-time variability in ADHD
entities.summary: Meta-analytic evidence finds greater reaction-time variability in ADHD than in typically developing groups, but smaller differences against some clinical comparison groups and in adults limit diagnostic specificity (multi-study review).

entities.name: Attentional stability
entities.summary: Attentional performance can fluctuate within a person with ADHD; variability is a dimensional phenotype rather than proof of one underlying circuit (multi-study review).

entities.name: Response inhibition dimension
entities.summary: Response inhibition is one dimension of ADHD research, but group-level stopping differences do not establish that every person has the same deficit or identify a single inhibitory node (human; review).

entities.name: Working-memory dimension
entities.summary: Working-memory difficulties occur in a subset of people with ADHD and vary with task demands; translational prefrontal studies show that catecholamine dose and receptor context can alter delay-period representations (human; nonhuman primate).

entities.name: Delay and reward sensitivity
entities.summary: Meta-analysis reports steeper monetary delay discounting in ADHD, while imaging and review literature links reward-pathway measures to motivational dimensions without making them a complete account of the disorder (human).

entities.name: Frontoparietal control system in ADHD
entities.summary: Control-related frontal and parietal systems support goals, working memory and flexible attention. ADHD studies report task- and population-dependent differences in their recruitment and coordination, not a universal isolated prefrontal deficit (human; review).

entities.name: Frontostriatal control system in ADHD
entities.summary: Frontal, striatal, pallidal and thalamic systems contribute to action selection, response regulation and motivation. Their ADHD relevance is convergent but distributed, so cognitive, motor and motivational territories should not be collapsed into one globally deficient loop (human; review).

entities.name: Default-mode/task-engaged interactions
entities.summary: ADHD studies implicate within-network organization, task-related deactivation and interactions between internally oriented and task-engaged systems. Default-mode interference is a model of lapses, not an established universal causal mechanism (human; review).

entities.name: Salience and monitoring system
entities.summary: Anterior insula and dorsal medial frontal systems are relevant to detecting important events, monitoring performance and allocating effort, but ADHD findings support a broader network account rather than a single failed switch (human; review).

entities.name: Reward and motivation system in ADHD
entities.summary: Ventral striatum, orbitofrontal/ventromedial cortex, anterior cingulate and midbrain dopamine systems contribute to reward processing. Anticipation, outcome valuation, prediction error, effort and delay should be kept as distinct measurements (human; review).

entities.name: Cerebellar participation in ADHD models
entities.summary: Cerebellar motor and association territories appear in distributed ADHD models involving timing, prediction and coordination with cognitive systems, but current evidence does not support a single cerebellar lesion or uniform subdivision effect (human; review).

entities.name: Recurrent prefrontal network mechanism
entities.summary: Recurrent excitation and inhibitory shaping support maintained prefrontal representations; catecholaminergic receptors modulate their stability and selectivity in a dose- and state-dependent manner (nonhuman primate; rat; review).

entities.name: Postsynaptic alpha2A prefrontal signaling
entities.summary: Guanfacine engages postsynaptic alpha2A-adrenoceptors in prefrontal cortex and reduces cAMP-related signaling, a translational mechanism that can strengthen recurrent network interactions supporting working memory (review).

entities.name: Prefrontal D1 gain control
entities.summary: Nonhuman-primate experiments support an inverted-U relationship in which moderate D1-receptor stimulation improves, and excessive stimulation impairs, delay-related prefrontal activity and working-memory performance (nonhuman primate).

entities.name: Medial-prefrontal glutamate measures
entities.summary: A spectroscopy meta-analysis found higher glutamate-plus-glutamine concentrations in right medial prefrontal cortex in children with ADHD, with substantial methodological and regional heterogeneity (human).

entities.name: Polygenic ADHD risk
entities.summary: A large genome-wide analysis identified 27 ADHD risk loci and implicated genes expressed during early brain development, including enrichment in neuronal populations; association does not establish a causal circuit edge (human).

entities.name: Developmental cortical morphology
entities.summary: Large coordinated imaging analyses report subtle age-dependent cortical and subcortical group differences, with stronger findings in children than adults; cross-sectional averages do not establish an individual maturation trajectory (human).

entities.name: ADHD measurement caveats
entities.summary: Reaction-time variability, EEG theta/beta ratio and ERP measures show heterogeneous group differences and should not be treated as universal diagnostic biomarkers or direct localizations of a neurotransmitter circuit (multi-study review).

entities.name: Treatment as circuit perturbation
entities.summary: Stimulants alter catecholamine transport and distributed brain networks, while acute treatment effects should be kept separate from claims about the developmental cause of ADHD or permanent circuit repair (human; review).
