corticospinal neurons of the caudal forelimb area control reaching, those of the rostral area grasping (mouse)
proposed to be essential for highly skilled movements, such as adaptive movements of the distal extremities
Chx10+ interneurons needed for skilled reaching, Vglut3+ for releasing food (mouse)
required to specify corticospinal and other subcerebral projection neurons (mouse)
Ctip2 is not expressed in Fezl-deficient cortex (mouse)
critical for corticospinal axons to reach the spinal cord (mouse)
Pten deletion (raising mTOR activity) lets injured corticospinal axons regenerate (mouse)
excess tonic inhibition in peri-infarct cortex; reducing it promotes recovery (mouse)
corticospinal tract integrity predicts the potential for recovery (human)
rehabilitative training preserves the hand map beside an infarct (monkey)
cortical hyperexcitability is an early feature of motor neuron disease (human)
intended movements still modulate motor cortex activity years after injury and can be decoded (human)
restores device control and communication after paralysis (pilot studies, human)
injured corticospinal axons regenerate poorly
a common Val108/158 Met variant accounts for a four-fold variation in COMT activity and dopamine catabolism (human)
the low-activity Met allele predicts fewer perseverative errors on the Wisconsin Card Sort and a more efficient prefrontal response during working memory (human)
the Val allele is transmitted more often to offspring with schizophrenia; the authors suggest it slightly raises risk by impairing prefrontal function (human)
D1-receptor stimulation sculpts delay activity along an inverted U: low levels sharpen spatial tuning, high levels reduce delay firing in all directions, eroding tuning (monkey)
links.note: Blocking prefrontal D1 receptors impairs memory-guided but not visually guided saccades (sawaguchi1991, monkey).

links.rel: D1-receptor actions on delay firing are mediated by cAMP signaling (monkeys and rats)
α2A-adrenoceptor stimulation inhibits cAMP and closes HCN channels, which are colocalized with the receptors in prefrontal spines (monkeys and rats)
closing HCN channels strengthens spatially tuned delay firing, while excessive cAMP collapses it (monkeys and rats)
Delay-cell persistent firing in dorsolateral PFC needs NR2B-containing NMDA receptors (monkey)
systemic ketamine abolished Delay-cell persistent firing in dorsolateral PFC, while many Response cells fired more (monkey)
builds spine synapses on prefrontal neurons: through mTOR in rats, and by rescuing spines lost in depression-related states in mice

in rodent models, blocking mTOR prevents ketamine’s synaptogenesis and behavioral effects (rat), and prefrontal spine formation is needed to maintain, though not to induce, its effects on motivated escape (mouse)
recurrent excitation among pyramidal Delay cells generates persistent firing (monkey)
dendritic spine density on deep layer 3 pyramidal neurons of DLPFC area 46 is 23% lower in schizophrenia than in controls (human)
depression-related behavior goes with branch-specific spine loss on prefrontal projection neurons (mouse)
excitatory synaptic strength onto layer V mPFC pyramidal neurons tracks dominance rank, and raising or lowering synaptic efficacy in dorsal mPFC moves rank up or down (mouse)
inhibiting parvalbumin interneurons suppresses gamma oscillations, and driving them is sufficient to generate gamma rhythmicity (mouse neocortex)
links.note: Review (lewis2005): in schizophrenia, reduced GABA synthesis in DLPFC parvalbumin interneurons alters perisomatic inhibition of pyramidal neurons, which contributes to a diminished capacity for gamma-frequency synchrony.

links.rel: convergent findings: in schizophrenia, deficient TrkB signaling reduces GABA synthesis in DLPFC parvalbumin interneurons (review)
inhibiting mPFC somatostatin (not parvalbumin) interneurons during encoding impairs spatial working memory (mouse)
inhibiting them during encoding decreases hippocampal-prefrontal synchrony (mouse)
persistent delay firing as the store of working memory
links.note: Prefrontal delay firing (fuster1971, monkey), tuned to the remembered direction (funahashi1989, monkey) and absent on error trials (bolkan2017, mouse), supports the view; lundqvist2016 instead finds brief gamma and beta bursts and argues that working memory is manifested by discrete oscillatory dynamics and spiking, not sustained activity (monkey).

links.rel: gamma bursts accompany encoding and re-activation (monkey); hippocampal-prefrontal gamma synchrony appears to mediate cue encoding (mouse); hippocampal-prefrontal theta coupling strengthens during spatial working memory (rat)
mixed-selectivity neurons carry information about all task-relevant aspects, and the dimensionality of this representation collapses on error trials (monkey)

single-neuron responses make sense as population dynamics that a trained recurrent network reproduces; the authors propose that context-dependent selection and integration of inputs are one dynamical process (monkey)
prefrontal neurons code abstract rules (monkey); theory casts prefrontal representations of goals and the means to achieve them as bias signals to other brain structures
mediodorsal input amplifies local prefrontal connectivity to sustain rule representations, without relaying categorical information (mouse)
the parvicellular mediodorsal nucleus connects with dorsolateral areas 46 and 9 (monkey)
the magnocellular mediodorsal nucleus connects with orbital and medial areas 11–14 (monkey)
mediodorsal input sustains mPFC delay activity during working memory and prefrontal rule representations during attention (mouse)
the mPFC-to-mediodorsal projection supports the choice that follows the delay (mouse)
direct hippocampal input supports the encoding of spatial cues in working memory (mouse); CA1-mPFC firing correlations and theta coupling strengthen during spatial working memory (rat)
hippocampal-formation neurons project mostly to medial, then orbital, prefrontal areas and only sparsely to lateral areas (monkey)
dense connections with posterior orbitofrontal cortex, whose caudal areas receive more amygdala input than they send (monkey)
cingulate area 24 sends comparatively more projections to the amygdala than it receives (monkey)
subgenual area 25 sends comparatively more projections to the amygdala than it receives (monkey)
basolateral amygdala firing entrains to mPFC theta input when mice recognize safety
proposed: prelimbic cortex turns transient amygdala input into a sustained output that drives conditioned fear (rat)
selectively activating mPFC neurons that project to the dorsal raphe had a profound, rapid and reversible effect on the selection of active behavior in a challenging situation (rat)
links.note: Activating mPFC principal neurons without regard to their projection had no detectable effect.

links.rel: dopaminergic projection from a distinct fast-firing population (mouse); phasic release in mPFC tunes its neurons to relevant cues during learning (mouse)
noradrenergic projection; LC cells projecting to PFC differ from those projecting to motor cortex and release more noradrenaline (rat)
frontal-parietal synchrony is stronger at lower frequencies during top-down and at higher frequencies during bottom-up attention (monkey)
prelimbic activity tracks freezing, and inactivating prelimbic cortex impairs the expression of conditioned fear (rat)
infralimbic activity signals extinction recall, stimulating it mimics extinction, and inactivating it impairs extinction learning and memory (rat)

an important component of the system for acquiring, storing and expressing fear memory (review); amygdala lesions interfere with fear conditioning to a tone and to the context, and inactivating the basolateral amygdala impairs fear expression and extinction memory (rat); a patient with bilateral amygdala damage did not acquire conditioned autonomic responses, and unilateral temporal lobectomy impairs fear conditioning (human)

hippocampal lesions impair fear conditioning to the context but not to a tone, and abolish contextual fear when made 1 day, but not 7 to 28 days, after training; inactivating the ventral hippocampus impairs fear expression and extinction memory (rat)
prelimbic lesions abolish sensitivity to goal value (rat)
infralimbic lesions keep actions goal-directed after extended training (rat)
medial frontal lesions selectively impair attentional set shifting (rat)
inhibiting mPFC somatostatin interneurons or hippocampal input during cue encoding, or mediodorsal input during maintenance, impairs spatial working memory (mouse)
its neurons hold directionally tuned delay activity for remembered locations, which depends on NR2B NMDA receptors (monkey)
lateral prefrontal (area 9) damage causes a loss of inhibitory control in attentional selection (marmoset)
DLPFC blood flow fails to rise during the Wisconsin Card Sort in patients and tracks their performance (human)
OFC neurons encode the value of offered and chosen goods, independent of spatial and motor factors (monkey)
value signals for the options under choice: in OFC neurons (monkey) and vmPFC activity (human)
orbital prefrontal removals attenuate the effect of reinforcer devaluation on choices, and fiber-sparing lesion results favor a role in value updating (monkey)
links.note: Theory (wilson2014) proposes that OFC labels the current task state for reinforcement learning elsewhere in the brain.

links.rel: needed for reversal learning? results depend on the lesion method (monkey; marmoset)
links.note: Surgical removals of orbital prefrontal cortex impaired object reversal learning (izquierdo2004, monkey), and OFC damage impaired inhibitory control in affective processing (dias1996, marmoset), but excitotoxic, fiber-sparing OFC lesions spared reversal learning, and a previously reported loss of inhibitory control was traced to damage to nearby fiber tracts (rudebeck2013, monkey).

links.rel: damage leaves patients oblivious to future consequences, and its activity encodes the values of specific options (human)
bilateral damage makes judgments on emotionally aversive moral dilemmas abnormally utilitarian (human)
conflict-related activity predicts prefrontal activity and behavioral adjustments (human); theory proposes that dorsal ACC allocates control according to its expected value
encodes the average value of the foraging environment and the cost of foraging (human)
reported to be metabolically overactive in treatment-resistant depression; chronic stimulation of the adjacent white matter was associated with sustained remission in four of six patients (human)
cortical maturation is delayed in ADHD, most prominently in prefrontal regions (human)
prefrontal neurons signal the attended location first during top-down attention (monkey), and mediodorsal-sustained prefrontal rule representations guide attention (mouse)
striatonigral projection: substance P neurons (human), which in rats also express D1 receptors
substance P-containing striatal neurons project to the internal pallidum: the 'direct' pathway
striatopallidal projection: enkephalin-containing neurons (human), which in rats also express D2 receptors
prototypic pallidal neurons, often parvalbumin-positive, target the subthalamic nucleus (rat): the 'indirect' pathway
arkypallidal neurons innervate only the striatum, its largest extrinsic GABAergic input, and respond to Stop cues (rat)
excitatory relay of the 'hyperdirect' and 'indirect' pathways to the pallidum
links.note: In patients with Parkinson's disease off medication, local potentials in the two nuclei are dominated by coherent activity below 30 Hz, which levodopa reduces (brown2001).

links.rel: 'hyperdirect' pathway: motor-related cortical areas excite the subthalamic nucleus, bypassing the striatum, with a shorter conduction time than paths through it
pallidal output to the thalamus closes the basal ganglia–thalamocortical 'motor' circuit
tonic GABA-mediated inhibition of saccade-related collicular cells; muscimol in the pars reticulata releases irrepressible saccades (monkey)
the ventromedial (limbic) striatum projects to a wide range of midbrain dopamine cells, part of an ascending striatonigrostriatal spiral (monkey)
acts on striatonigral neurons through D1 receptors: dopamine loss lowers their D1-receptor and substance P mRNAs, which a D1 agonist reverses (rat)
acts on striatopallidal neurons through D2 receptors: dopamine loss raises their D2-receptor and enkephalin mRNAs, which a D2 agonist reverses (rat)
complementary actions in D1 and D2 neurons keep corticostriatal plasticity bidirectional and Hebbian; unidirectional in Parkinson's disease models (mouse)
nigral stimulation at self-stimulation parameters potentiates corticostriatal synapses through dopamine receptors (rat)
proposed to reinforce learned actions: the potentiation correlated with the time rats took to learn self-stimulation (rat)
the fluctuating output of dopamine neurons apparently signals reward prediction errors (primate)
activating dopamine neurons at reward delivery, mimicking a prediction error, is sufficient for long-lasting increases in cue-elicited reward seeking (rat)
activating direct-pathway neurons reduces freezing and increases locomotion, and rescues locomotor initiation in a Parkinson's disease model (mouse)
links.note: Both pathways are transiently active when actions start (cui2013), and manipulating striatonigral neurons before a learned sequence slows its initiation (tecuapetla2016).

links.rel: classically inhibits movement: bilateral activation produces freezing and fewer locomotor initiations (mouse); yet indirect-pathway neurons are also active when actions start
links.note: kravitz2010 supports the classical opposing model. cui2013 found direct- and indirect-pathway neurons concurrently active at action initiation, and tecuapetla2016 found both pathways necessary for initiating and executing learned sequences (manipulating the striatopallidal pathway before initiation aborted it), and suggests a supportive versus permissive model rather than opposition.

links.rel: inhibiting dopamine neurons while mice are immobile lowers, and activating them raises, the probability of future movements; rapid signals in striatal dopamine axons can trigger locomotion (mouse)
pre-movement dopamine neuron activity relates to, and manipulating it changes, the vigour of future movements; dopamine depletion reduces vigor (mouse)
distinct dorsal striatal neuron classes represent vigor, and suppressing striatal activity during movement reduces it (mouse)
dorsolateral (not dorsomedial) striatum lesions keep actions sensitive to outcome devaluation: it is necessary for habit formation (rat)
start/stop activity emerges in nigrostriatal circuits during sequence learning, and both striatal pathways are needed to initiate and execute learned sequences (mouse)
arkypallidal neurons respond early and selectively to Stop cues, proposed to cancel actions in preparation via their projection to striatum (rat)

muscimol in the pars reticulata, releasing collicular cells from its tonic inhibition, causes irrepressible saccades and most disrupts saccades to remembered targets; suggested to apply to skeletal movements too (monkey)
a mutation in its gene occurs in families with autosomal dominant Parkinson's disease, and it forms the major filamentous component of Lewy bodies
loss of nigral dopamine neurons underlies the disease and causes deficits in movement initiation and slowness of movement
links.note: MPTP, which caused marked parkinsonism in people who injected it, is proposed to damage substantia nigra cells selectively (langston1983).

links.rel: excess subthalamic activity is implicated: lesioning the nucleus reduces akinesia, rigidity and tremor in MPTP-treated monkeys
classic model: changes in striatal projection neuron subpopulations that increase basal ganglia output are hypothesized to cause hypokinetic disorders
classic model: hyperkinetic disorders are postulated to result from selective impairment of striatal neurons projecting to the lateral pallidum
off medication, subthalamic and internal pallidal potentials are dominated by coherent activity below 30 Hz (four patients)
reduces subthalamic–pallidal activity below 30 Hz and brings a new peak near 70 Hz (four patients)
reduces symptoms; in early disease parkinsonism worsened less than with placebo over 42 weeks, but whether levodopa alters progression is uncertain (RCT)
links.note: Striatal dopamine-transporter uptake declined more with levodopa than with placebo, which may mean faster loss of nigrostriatal terminals or a pharmacologic effect on the transporter (fahn2004). In many patients, treatment is complicated by fluctuations between off and on periods, often with debilitating dyskinesias (limousin1998).

links.rel: subthalamic or pallidal stimulation improves motor function and quality of life more than best medical therapy (RCTs), with more serious adverse events
links.note: Stimulating only when local field potentials from the electrodes show pathological activity (adaptive DBS) beat continuous stimulation, with 56 percent less stimulation time, in 8 patients (little2013).

links.rel: therapeutic effects within the subthalamic nucleus can be accounted for by selective stimulation of afferent axons projecting to it (parkinsonian rodents)
an expanded, unstable CAG repeat in IT15 on 4p16.3, found on disease chromosomes in all 75 families examined
enkephalin-containing striatal neurons projecting to the external pallidum are much more affected in early and middle stages than substance P neurons projecting to the internal pallidum (post-mortem)
links.note: albin1989 postulates that hyperkinetic disorders result from selective impairment of striatal neurons projecting to the lateral pallidum.

links.rel: perforant path: entorhinal layer II gives rise to the major excitatory input to the hippocampus, which reaches the dentate gyrus first in the trisynaptic pathway
the dentate gyrus projects to CA3, the second step of the trisynaptic pathway
CA3 projects to CA1, the third step of the trisynaptic pathway; CA3's recurrent excitation generates sharp waves that drive ripples in CA1
entorhinal input to CA2, the first arm of a disynaptic circuit linking entorhinal input with CA1 output
CA2 output to CA1, the second arm of that disynaptic circuit
entorhinal layer IV receives a major hippocampal efferent projection; CA1 is the main hippocampal output
inactivating the medial septum (muscimol, or intraseptal lidocaine) reduces theta oscillations (rat)
when theta is reduced, grid cells lose their spatial periodicity, while head-direction cells keep their selectivity and place cells retain their firing patterns to a larger extent (rat)

as a rat crosses a place field, the theta phase of firing moves progressively forward on each cycle (phase precession); using the phase as well as the firing rate can improve the accuracy of place coding (rat)
place cells fire at particular locations, preliminary evidence that the hippocampus acts as a spatial map (rat); cells that respond at specific locations are found mainly in the human hippocampus
grid cells tile the environment with a triangular grid and may form a path-integration-based map (rat); grid-like cells occur in humans navigating a virtual environment
the dorsal (posterior) hippocampus performs primarily cognitive functions (review); posterior hippocampi are larger in London taxi drivers, and their volume correlates with time spent driving (human)

the ventral (anterior) hippocampus relates to stress, emotion and affect (review); raising ventral dentate activity suppresses innate anxiety, and ventral CA1 anxiety cells are required for avoidance (mouse)
links.note: The dorsal–ventral dichotomy may need revision: gene expression shows discrete domains along the long axis, whereas anatomy and rodent recordings suggest gradients (strange2014).

links.rel: ventral CA1 neurons projecting to prefrontal cortex show increased anxiety-related firing (rat); inhibiting ventral hippocampal input to medial prefrontal cortex disrupts anxiety-related behavior and theta synchrony (mouse)
goal-directed firing is most prominent in ventral CA1 neurons that target the nucleus accumbens (rat)

ventral CA1 projects to the basal amygdala, and activating these terminals impairs contextual fear memory (mouse); triple-projecting ventral CA1 neurons target the amygdala, prefrontal cortex and nucleus accumbens (rat)
ventral CA1 neurons projecting to the lateral hypothalamic area are enriched in anxiety cells, and activating their terminals there increases anxiety and avoidance (mouse)
blocking NMDA receptors with AP5 suppresses hippocampal LTP (rat); deleting them from CA1 pyramidal cells abolishes CA1 LTP (mouse)
AP5 impairs place learning, but not visual discrimination, while suppressing LTP (rat); mice lacking CA1 NMDA receptors lack CA1 LTP and have impaired spatial memory
links.note: Morris et al. conclude that LTP is involved in some, but not all, forms of learning; one-trial inhibitory avoidance learning itself induces LTP in CA1 (rat; whitlock2006).

links.rel: minimal changes to an environment alter dentate activity patterns (rat); deleting dentate NMDA receptors impairs telling similar contexts apart (mouse); human CA3/dentate gyrus activity is biased toward pattern separation
ablating adult neurogenesis impairs discrimination between nearby locations, and increasing the survival of adult-born neurons improves discrimination between similar contexts (mouse)
deleting NMDA receptors from CA3 pyramidal cells impairs recall from a fraction of the original cues (mouse)
place cells that fired together during behavior fire together more in later slow-wave sleep (rat); sharp wave-ripples replay fragments of waking sequences in compressed form (review)
selectively suppressing ripples after training impairs spatial memory, and disrupting ripple-associated activity during rest slows learning (rat)
before goal-directed navigation, hippocampal sequences depict paths from the current location to a remembered goal and predict immediate future behavior (rat)

loss of recent memory follows bilateral hippocampal lesions, a lesion limited to CA1 caused enduring anterograde amnesia, and hippocampal amnesia also impairs imagining new experiences (human); the medial temporal lobe system is essential for declarative memory (review)

the hippocampus's role is temporary: lesions abolish contextual fear when made 1 day, but not 7 to 28 days, after training (rat), and when a neocortical schema exists, new associations become hippocampal-independent rapidly (rat)
optogenetically reactivating dentate engram cells tagged during fear conditioning induces freezing, and reactivating a context's engram during fear conditioning creates a false fear memory (mouse)
prefrontal engram cells for remote contextual fear form during learning and mature with time with support from hippocampal engram cells, which gradually become silent (mouse)
input from the hippocampal–entorhinal network helps generate prefrontal engram cells for remote contextual fear memory during learning (mouse)
genetically inactivating CA2 pyramidal neurons causes a pronounced loss of social memory without changing sociability or spatial and contextual memory (mouse)
time cells encode successive moments during a gap between key events, bridging discontiguous events in memory (rat)
chronic antidepressants increase adult hippocampal neurogenesis; fluoxetine has no neurogenic effect in serotonin 1A receptor null mice (mouse)

disrupting antidepressant-induced neurogenesis blocks behavioral responses to antidepressants, but increasing neurogenesis alone does not produce an antidepressant- or anxiolytic-like response (mouse)
hippocampal volumes are smaller after recurrent major depression, and the reduction correlates with its total duration (human)

in monozygotic twins discordant for trauma exposure, PTSD severity correlated with smaller hippocampi in both the exposed twin and the unexposed co-twin, evidence that smaller hippocampi are a risk factor for stress-related psychopathology (human)
neurofibrillary changes begin in the transentorhinal region and then involve the entorhinal cortex proper, and layer II entorhinal neurons are already 60% fewer in very mild disease (human)
pathology of the subiculum and entorhinal layers II and IV isolates the hippocampal formation from much of its input and output and probably contributes to the memory disorder (human)
loss of recent memory follows bilateral hippocampal lesions; a lesion limited to CA1 caused marked anterograde amnesia (human)

the lateral amygdala is a major subcortical target of the auditory thalamus; fear conditioning potentiates this input and increases the shortest-latency tone responses of lateral amygdala neurons (rat)
links.note: Destroying either the direct thalamo-amygdala or the thalamo-cortico-amygdala pathway alone leaves auditory fear conditioning intact; destroying both disrupts it (romanski1992).

links.rel: during fear expression the lateral amygdala is thought to engage the central nucleus (rat); fear conditioning induces cell-specific plasticity of lateral amygdala inputs onto inhibitory neurons of the lateral central amygdala (mouse)
stimulating basolateral terminals in the central amygdala reduces anxiety-related behavior, and basolateral neurons projecting to the centromedial amygdala support negative reinforcement (mouse)
intercalated cells receive information about the conditioned stimulus from the basolateral amygdala (rat)
inhibitory projections to the central nucleus that could reduce the impact of basolateral input after extinction (rat)
an inhibitory pathway to the ventrolateral PAG produces freezing (mouse); midbrain central gray lesions disrupt conditioned freezing but not the arterial pressure response (rat)
lesions of the lateral hypothalamic area, a central amygdala target, interfere with the conditioned arterial pressure response but not freezing (rat)

stimulating hypothalamic oxytocin axons activates a local GABAergic circuit that inhibits neurons in the central amygdala output region (in vitro), and evoked oxytocin release there decreases freezing; oxytocin reduces freezing without affecting the cardiovascular response (rat)
intranasal oxytocin reduces amygdala activation by fear-inducing visual stimuli and the amygdala's coupling to brainstem regions implicated in fear (human)
mice work to earn stimulation of basolateral inputs to the accumbens, which requires accumbal D1 receptors, and accumbens-projecting basolateral neurons support positive reinforcement (mouse)
monosynaptic glutamatergic input to ventral hippocampal pyramidal neurons; activating it increases anxiety-related behavior and inhibiting it decreases it (mouse)
firing is directed mainly from the amygdala to prelimbic cortex during a shock cue, and stimulating this projection increases freezing while inhibiting it reduces freezing (rat)

lesions interfere with auditory fear conditioning, and pairing a tone with optogenetic activation of lateral amygdala pyramidal neurons makes the tone elicit fear (rat); deleting, after learning, the lateral amygdala neurons that overexpressed CREB blocks expression of the memory (mouse)

needed for acquiring and expressing conditioned fear (rat); lateral central amygdala activity is required for acquisition and medial output neurons drive conditioned fear responses (mouse); lesions reduce fear-related behavior (monkey)

bilateral lesions reduce fear-related behavior and freezing toward a human intruder and lower cerebrospinal fluid CRF and plasma ACTH, suggesting a role in fear- and anxiety-related behavioral and pituitary–adrenal responses (monkey)
links.note: The same lesions did not change asymmetric frontal brain electrical activity (kalin2004).

links.rel: partial lesions of intercalated cells impair the expression of fear extinction, more the fewer intercalated neurons survive (rat)

transitions between high fear (renewal) and low fear (extinction) are triggered by a switch in the balance of activity between two populations of basal amygdala neurons, and inactivating the basal amygdala prevents them; inhibiting centromedial-projecting basolateral neurons impairs fear conditioning (mouse)

fear conditioning potentiates thalamic input to the lateral amygdala and drives AMPA receptors into its synapses; blocking that delivery reduces the memory, and optogenetic LTD of auditory inputs inactivates it while LTP reactivates it (rat)

changing CREB function alters the probability that lateral amygdala neurons are recruited into a fear memory, and deleting, after learning, the neurons that overexpressed CREB blocks expression of the memory (mouse)
activating SOM+ neurons of the lateral central amygdala drives fear responses and is needed for recall, and activating SOM+ central amygdala neurons initiates freezing (mouse)
CRF+ central amygdala neurons mediate conditioned flight, competing with SOM+ neurons that initiate freezing (mouse)
probably the CEl 'off' units, inhibited by the conditioned stimulus, of an inhibitory microcircuit that gates central amygdala output to control conditioned freezing (mouse)
activated by diverse anorexigenic signals, required for them to inhibit feeding, and suppress food intake when activated (mouse)

accumbens-projecting neurons support positive and centromedial-projecting neurons negative reinforcement, and two genetically distinct populations take part in positive- and negative-valence behaviors (mouse)

distinct populations of neurons encode the positive and negative values of images (monkey), and two people with focal bilateral lesions showed a dramatic reduction in loss aversion in monetary gambles (human)

excitotoxic lesions impair choices after a food is devalued but not object reversal learning (monkey); its role in stimulus–reward learning might be as important as its role in fear conditioning (review)

the basolateral complex mediates the memory-modulating effects of adrenal stress hormones (review), and blocking protein synthesis in the lateral and basal amygdala after a fear memory is reactivated causes amnesia (rat)
a patient with selective bilateral damage was impaired at recognizing fear in faces, and in patient SM impaired fear recognition stems from not making normal use of the eye region of faces (human)
a GABAergic subpopulation promotes aggression and two other social behaviors, whereas neighboring glutamatergic neurons promote self-grooming and inhibit social interactions (mouse)
exaggerated amygdala responses to masked fearful faces in veterans with PTSD, and greater amygdala activity in PTSD across imaging studies (meta-analysis) (human)
greater amygdala activity in social anxiety disorder and specific phobia than in comparison subjects (meta-analysis, human)
larger amygdalae in boys with autism aged 7.5 to 12.5 years but not in adolescents, because the typical age-related increase in volume is missing (human)
hypoactivation of the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, and of the dorsal and rostral anterior cingulate, in PTSD but not in social anxiety disorder or specific phobia (meta-analysis, human)

retinal input reaches V1 through the lateral geniculate; in primates its parvocellular and magnocellular subdivisions, which differ already in the retina in colour selectivity, contrast sensitivity, temporal properties and spatial resolution, and a third, koniocellular channel are likely to carry different aspects of the image (review)

geniculate neurons connect monosynaptically to simple cells of matching on or off signature (cat); koniocellular layers relay short-wavelength cone input to the blobs and low-acuity input to layer I (review); monocular deprivation alters geniculocortical as well as intracortical connections (mouse)

the specificity of geniculate connections implies that simple receptive fields and their orientation selectivity are laid down at the first thalamocortical synapse, and the orientation tuning of geniculate input to simple cells survives inactivation of the cortex (cat)
sharpening orientation tuning by activating PV+ interneurons improved orientation discrimination (mouse)
activating PV+ interneurons sharpens orientation tuning and direction selectivity, whereas activating SOM+ or VIP+ interneurons does not (mouse)
excited preferentially by horizontal cortical axons, SOM+ interneurons contribute to the surround suppression of pyramidal cells (mouse)
nicotinic input from the basal forebrain largely mediates the activation of VIP interneurons by locomotion (mouse)
activating VIP interneurons increases V1 visual responses, and damaging them abolishes the enhancement of those responses by locomotion (mouse)
layer 2/3 neurons respond to mismatch between actual and expected visual flow during locomotion, suggesting predictive coding (mouse)
nearly half of V1 neurons combine visual speed and run speed during virtual navigation (mouse)
in the monkey, V1 and V2 feed area V5 (MT)
in the monkey, V1 and V2 feed area V4
the ventral stream runs from striate to inferotemporal cortex and is proposed to play the major role in identifying objects (review)
the dorsal stream runs from striate to posterior parietal cortex and is proposed to mediate the sensorimotor transformations for visually guided action (review)
V1 projects to 15 cortical fields, at least nine of them distinct areas with complete maps of the visual field (mouse)
stimulating a frontal eye field site below saccade threshold enhances the visual responses of V4 neurons at the corresponding location and can suppress them at non-corresponding locations (monkey)

amygdala damage abolishes the larger response of fusiform and occipital cortex to fearful than to neutral faces, and the fusiform emotional response is parametrically related to the extent of the damage (human)
motion perception: MT lesions raise motion but not contrast thresholds and most MT neurons match the animal's sensitivity to motion (monkey), and visual motion activates V5 (human)
colour activates area V4 in the lingual and fusiform gyri (human)
attention filters unattended stimuli from the receptive fields of V4 neurons (monkey), and frontal eye field stimulation enhances V4 responses at the corresponding location (monkey)

object recognition: the ventral stream to inferotemporal cortex is proposed to play the major role in identifying objects (review), and many inferotemporal neurons are selective for shape, colour or texture (monkey)
a population of inferotemporal neurons responds selectively to faces, depending on the configuration of facial features (monkey)
more active for faces than for objects, houses or hands and for intact than scrambled faces (human)

visually guided action: the dorsal stream is proposed to mediate the sensorimotor transformations for visually guided actions such as grasping (review), and a patient who could not perceive object shape, size and orientation grasped the objects accurately (human)
spatial localization: a dot-location matching task activated lateral superior parietal cortex (human)
each area encodes a distinct combination of spatiotemporal features, perhaps forming motion- and pattern-related groups (mouse)

after a restricted occipital ablation some visual capacity remains in the hemianopic field, and some patients with extensive V1 damage can point or make saccades toward stimuli in the blind field (human)
koniocellular geniculate neurons that innervate extrastriate cortex are likely to sustain some visual behaviours in the absence of V1 (review)
in the early blind, Braille reading activates primary visual cortex, and occipital magnetic stimulation disrupts it (human)

disrupting one isoform of glutamic acid decarboxylase prevents the loss of responses to a deprived eye and benzodiazepines restore it; a threshold level of inhibition may trigger the critical period (mouse)
perineuronal nets form as the critical period ends, and degrading their proteoglycans lets monocular deprivation shift ocular dominance in adults (rat)

early experimental strabismus or anisometropia often causes amblyopia, with reduced cortical binocularity and, in severe cases, lower spatial resolution of neurons driven by the amblyopic eye (monkey)
during visual aura in three people, changes with the characteristics of cortical spreading depression start in area V3A and spread over occipital cortex in register with the percept (human)
five patients had a progressive dementia heralded by disorders of higher visual function, with predominant parieto-occipital atrophy on imaging in two of them (human)
bilateral damage attributed to the lateral temporo-occipital cortex disturbed movement vision in a rather pure form (human)
extrastriate areas concerned mainly with spatial vision, visual motion and the peripheral field project to the pontine nuclei, but areas for object identification and central vision do not (monkey)
only a few corticopontine cells, in the part of area 17 that represents the lower peripheral visual field (monkey)
the thalamic taste area, the parvicellular ventral posteromedial nucleus, projects to insular-opercular cortex (review)

the insula connects with the lateral, basolateral, central, cortical and medial amygdaloid nuclei (review), giving somatosensory, auditory, gustatory, olfactory and visceral sensations a route to the limbic system (monkey)

sweet- and bitter-responsive taste cortex project to distinct parts of the amygdala; manipulating these inputs imposes or reverses taste valence, and silencing amygdala neurons abolishes valence-related behaviour but not taste discrimination (mouse)

direct excitatory projection to the lateral central amygdala; inhibiting it prevents learning to withhold licking for an aversive taste, and activating it suppresses licking and can instruct avoidance (mouse)
the posterior insula projection to the central amygdala mediates anxiety-related behaviours (mouse)
an accumbens-projecting posterior insula pathway regulates feeding upon changes in bodily state (mouse)

hunger signals from hypothalamic AgRP neurons reach insular cortex via the paraventricular thalamus and basolateral amygdala (mouse), and insular cortex appears to combine visceral signals with this hypothalamus-gated amygdala input (mouse)
at rest the anterior insula is coupled with the anterior cingulate cortex (human), and a right fronto-insular and anterior cingulate network is activated by salient events (human)
the orbital frontoinsular cortex anchors the salience network with the dorsal anterior cingulate (human), and the anterior insula is proposed as its hub (review)
the dorsal anterior cingulate is the other anchor of the salience network, and its connectivity correlates with prescan anxiety (human)

Granger causality analysis indicates that the right fronto-insular cortex drives switching between the central-executive and default-mode networks (human); the network is proposed to give salient events access to attention and working memory (review)

right anterior insula activity predicts the accuracy of heartbeat detection, and its gray matter volume correlates with interoceptive accuracy and visceral awareness (human); proposed to re-represent interoception as a basis for feelings (review)
graded cooling activates the dorsal margin of the middle/posterior insula, which the authors consider an interoceptive area of limbic sensory cortex (human)

neurons expressing a given receptor converge on one or a few glomeruli at positions constant across individuals (rat), two fixed loci among about 1800 in the mouse bulb (mouse), forming a fine spatial map (mouse)
axons from individual glomeruli project diffusely across piriform cortex, and piriform neurons sample the whole bulb without obvious spatial bias (mouse)
projections from individual glomeruli form spatially stereotyped patches in the cortical amygdala, which prefers dorsal bulb input (mouse)

reciprocal dendrodendritic synapses: mitral glutamate excites granule dendrites, which return NMDA receptor-dependent GABAergic inhibition that can mediate lateral inhibition between mitral cells (rat)
individual olfactory cortex neurons receive input from multiple mitral cells representing broadly distributed glomeruli (mouse)
olfactory bulb signals reach the lateroposterior orbitofrontal cortex through the anterior piriform cortex (probably with the medial amygdala) and the hypothalamus, not the thalamus (monkey)

a visuo-motor centre that regulates visuomotor behaviour (octopus)
thought to receive input from the olfactory organ (octopus)

gustatory projections are segregated by taste category and by body location (fly), and Gr5a cells respond to sugars and Gr66a cells to bitter compounds (fly)

a pair of subesophageal motor neurons controls a subprogram of a simple taste behaviour (fly)

sugar- and bitter-sensing taste cells drive acceptance or avoidance (fly), the gustatory connectome traces complete pathways from them to feeding motor neurons (fly), and a connectome-based model predicts the neurons that respond to tastes and are required for feeding initiation (fly)

the whole-brain connectome traces synaptic pathways from a subset of photoreceptors to descending motor pathways (fly)

supply dopamine to the mushroom body: 20 types, each confined to one or at most two compartments (fly); the 12 PPL1 neurons carry aversive reinforcement to the vertical lobes and heel (fly)

express the amnesiac gene product strongly (fly)

leucokinin acts through LkR in the fan-shaped body and clock-associated circuits to regulate sleep and post-feeding water balance (fly)
Allatostatin A acts through AstA-R1 to inhibit sugar-sensing dopaminergic neurons, terminating feeding and switching flies to foraging locomotion (fly)
drosulfakinin stimulates DskR1 on insulin-producing cells to trigger insulin-like peptide release and promote satiety (fly)
insulin-producing cells synthesize and secrete DILP2, DILP3, and DILP5 (fly)
circulating and centrally released DILPs act on InR in the fan-shaped body to modulate metabolic sleep and nutrient homeostasis (fly)
adipokinetic hormone acts on AKHR in gnathal ganglion circuits to promote food search and taste responsiveness (fly)
adenosine receptor AdoR in neurons and glia mediates purinergic homeostatic sleep regulation and metabolic stress resistance (fly)
nitric oxide cotransmission in mushroom body dopamine neurons regulates memory decay and updating (fly)
retrograde carbon monoxide from Kenyon cells regulates on-demand dopamine release during memory formation (fly)
short neuropeptide F presynaptically sensitizes olfactory receptor neurons during hunger (fly)
SIFamide hub neurons arbitrate competing reward and metabolic priorities between feeding and mating (fly)
pigment-dispersing factor sets circadian phase and paces morning locomotor anticipation (fly)
fast histaminergic transmission from photoreceptors to lamina neurons initiates visual processing (fly)
tyramine signaling regulates motor program switching and flight initiation (fly)
tachykinin modulates male-male aggressive encounters (fly)
leucokinin coordinates postprandial satiety and meal termination (fly)
drosulfakinin signaling induces satiety and suppresses meal consumption (fly)
insulin-like peptides coordinate nutrient satiety and metabolic energy balance (fly)
adipokinetic hormone mobilizes energy stores and stimulates hungry food search (fly)
purinergic signaling via AdoR regulates sleep depth and homeostatic sleep pressure (fly)
dopaminergic projections from protocerebral clusters innervate the central complex ellipsoid body to modulate locomotor arousal and sleep (Drosophila)
nitric oxide synthase (NOS)-expressing dopamine neurons project axons toward the lateral horn and superior protocerebrum (Drosophila)
serotonergic afferents supply the central complex ellipsoid body to regulate visual pattern memory and sleep architecture (Drosophila)
tyraminergic descending pathways from gnathal ganglia coordinate locomotor gait switching and flight in the ventral nerve cord, distinct from octopamine (Drosophila)
histaminergic transmission from photoreceptor axons terminates in the lamina and outer medulla to mediate fast visual contrast detection (Drosophila)
SIFamide hub neurons in the pars intercerebralis send wide arborizations to the antennal lobe to modulate odor sensitivity during starvation (Drosophila)
SIFamide hub neurons project throughout the central complex to bias behavioral prioritization toward feeding over courtship (Drosophila)
pigment-dispersing factor (PDF) from ventrolateral clock pacemakers signals to central complex ring neurons to pace morning locomotor anticipation (Drosophila)
PDF transmission from clock neurons modulates fan-shaped body dorsal neurons to gate sleep and arousal rhythms (Drosophila)
tachykininergic projection pathways from antennal lobe local interneurons modulate innate odor processing in the lateral horn (Drosophila)
leucokinergic neurons projecting to the fan-shaped body coordinate context-dependent post-feeding sleep and water balance (Drosophila)
insulin-producing cells (IPCs) secrete DILPs to modulate metabolic sleep and energy state in the fan-shaped body (Drosophila)
protocerebral dopamine clusters (PPM3/PAM) innervate dorsal layers of the fan-shaped body to gate sleep-wake homeostasis and courtship arousal (Drosophila)
serotonergic widefield protocerebral neurons extend dense arborizations into the antennal lobe to tune presynaptic olfactory gain and behavioral sensitivity (Drosophila)
drosulfakinin (DSK) peptidergic hub transmission from pars intercerebralis projects to subesophageal feeding motor networks to terminate feeding and signal satiety (Drosophila)
short neuropeptide F (sNPF) transmission from local and projection neurons signals to mushroom body calyces to enhance hunger-dependent food odor attraction (Drosophila)
allatostatin-A (AstA) inhibitory peptidergic afferents from the lateral protocerebrum innervate the central complex ellipsoid body to suppress foraging and promote quiescence (Drosophila)
Kenyon cells produce diffusible carbon monoxide (CO) via heme oxygenase to act as a retrograde messenger regulating presynaptic dopaminergic release and memory longevity (Drosophila)
adenosine signaling through AdoR modulates visual compass ring neuron transmission between the anterior optic tubercle and ellipsoid body (Drosophila)
optic lobe projection neurons send retinotopically organized axons through the optic tract toward the central brain (octopus)
the optic tract delivers processed visual signals into the superior frontal lobe to initiate visual memory storage (octopus)
optic tract collaterals innervate anterior and lateral basal lobes to drive rapid visually guided motor orienting and camouflage (octopus)
optic lobe cholinergic interneurons project to the peduncle lobe for visuomotor integration and compensatory eye movements (octopus)
vertical lobe large output neurons project through the subvertical tract into the subvertical lobe to convey consolidated memory signals (octopus)
the subvertical lobe relays learning-derived executive decisions to anterior and median basal motor control centers via dopaminergic projections (octopus)
median superior frontal axons send direct collateral projections to the subvertical lobe bypassing the vertical lobe matrix (octopus)
anterior and median basal lobes project to the pedal lobe to command funnel steering and jet-propulsion locomotion (octopus)
anterior basal motor pathways project to the brachial lobe to direct goal-oriented arm extension and sucker grasping via dopamine (octopus)
subvertical lobe descending tracts innervate the palliovisceral lobe to modulate autonomic tone, respiration and mantle pumping (octopus)
reciprocal tracts link the pedal and palliovisceral subesophageal motor centers to coordinate jetting with mantle cavity contraction (octopus)
subesophageal tracts connect the pedal and brachial lobes to synchronize crawling gait and sucker adhesion with mantle movement (octopus)
brachial lobe motor neurons descend along the cerebrobrachial tracts into axial nerve cords of the eight arms with tyraminergic modulation (octopus)
axial arm nerve cords send ascending sensory and proprioceptive fibers back into the central brachial lobe (octopus)
brachial lobe sensory relays ascend into the inferior frontal lobe chemotactile learning matrix (octopus)
associative inter-lobe tracts link the inferior frontal tactile system with the superior frontal visual system (octopus)
inferior frontal output tracts innervate anterior basal motor centers to trigger arm grasping or tactile avoidance (octopus)
inferior frontal learning outputs project to the subvertical lobe for tactile memory consolidation (octopus)
inferior frontal lobe projects to the superior buccal lobe to initiate beak biting and radula rasping upon food recognition (octopus)
subpedunculate and peduncle complex fibers supply inhibitory FMRFamide-related neuropeptides to the optic gland to halt premature reproduction and senescence (octopus)
subvertical lobe neuroendocrine fibers reach the optic gland to modulate hormonal release during sexual maturation (octopus)
anterior and median basal lobes project to the palliovisceral lobe to drive dynamic chromatophore skin patterning during active sleep and camouflage (octopus)
large output neurons of the vertical lobe converge their axons to project into the subvertical lobe (octopus)
subpedunculate and peduncle lobe fibers express FMRFamide-related neuropeptides that tonically inhibit optic gland secretion (octopus)
median superior frontal lobe terminals synthesize and release glutamate to excite vertical lobe amacrine interneurons (octopus)

septal cholinergic input selectively suppresses recurrent CA3-CA3 associative collateral transmission via presynaptic muscarinic M4 receptors while preserving mossy fiber afferents, preventing interference and promoting encoding of novel spatial info (rodent)
cholinergic and GABAergic septal inputs to the dentate gyrus modulate granule cell excitability and pattern separation (mouse)
cholinergic innervation of the subiculum modulates hippocampal output gating to the mammillary bodies, thalamus, and prefrontal cortex (rodent)
septal cholinergic and GABAergic fibers to the medial entorhinal area pace grid cell theta firing and maintain spatial representation stability (mouse, rat)
CA1 pyramidal neurons project topographically to the dorsal and intermediate lateral septum, conveying spatial contextual representations (rodent)
subiculum efferents innervate the lateral septum to link hippocampal output with septal motivational and autonomic stations (rodent)
mesolimbic dopaminergic fibers from the VTA innervate the medial septum, acting on D1/D2 receptors to modulate theta rhythm power and exploratory locomotion (rodent)
locus coeruleus noradrenergic terminals innervate the basal forebrain, depolarizing cholinergic neurons via alpha1 and beta adrenoceptors to promote cortical arousal and wakefulness (rodent)
dorsal raphe serotonergic axons innervate basal forebrain cholinergic neurons, hyperpolarizing them via 5-HT1A receptors to modulate sleep-wake transitions (rodent)
subsecond acetylcholine transients in prelimbic cortex time cue detection in sustained attention tasks; optogenetic cholinergic activation improves attentional accuracy (mouse, rat)
cholinergic innervation of infralimbic cortex gates extinction learning and behavioral flexibility (rodent)
cholinergic input to anterior cingulate cortex signals attentional effort, error monitoring, and unexpected reward/punishment (mouse, primate)
cholinergic innervation of orbitofrontal cortex modulates outcome expectancy, value updating, and reversal learning (rodent, primate)

layer 5/6 pyramidal neurons of prelimbic cortex project top-down to substantia innominata and nucleus basalis, exerting executive control over cholinergic arousal and cue-directed attention (rat, mouse)
anterior cingulate cortex sends top-down projections to the basal forebrain to drive cholinergic transients during effortful cognitive control (rodent)
medial prefrontal cortex sends descending glutamatergic projections to the basal forebrain to modulate cholinergic and non-cholinergic projection neurons (mouse, rat)
cholinergic input from nucleus basalis to primary motor cortex is required for motor skill learning and map plasticity (rat, mouse)
cholinergic projections to primary somatosensory cortex enhance sensory acuity and tune whisker-barrel receptive fields (mouse, rat)

chains.name: Cerebro-cerebellar loop
chains.desc: Prefrontal cortex → pontine nuclei → cerebellar cortex → nuclei → thalamus → prefrontal cortex: the closed loop behind nonmotor cerebellar functions.

chains.name: Climbing fibers teach motor learning
chains.desc: The classic Marr–Albus–Ito chain. The final step (LTD is necessary for learning) is debated.

chains.name: Autism gene → Purkinje → mPFC circuit
chains.desc: Purkinje-cell Tsc1 loss and Crus I → nuclei → VM thalamus → mPFC circuits regulate social behavior in mice.

chains.name: Reward signals → VTA → social behavior
chains.desc: Climbing fibers signal reward; the nuclei excite VTA. Whether cerebellar reward signals shape this output is untested.

chains.name: Vermis → fastigial → PAG fear circuit
chains.desc: Fastigial neurons projecting to ventrolateral PAG control the strength of fear memories.

chains.name: Cerebellar plasticity shapes place cells
chains.desc: PKC-dependent Purkinje-cell plasticity is needed for hippocampal place coding from self-motion cues; the pathway between them is not mapped.

chains.name: Gut → anterior DCN → striatal dopamine → satiation
chains.desc: Discovered by reverse translation from Prader–Willi syndrome; both the afferent route and the route to striatal dopamine are unknown.

chains.name: Cerebellum–DLPFC network in schizophrenia
chains.desc: Cerebellum–right DLPFC connectivity tracks negative symptoms; TMS that restores it reduces them.

chains.name: Dentate → striatum in dystonia
chains.desc: A short-latency dentate → thalamus → striatum path relays aberrant cerebellar activity that causes dystonia in mice.

chains.name: D1R+ nuclear neurons and executive function
chains.desc: A dopamine-receptive population in the lateral nucleus supports working memory and response inhibition.

chains.name: Essential tremor: unpruned climbing fibers
chains.desc: Too little GluD2 leaves surplus climbing fibers unpruned. The extra climbing fiber–Purkinje synapses drive cerebellar oscillations that generate tremor (mice and patient tissue).

chains.name: Cerebellum → substantia nigra → striatal dopamine
chains.desc: Cerebellar nuclei excite nigral dopamine neurons monosynaptically, raising striatal dopamine and locomotion. The pathway is active before movement and for reward.

chains.name: Exercise → dentate → amygdala → less anxiety
chains.desc: Rotarod exercise engages glutamatergic dentate neurons that drive PKCδ+ amygdala neurons and reduce anxiety (mouse).

chains.name: SCN2A → granule-cell LTP → VOR learning
chains.desc: Losing NaV1.2 in granule cells weakens high-frequency transmission and LTP at parallel fiber–Purkinje synapses, and the VOR becomes hypersensitive. Seen in mice and in children with SCN2A loss-of-function variants; raising Scn2a expression rescued VOR plasticity in mice.

chains.name: Rhombic-lip origins of medulloblastoma
chains.desc: Atoh1 specifies the glutamatergic rhombic-lip lineage, which is expanded in humans. Group 3 and 4 medulloblastomas carry signatures of this lineage, and Group 4 tumors resemble rhombic-lip progenitors stalled in development.

chains.name: Climbing-fiber disinhibition gates learning
chains.desc: Synchronous climbing fibers excite MLI2 interneurons, which silence MLI1s and disinhibit Purkinje dendrites. The larger calcium signal permits LTD and learning.

chains.name: Noradrenaline, glia and pain
chains.desc: Noxious stimuli release noradrenaline from locus coeruleus terminals in the cerebellar cortex. Bergmann glia respond through α1-adrenergic receptors, and this glial signaling promotes nocifensive behavior and neuropathic pain (mouse).

chains.name: Stress-triggered ataxia attacks
chains.desc: In tottering mice, a model of episodic ataxia type 2, stress-released noradrenaline acts on Purkinje-cell α1-adrenergic receptors and, through casein kinase 2, disrupts pacemaking. The erratic firing triggers attacks; blocking the cascade prevents them.

chains.name: Olivary CRF
chains.desc: Inferior-olive neurons express very high levels of CRF. CRF-expressing olivary neurons excite glutamatergic interpositus neurons through CRF1 and CRF2 receptors, and olivo-cerebellar CRF deficiency causes motor deficits.

chains.name: Endocannabinoids and LTD
chains.desc: Purkinje cells release the endocannabinoid 2-AG, which acts retrogradely on presynaptic CB1 receptors; parallel-fiber LTD requires both.

chains.name: From cortical layers to the spinal cord
chains.desc: Layer 2/3 neurons drive layer 5 pyramidal-tract neurons, whose corticospinal axons contact spinal premotor interneurons needed for skilled reaching (mouse).

chains.name: From plan to command
chains.desc: Preparatory activity underlies motor planning; in mice, two types of pyramidal-tract neuron carry it at different times: the type projecting to the thalamus early, the type projecting to the medulla late, together with motor commands.

chains.name: ALM–thalamus loop
chains.desc: ALM and the thalamus are connected in both directions, and photoinhibiting either diminishes activity in the other, suggesting that the persistent preparatory activity behind motor planning requires reciprocal excitation across areas (mouse).

chains.name: Go cue → movement
chains.desc: Ascending glutamatergic neurons of the midbrain reticular and pedunculopontine nuclei show short-latency, phasic changes in firing selective for an auditory Go cue; the signal reaches motor cortex via the thalamus and switches it from planning-related activity to a motor command (mouse).

chains.name: Spines as skill memories
chains.desc: Somatostatin interneurons regulate learning-related spine changes on layer 2/3 dendrites, and new spines stabilized during training are associated with durable skill memory (mouse).

chains.name: Dopamine and skill learning
chains.desc: In rat M1, dopamine acting on D1/D2 receptors supports LTP, and LTP-like strengthening of synapses accompanies skill learning.

chains.name: Building and repairing the corticospinal tract
chains.desc: Fezl is needed for Ctip2 expression, and Ctip2 for corticospinal axons to reach the spinal cord (mouse); after spinal cord injury these axons regenerate poorly, which Pten deletion partly overcomes in mice.

chains.name: Reading out motor cortex after paralysis
chains.desc: Movement intentions still modulate motor cortex years after spinal cord injury and can be decoded to control devices or produce text (human pilot studies).

chains.name: Map plasticity and stroke recovery
chains.desc: BDNF val66met carriers show less training-dependent map reorganization (human), and rehabilitative training preserves the hand map beside an infarct (monkey).

chains.name: Cerebellar input to motor cortex
chains.desc: Cerebellar nuclear output reaches motor cortex through the thalamus, where thalamic input drives inhibitory cells through GluR2-lacking AMPA receptors and PV interneurons fire before pyramidal cells (monkey).

chains.name: COMT, dopamine and working memory
chains.desc: A common COMT variant accounts for a four-fold variation in the enzyme's activity and in dopamine breakdown (human); D1-receptor stimulation tunes delay activity along an inverted U (monkey); and delay activity is one proposed store of working memory, although whether sustained firing holds the memory is debated.

chains.name: Noradrenaline, HCN channels and working memory
chains.desc: α2A adrenoceptors inhibit cAMP and close HCN channels, which strengthens the delay firing of prefrontal networks; blocking HCN1 channels in PFC improved working memory (monkeys and rats).

chains.name: Mediodorsal thalamus and medial PFC
chains.desc: Mediodorsal thalamic input sustains medial prefrontal delay activity, and inhibiting mediodorsal or hippocampal input to medial PFC, or its somatostatin interneurons, impairs spatial working memory (mouse).

chains.name: Interneurons, gamma and working memory
chains.desc: Inhibiting parvalbumin interneurons suppresses gamma rhythms, and driving them generates gamma (mouse neocortex); gamma bursts and synchrony accompany working memory (monkey, mouse). A review links reduced GABA synthesis in these interneurons, through weaker gamma synchrony, to working-memory deficits in schizophrenia.

chains.name: Amygdala → prelimbic cortex → fear
chains.desc: Proposed: prelimbic cortex turns brief amygdala responses to a tone into the sustained output that drives freezing; inactivating prelimbic cortex impairs fear expression (rat).

chains.name: Ketamine and prefrontal spines
chains.desc: Ketamine builds spine synapses on prefrontal neurons (rat, mouse), and loss of these spines accompanies depression-related behavior (mouse).

chains.name: Value in the orbitofrontal cortex
chains.desc: Orbitofrontal neurons encode the value of offered and chosen goods (monkey), a candidate basis for economic choice.

chains.name: Dentate → thalamus → prefrontal cortex
chains.desc: Dentate output reaches prefrontal area 46 through the thalamus (monkey), one route by which the cerebellum could reach prefrontal control circuits.

chains.name: Direct pathway
chains.desc: Striatal neurons of the direct pathway (substance P; D1 receptors in rats) project to the internal pallidum, whose output reaches the thalamus of the basal ganglia–thalamocortical motor circuit. In a proposed model, this pathway disinhibits the thalamic and cortical targets of the selected motor program.

chains.name: Indirect pathway
chains.desc: Striatopallidal neurons (enkephalin; D2 receptors in rats) project to the external pallidum, whose prototypic neurons target the subthalamic nucleus (rat), which in turn excites the internal pallidum. In the classic model, selective impairment of these striatal neurons is postulated to cause hyperkinetic disorders, and in Huntington disease they are much more affected in early and middle stages than substance P neurons projecting to the internal pallidum (post-mortem).

chains.name: Hyperdirect pathway
chains.desc: Motor-related cortical areas excite the subthalamic nucleus, which excites the pallidum, bypassing the striatum with a shorter conduction time than the paths through it. A proposed center–surround model has this signal first inhibit large areas of thalamus and cortex, before the direct pathway releases only the selected motor program.

chains.name: Reward prediction error → learning
chains.desc: The fluctuating output of primate dopamine neurons apparently signals errors in reward prediction, and in rats, activating dopamine neurons at the moment of reward, mimicking such an error, is sufficient for long-lasting increases in cue-elicited reward seeking.

chains.name: Nigral dopamine → corticostriatal plasticity
chains.desc: Stimulating the substantia nigra with the parameters optimal for self-stimulation potentiates corticostriatal synapses through dopamine receptors, and the amount of potentiation correlated with the time the rats took to learn; the authors propose that this potentiation reinforces the learned action (rat).

chains.name: Limbic → motor striatal spiral
chains.desc: In monkeys, the ventromedial (limbic) striatum projects widely onto midbrain dopamine cells, and the dorsolateral striatum receives input from a broad expanse of them; across these striatonigrostriatal connections the shell influences the core, the core the central striatum and the central striatum the dorsolateral striatum, an anatomical basis for a limbic–cognitive–motor interface.

chains.name: Striatum → nigra → colliculus (saccades)
chains.desc: Striatonigral neurons project to the substantia nigra pars reticulata, which holds saccade-related cells of the superior colliculus under tonic GABA-mediated inhibition; muscimol in the pars reticulata releases irrepressible saccades (monkey).

chains.name: Parkinson's disease and the subthalamic nucleus
chains.desc: Parkinson's disease results from a loss of nigral dopamine neurons. Excessive subthalamic activity is implicated in its motor signs: lesioning the subthalamic nucleus reduces akinesia, rigidity and tremor in MPTP-treated monkeys, and stimulating it improves motor scores in patients, an effect that in parkinsonian rodents can be accounted for by stimulating its afferent axons.

chains.name: Huntington's disease
chains.desc: The Huntington's disease mutation is an expanded, unstable CAG repeat in the IT15 gene on 4p16.3. In the disease, enkephalin-containing striatal neurons projecting to the external pallidum are much more affected in early and middle stages than substance P neurons projecting to the internal pallidum (post-mortem), and impairment of these neurons is postulated to cause hyperkinetic disorders.

chains.name: Indirect pathway → subthalamic nucleus → cerebellum
chains.desc: The indirect pathway runs from striatopallidal neurons through the external pallidum to the subthalamic nucleus, which also reaches the cerebellar cortex disynaptically through the pontine nuclei (monkey), one of the disynaptic projections that link the basal ganglia and cerebellum.

chains.name: Trisynaptic pathway
chains.desc: Entorhinal cortex → dentate gyrus → CA3 → CA1: the classic route through the hippocampus. The perforant path from entorhinal layer II is the major source of excitatory input to the hippocampus, and CA1 is the main hippocampal output.

chains.name: Septal theta and grid cells
chains.desc: Inactivating the medial septum reduces theta oscillations, and entorhinal grid cells then lose their spatial periodicity while head-direction cells keep their selectivity (rat). Grid cells tile the environment and may form a path-integration-based map.

chains.name: Replay and consolidation
chains.desc: Place cells that fired together during behavior fire together more in later slow-wave sleep (rat); sharp wave-ripples replay compressed fragments of waking sequences (review), and suppressing them after training impairs spatial memory (rat).

chains.name: NMDA receptors, LTP and spatial memory
chains.desc: Blocking hippocampal NMDA receptors with AP5 suppresses LTP and impairs place learning (rat), and deleting them from CA1 pyramidal cells abolishes CA1 LTP and impairs spatial memory (mouse).

chains.name: Pattern separation in the dentate gyrus
chains.desc: Entorhinal input reaches the dentate gyrus, where minimal changes to an environment alter granule-cell activity patterns (rat) and deleting granule-cell NMDA receptors impairs telling similar contexts apart (mouse).

chains.name: Antidepressants and adult neurogenesis
chains.desc: Chronic antidepressants increase adult hippocampal neurogenesis, and disrupting that neurogenesis blocks their behavioral effects; increasing neurogenesis alone does not produce an antidepressant-like response (mouse).

chains.name: Ventral hippocampus, prefrontal cortex and amygdala
chains.desc: Inhibiting ventral hippocampal input to the medial prefrontal cortex disrupts anxiety-related behavior and theta synchrony (mouse), and medial prefrontal theta input entrains the basolateral amygdala when mice recognize safety.

chains.name: From a tone to freezing
chains.desc: The lateral amygdala is a major subcortical target of the auditory thalamus, and fear conditioning potentiates this input (rat). During fear expression the lateral amygdala is thought to engage the central nucleus, the principal output for conditioned fear (rat), whose inhibitory pathway to the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray produces freezing (mouse).

chains.name: A separate output for blood pressure
chains.desc: Different central amygdala outputs appear to mediate the behavioral and autonomic parts of conditioned fear: lesions of the lateral hypothalamic area interfere with the conditioned arterial pressure response but not freezing (rat).

chains.name: Intercalated cells and extinction
chains.desc: Intercalated cells receive conditioned-stimulus information from the basolateral amygdala and inhibit the central nucleus; after extinction training they could reduce the impact of basolateral input on the central nucleus, and partial lesions impair the expression of extinction (rat).

chains.name: Oxytocin damps freezing
chains.desc: Stimulating hypothalamic oxytocin axons in the central amygdala activates a local GABAergic circuit that inhibits neurons in its output region (in vitro), and evoked oxytocin release there decreases freezing in fear-conditioned rats; oxytocin decreases freezing without affecting the cardiovascular response (rat).

chains.name: Basolateral amygdala to prelimbic cortex
chains.desc: Stimulating the basolateral projection to prelimbic cortex increases freezing (rat), and prelimbic activity tracks freezing second by second; inactivating prelimbic cortex impairs the expression of conditioned fear (rat).

chains.name: Basolateral amygdala to ventral hippocampus
chains.desc: Activating basolateral amygdala synapses in the ventral hippocampus increases anxiety-related behavior (mouse), and ventral CA1 anxiety cells, activated by anxiogenic environments, are required for avoidance (mouse).

chains.name: From the retina to oriented edges
chains.desc: Retinal input reaches V1 through the lateral geniculate nucleus (review). Geniculate neurons connect to simple cells by on or off signature, which implies that orientation selectivity is laid down at the first thalamocortical synapse (cat), and sharpening that tuning by activating PV+ interneurons improves orientation discrimination (mouse).

chains.name: Seeing motion
chains.desc: In the monkey, V1 and V2 feed area MT (V5); MT lesions raise motion thresholds and most MT neurons match the animal's sensitivity to motion (monkey), and motion activates V5 in humans.

chains.name: The ventral stream to faces
chains.desc: The ventral stream runs from striate to inferotemporal cortex and is proposed to play the major role in identifying objects (review), and a population of inferotemporal neurons responds selectively to faces (monkey).

chains.name: Vision for action
chains.desc: The dorsal stream from striate to posterior parietal cortex is proposed to mediate visually guided action (review); a patient who could not perceive the shape, size and orientation of objects grasped them accurately (human).

chains.name: Attention from the frontal eye field
chains.desc: Stimulating a frontal eye field site below saccade threshold enhances V4 responses at the corresponding location (monkey), and attention filters unattended stimuli from the receptive fields of V4 neurons (monkey).

chains.name: Running turns up V1
chains.desc: Locomotion activates VIP interneurons in V1, largely through nicotinic input from the basal forebrain, and these neurons are needed for the enhancement of V1 visual responses by running (mouse).

chains.name: Inhibition and the critical period
chains.desc: Without one isoform of glutamic acid decarboxylase, a deprived eye does not lose its cortical responses, and benzodiazepines restore this plasticity (mouse); abnormal visual experience early in life (experimental strabismus or anisometropia) often causes amblyopia, with reduced cortical binocularity (monkey).

chains.name: Visual cortex to the cerebellum
chains.desc: Extrastriate areas concerned mainly with spatial vision, motion and the peripheral field project to the pontine nuclei (monkey), whose crossed mossy fibers reach the cerebellar cortex.

chains.name: The amygdala and faces
chains.desc: The larger fusiform response to fearful than to neutral faces is absent after amygdala damage (human), and the fusiform face area is selectively involved in face perception (human).

chains.name: From taste to its value
chains.desc: The thalamic taste area projects to insular-opercular cortex (review). Sweet- and bitter-responsive taste cortex projects to distinct parts of the amygdala, and these inputs assign taste valence (mouse); amygdala neurons encode positive and negative values (monkey).

chains.name: The posterior insula and anxiety
chains.desc: The posterior insula projection to the central amygdala mediates anxiety-related behaviours (mouse), and bilateral central amygdala lesions suggest a role for it in fear- and anxiety-related responses (monkey).

chains.name: Hunger reaches the insula
chains.desc: Signals from hypothalamic AgRP hunger neurons reach insular cortex via the paraventricular thalamus and basolateral amygdala and bias insular neurons toward food cues (mouse).

chains.name: Salience and switching
chains.desc: The frontoinsular cortex anchors the salience network with the dorsal anterior cingulate (human), and the right fronto-insular cortex appears to drive switches between the central-executive and default-mode networks (human).

chains.name: From receptor genes to cortex
chains.desc: Odorant receptors, a large gene family expressed in the olfactory epithelium (rat), encode odours combinatorially (mouse); neurons expressing one receptor converge on one or a few glomeruli (rat, mouse), and each glomerulus projects diffusely across piriform cortex (mouse).

chains.name: Innate odour responses
chains.desc: Glomeruli project in stereotyped patches to the cortical amygdala (mouse), and this circuit is necessary for innate aversive and appetitive odour responses (mouse).

chains.name: Learned odour meaning
chains.desc: Glomeruli project diffusely to piriform cortex (mouse), where arbitrary ensembles of neurons can acquire learned appetitive or aversive meaning (mouse).

chains.name: Smell in the orbitofrontal cortex
chains.desc: Olfactory bulb signals reach the lateroposterior orbitofrontal cortex through the anterior piriform cortex and the hypothalamus, and removing that area strikingly impairs odour discrimination (monkey).

chains.name: From the eye to the vertical lobe
chains.desc: Retinal photoreceptors project to the optic lobe, whose fibres reach the superior frontal lobe (HRP tracing); the median superior frontal lobe sends the glutamatergic input of the vertical lobe, whose LTP supports long-term memory (octopus).

chains.name: The vertical lobe's fan-out fan-in network
chains.desc: About 1.8 million input axons from the median superior frontal lobe innervate the amacrine interneurons, most of the lobe's roughly 25 million cells, which converge sharply onto large output neurons; plasticity sits at the input layer in the octopus and at the output layer in the cuttlefish, yet both networks perform the same computation (octopus, cuttlefish).

chains.name: From the eye to an arm
chains.desc: The optic lobe receives retinal input and exchanges fibres with the basal lobes, the higher motor centres, whose stimulation evokes movements without a body map; octopuses use vision to guide a single arm to a goal (octopus).

chains.name: From receptor neurons to learned odour value
chains.desc: Olfactory receptor neurons feed projection neurons in their glomerulus; each Kenyon cell combines a random set of glomerular inputs; Kenyon cells converge onto output neurons in 15 compartments, whose activation drives attraction or repulsion and whose ensemble is suggested to represent valence (fly).

chains.name: Octopamine and dopamine in reward
chains.desc: Octopamine reinforces short-term appetitive memory through mushroom-body-targeted dopamine neurons, partly via their OAMB receptor, and activating a subset of these dopamine neurons can substitute for sugar (fly); PAM-cluster dopamine neurons signal sugar reward (fly).

chains.name: The anterior visual pathway to the compass
chains.desc: Medulla visual projection neurons feed neurons that connect the anterior optic tubercle with ring neurons, whose axons largely form the ellipsoid body; neurons tiling the ellipsoid body encode heading, and its neurons are needed for visual place learning (fly).

chains.name: From the eye to escape
chains.desc: Photoreceptor signals split in the lamina into parallel pathways; L1 and L2 start the ON and OFF pathways to T4 and T5 motion detectors in the lobula plate; LPLC2 looming detectors ramify in the T4/T5 layers and terminate on the giant fibre, which triggers escape take-off (fly).

chains.name: From taste neurons to a taste motor program
chains.desc: Sugar stimulation of gustatory neurons activates, and bitter compounds inhibit, a pair of subesophageal motor neurons that control a subprogram of a simple taste behaviour, with no direct connection from the sensory neurons detected (fly).

chains.name: Sleep and long-term memory
chains.desc: Activating neurons that include dorsal fan-shaped body projections induces sleep, and sleep induced after training that alone does not produce long-term memory lets flies form one (fly).

chains.name: Dopamine writes an odour memory
chains.desc: Dopamine neurons supply dopamine to single mushroom body compartments; acting on Kenyon cells through DopR1, dopamine that follows an odour raises cAMP through rutabaga and depresses that odour’s synapses onto the compartment’s output neurons, which changes the fly’s learned response to the odour (fly).

chains.name: Hunger gates sugar memory
chains.desc: Neuropeptide F, the fly orthologue of NPY, acts on six dopamine neurons of the mushroom body to release the expression of sugar-reward memory in hungry flies (fly).

chains.name: Septohippocampal theta & ripple pacing
chains.desc: Medial septal ChAT/GABA neurons co-transmit acetylcholine and GABA to CA1 pyramidal cells and interneurons, pacing theta rhythms and suppressing sharp-wave ripples; CA1/CA3 output returns topographically to lateral septum.

chains.name: Striato-basal forebrain salience gating
chains.desc: Nucleus accumbens D1 MSNs disinhibit substantia innominata cholinergic neurons to evoke acetylcholine release in the basolateral amygdala during salient cue processing, while D2 MSNs suppress release.

chains.name: Basal forebrain attentional selection
chains.desc: Anterior-medial basal forebrain (horizontal and vertical diagonal band) cholinergic projection to prelimbic prefrontal cortex optimizes attentional focus and cued response execution.

chains.name: Ascending reticular arousal loop
chains.desc: Ascending brainstem and midbrain tegmental arousal projections engage VTA, thalamus, and basal forebrain to modulate cortical default mode network coupling and sustain wakeful awareness.

chains.name: Nitric oxide cotransmission updates mushroom body memory
Kenyon cell retrograde carbon monoxide signaling
ADHD phenotypic dimensions before circuits
chains.desc: Phenotypic dimensions come first: ADHD is heterogeneous, response-time variability can accompany attentional instability, and these dimensions are mapped onto distributed control systems rather than one universal deficit.

chains.name: Control and default-mode interactions
chains.desc: Frontoparietal control and default-mode/task-engaged interactions are candidate network mechanisms for lapses, but the model remains an interpretation of group-level findings.

chains.name: Delay sensitivity and reward circuitry
chains.desc: Delay-discounting and reward-related findings connect motivational phenotypes to ventral-striatal and frontal systems without reducing ADHD to a single reward deficit.

chains.name: Catecholamine modulation of prefrontal representations
