chains.desc: D1 and alpha2A mechanisms provide a translational chain from catecholamine modulation to recurrent prefrontal physiology and working-memory performance; this does not establish a universal receptor abnormality in ADHD.

chains.name: Polygenic risk and developmental trajectories
chains.desc: Polygenic risk and age-dependent imaging differences support developmental models with heterogeneous pathways rather than a fixed brain-age or single-circuit explanation.

questions.title: One computation or many?
questions.text: Is the same computation applied to different inputs across the cerebellar cortex ('universal transform'), or do zebrin modules, cell-type gradients and nuclear classes implement different computations?
approaches: Compare plasticity rules and Purkinje-cell dynamics between anterior motor and posterior association lobules with identical protocols.
Test whether one model class (e.g., forward model) fits responses across a multi-domain fMRI battery.
Relate posterior Purkinje-cell subtypes to their projection targets.

questions.title: What do climbing fibers teach outside the motor domain?
questions.text: Climbing fibers signal reward, reward omission and learned predictions. Do these signals drive plasticity that changes social or reward-guided behavior?
approaches: Image climbing fibers during social and reward tasks.
Closed-loop olive stimulation or suppression timed to reward prediction errors.
Test whether reward-related microzones project to VTA-targeting nuclear neurons.

questions.title: How necessary is LTD for learning?
questions.text: Mice lacking LTD expression learn normally. Is this compensation by other plasticity sites, module-specific learning rules, or evidence that LTD is not the main memory mechanism?
approaches: Acute, inducible LTD block in adults to avoid developmental compensation.
Separate manipulations of zebrin-positive and zebrin-negative modules.
Measure which plasticity sites change first during learning.

questions.title: Does the cerebellum instruct cortical development?
questions.text: Juvenile perturbation of posterior cerebellum has lasting nonmotor effects. Through which circuits does early cerebellar activity shape prefrontal maturation?
approaches: Time-limited juvenile perturbation with longitudinal prefrontal recordings.
Preterm cohorts with cerebellar injury followed with longitudinal connectivity imaging.
Rescue experiments that restore activity in the relay (VM thalamus) during the sensitive period.

questions.title: Which nuclear cell types carry nonmotor signals?
questions.text: Fastigial and dentate neurons fall into output-specific classes. Which classes carry signals for fear, reward, feeding and cognition, and are they the same across species?
approaches: Class-specific manipulation with intersectional genetics.
Projection-tagged recording during nonmotor tasks.
Cross-species comparison of human dentate classes.

questions.title: How do cerebellum and basal ganglia cooperate?
questions.text: Disynaptic links connect the two systems in both directions. What computation does the network perform during learning, and how does it fail in dystonia and Parkinson's disease?
approaches: Simultaneous recording of nuclei and striatum during learning.
Silence the intralaminar thalamic relay at defined learning stages.
Patient imaging of cerebello-striatal connectivity.

questions.title: What is special about the human cerebellum?
questions.text: Human Crus I/II, the frontal-projecting dentate class and the rhombic lip are all expanded. Which of these differences matter for human cognition and disease?
approaches: Comparative single-cell atlases across primates.
Organoid or xenograft models of the human rhombic lip.
Relate individual differences in Crus I/II size to cognition.

questions.title: Can cerebellar stimulation treat nonmotor disorders?
questions.text: Cerebellar TMS restored connectivity and reduced negative symptoms; Crus I stimulation rescued social deficits in mice. Can cerebellar neuromodulation become a targeted therapy?
approaches: Sham-controlled trials with connectivity-defined targets.
Animal models that map which cells TMS-like stimulation recruits.
Biomarkers that predict responders.

questions.title: How does gut information reach the cerebellar nuclei?
questions.text: Gut nutrients activate anterior DCN neurons that end meals through striatal dopamine. The route in is unknown; the route out could be the direct nuclear projection to substantia nigra dopamine neurons or a thalamic relay.
approaches: Trans-synaptic tracing from satiation-related anterior DCN neurons.
Vagal or spinal afferent manipulation during nutrient infusion.
Test whether the dopamine effect requires VTA/SNc or a thalamic relay.

questions.title: Do functional boundaries follow anatomical modules?
questions.text: Task-based parcellations do not follow lobular boundaries. Do they follow zebrin modules, climbing-fiber zones or cerebral connectivity instead?
approaches: High-resolution fMRI compared with zebrin maps in primates.
Individual-level parcellations in dense-sampling datasets.
Map climbing-fiber zones in tasks that span domains.

questions.title: Two dopamine routes?
questions.text: Cerebellar nuclei excite both VTA and substantia nigra dopamine neurons. Do the two routes carry different signals (reward versus movement vigor), and does either carry the satiation signal from the anterior nuclei?
approaches: Record cerebellar axons in VTA and SNc in one task with reward, movement and satiety epochs.
Silence each route during feeding and during reward learning while measuring striatal dopamine with sensors.
Map which nuclear output classes project to each target.

questions.title: When does a climbing fiber teach?
questions.text: Climbing fibers fire all the time, yet learning needs strong Purkinje calcium. Synchrony recruits MLI2 disinhibition. Is synchrony the gate, and what sets it: olivary coupling, error salience or reward?
approaches: Change olivary gap-junction coupling and measure MLI2 recruitment and learning.
Image Purkinje dendritic calcium with MLI2s silenced, for errors versus rewards.
Model whether synchrony-gated plasticity explains learning-rate differences across microzones.

questions.title: What drives non-motor cerebellar behaviors?
questions.text: Silencing granule-cell signaling spares social preference and anxiety, but silencing Purkinje output does not. Are these behaviors driven by intrinsic Purkinje firing, climbing fibers, or downstream compensation?
approaches: Silence climbing fibers or granule cells acutely in adults versus during development.
Clamp Purkinje firing patterns optogenetically while social behavior is tested.
Trace downstream compensation after early cerebellar lesions with whole-brain imaging.

questions.title: Is the cerebellum a cognitive reserve?
questions.text: Greater cerebellar volume goes with better cognition in older adults, and in Alzheimer's disease while amyloid burden is still low. Is that causal compensation through cerebro-cerebellar loops, or a marker of overall brain health?
approaches: Track cerebellar–cortical connectivity longitudinally as amyloid accumulates.
Test whether cerebellar TMS improves cognition more in people with low amyloid burden.
Compare cerebellar lesions acquired before versus after cortical pathology.

questions.title: Does behavioral state gate cerebellar learning?
questions.text: Locomotion enhances delay eyeblink conditioning by increasing mossy-fiber activity, and the eyeblink deficit of CB1-knockout mice disappears when they walk. Noradrenaline lowers climbing-fiber release and associative plasticity in slices, and β-adrenergic blockade impairs acquisition of eyeblink conditioning. Do neuromodulators decide when and where the cerebellum learns, or do they act through changes in movement and arousal?
approaches: Record locus coeruleus, serotonergic and cholinergic activity during eyeblink or VOR learning and relate it trial by trial to the learning rate.
Hold locomotion constant (treadmill) while removing one modulator's receptors from a single cerebellar cell type.
Compare how each modulator changes plasticity rules in slices with how it changes learning in vivo.

questions.title: What do co-released peptides add?
questions.text: Climbing fibers contain CRF (and, during development, CGRP), Golgi cells and mossy fibers contain enkephalin, and more than 30 neuropeptides have been found in the cerebellum. CRF is permissive for LTD and excites nuclear neurons, but the specific functions of most cerebellar peptides remain poorly understood. When are they released, and do they change what the fast transmitters compute?
approaches: Image peptide release during behavior with genetically encoded peptide sensors, where they exist.
Delete a peptide gene only in olivary or Golgi neurons and test motor learning and performance.
Map peptide receptors across cerebellar cell types with single-cell transcriptomics.

questions.title: Where does cerebellar serotonin come from?
questions.text: In rats, double labeling placed most serotonergic afferents in reticular nuclei rather than the raphe. Serotonin excites Lugaro cells and depolarizes Golgi cells, so it could switch inhibition in the granular layer. Which brainstem neurons supply cerebellar serotonin in mice and primates, and when are they active?
approaches: Trace serotonergic inputs to the cerebellum with intersectional genetic tools (for example Sert-Cre or Pet1-Cre) in mice.
Record these neurons across sleep, arousal and locomotion.
Delete serotonin receptors in Lugaro or Golgi cells and test granular-layer timing tasks.

questions.title: Does motor cortex execute learned skills, or only teach them?
questions.text: Motor cortex lesions after training spare a learned, precisely timed movement sequence in rats, yet sudden cortical inhibition blocks a learned prehension skill in mice. Which skills need motor cortex for execution, and why: dexterity, the kind of learning, or recovery after a chronic lesion?
approaches: Compare acute optogenetic inactivation with chronic lesions in the same animals and task.
Train tasks that differ only in dexterity and test whether execution still needs cortex after learning.
Track whether learning-related spines persist once execution no longer needs motor cortex.

questions.title: Representation or dynamics?
questions.text: Do motor cortex neurons represent movement parameters such as direction, or are they parts of a dynamical system whose state generates the movement pattern? If dynamics, are they generated locally or driven by thalamic input? In mouse ALM, planning activity shows discrete attractor dynamics, yet it collapses when the thalamus is silenced.
approaches: Perturb the cortical state optogenetically and test whether activity returns along the predicted dynamics.
Silence thalamic input at different movement phases while recording cortical populations.
Fit tuning-based and dynamical models to the same population recordings and compare their predictions for new movements.

questions.title: What releases a planned movement?
questions.text: In mice, a Go-cue signal from the midbrain reaches motor cortex through the thalamus and switches it from planning to a motor command, and choice activity collapses across the brain at movement initiation. Before licks in a flexible timing task, frontal cortex and striatum ramp in a way consistent with an adjustable timer. Do cued and timed movements converge on the same thalamocortical switch, and what sets the moment of release?
approaches: Record and silence midbrain reticular → thalamus neurons in the flexible lick-timing task and compare with the cued task.
Stimulate the midbrain–thalamus pathway at different points of the striatal ramp and test whether it releases the movement early.
Compare population dynamics at the onset of cued and self-timed reaches in monkeys to test whether the collapse of choice activity is shared.

questions.title: What do direct cortico-motoneuronal connections add?
questions.text: CM cells occupy a caudal 'new' M1 present only in some higher primates and humans, while the corticospinal output of 'old' M1, the standard for many mammals, must use the integrative mechanisms of the spinal cord. Which movements need the direct route, and can interneuron circuits substitute for it?
approaches: Selectively silence CM versus indirect corticospinal routes in primates and compare dexterity deficits.
Map corticospinal synapses onto spinal interneuron classes across species.
Test whether rodent corticospinal–interneuron circuits support independent digit control.

questions.title: What does the somato-cognitive action network do?
questions.text: Human M1 contains inter-effector regions coupled to the cingulo-opercular network. Are they needed for whole-body action planning and physiological control, and do they differ from effector regions in corticospinal output and in cerebellar connectivity?
approaches: Compare the effects of stimulating inter-effector versus effector regions on axial movement and action planning.
Trace inter-effector connectivity to brainstem and spinal targets in macaques.
Test whether cerebellar functional connectivity separates inter-effector from effector regions in precision fMRI.

questions.title: How do neuromodulators gate skill learning in M1?
questions.text: Dopamine from the VTA and acetylcholine from the basal forebrain are each needed for skill-related plasticity in rat motor cortex. Do they carry different signals, act on different cells, or gate different phases of learning?
approaches: Record dopamine and acetylcholine release in M1 across days of skill learning.
Block D1/D2 or cholinergic receptors in different learning phases and track spine formation.
Identify which M1 cell types express the receptors needed for learning.

questions.title: Is working memory held by persistent firing?
questions.text: Monkey prefrontal neurons fire through memory delays with activity tuned to the remembered location (funahashi1989), and this persistent firing depends on NR2B NMDA receptors (wangm2013); in mice, medial prefrontal delay firing needs mediodorsal thalamic input (bolkan2017). In monkey PFC, however, brief gamma bursts accompany the encoding and re-activation of remembered items while beta bursts mark a default state that encoding and decoding interrupt, and the authors argue that working memory is carried by discrete oscillatory dynamics and spiking rather than sustained activity (lundqvist2016). Which mechanism stores the item?
approaches: Silence prefrontal delay activity optogenetically for brief windows at different delay times and test whether the memory survives each gap.
Record large prefrontal and mediodorsal populations and ask whether the remembered item can be decoded continuously on single trials or only around bursts.
Compare local NR2B blockade with manipulations of short-term synaptic facilitation in the same task to see which one erases the memory.

questions.title: What does the orbitofrontal cortex compute?
questions.text: Monkey OFC neurons encode the value of offered and chosen goods (padoaschioppa2006). Surgical removal of orbital prefrontal cortex impaired reversal learning and blunted the effect of reinforcer devaluation (izquierdo2004), but excitotoxic, fiber-sparing OFC lesions spared reversal learning (rudebeck2013). Theory proposes instead that OFC represents the current task state for reinforcement learning (wilson2014). Is OFC a value signal, a map of task states, or both?
approaches: Compare excitotoxic, aspiration and chemogenetic OFC inactivation in the same animals on reversal and devaluation tasks.
Record OFC in a task where hidden task states and option values vary independently, and test which one its neurons track.
Inactivate OFC while recording midbrain dopamine neurons, and test whether prediction errors lose information about the hidden task state.

questions.title: What decides whether extinction holds?
questions.text: Infralimbic neurons respond to the tone when rats recall extinction, stimulating it mimics extinction, and inactivating it impairs extinction memory (milad2002; sierramercado2011). Prelimbic responses that persist after extinction go with failure to express it (burgosrobles2009). In mice, basolateral amygdala firing entrains to medial prefrontal theta input when animals recognize safety (likhtik2014). What sets the balance between prelimbic and infralimbic influence after extinction?
approaches: Silence prelimbic or infralimbic projections to the basolateral amygdala separately during extinction recall.
Image prelimbic and infralimbic ensembles across conditioning, extinction and recall, and test which ones predict the return of fear.
Drive theta-frequency input from medial PFC to the amygdala during safety cues and test whether extinction recall improves.

questions.title: How does ketamine produce lasting antidepressant effects?
questions.text: In rats, ketamine rapidly adds prefrontal spine synapses through mTOR, and blocking mTOR prevents its behavioral effects (li2010). In mice, ketamine rescues spines lost on prefrontal projection neurons, and these new spines maintain, but do not start, its effects on motivated escape (modasava2019). In monkeys, systemic ketamine abolishes the persistent firing of prefrontal Delay cells (wangm2013). What starts the antidepressant response, and how does it relate to ketamine’s effects on prefrontal firing?
approaches: Image prefrontal spines and ensemble activity in the first hours after ketamine to find what precedes the first behavioral change.
Block NMDA receptors only in defined prefrontal cell types to see which population starts the response.
Compare doses that abolish delay firing with antidepressant doses in the same animals.

questions.title: Do the direct and indirect pathways oppose each other or work together?
questions.text: The classical model has the direct pathway facilitate movement and the indirect pathway inhibit it, and in mice, optogenetically activating each fits that picture (kravitz2010). Yet both pathways are transiently active together when mice start an action (cui2013), and both are needed to initiate and execute learned action sequences, which led one group to propose that coordinated patterns of activity, rather than the relative amount of activity in each pathway, regulate movement (tecuapetla2016). What does each pathway contribute at the moment an action is chosen?
approaches: Record identified direct- and indirect-pathway neurons at cellular resolution while mice choose among several actions, and test whether indirect-pathway activity tracks the actions not taken.
Replay or scramble each pathway's natural activity pattern at action onset with patterned optogenetics, instead of driving it uniformly.
Compare how the two pathways coordinate in dopamine-depleted mice before and after levodopa.

questions.title: Is phasic dopamine a learning signal, a movement signal, or both?
questions.text: The output of primate dopamine neurons apparently signals reward prediction errors (schultz1997), and activating dopamine neurons at reward delivery is enough to strengthen cue–reward learning in rats (steinberg2013). In mice, though, many SNc dopamine neurons fire before self-paced movements and change their probability and vigour when manipulated (dasilva2018), striatal dopamine axons carry rapid locomotion signals (howe2016), and dopamine is needed for the striatal representation of vigor (panigrahi2015); the movement-related neurons and axons are largely separate from the reward-responsive ones. How are the two signals divided among dopamine neurons and their striatal targets, and do they interact?
approaches: Map, by projection target and genetic subtype, which dopamine neurons carry movement versus reward signals, then silence each group in a task that needs both.
Measure dopamine release in dorsal and ventral striatum during self-paced movements that are, or are not, followed by unexpected reward.
Test whether movement-related dopamine bursts change corticostriatal plasticity, as nigral stimulation at self-stimulation parameters does.

questions.title: How does deep brain stimulation relieve parkinsonism?
questions.text: Subthalamic or pallidal stimulation improves motor function and quality of life in Parkinson disease in randomized trials (weaver2009, schuepbach2013). In parkinsonian rodents, its therapeutic effects in the subthalamic nucleus can be accounted for by stimulating afferent axons there (gradinaru2009). In patients, the subthalamic nucleus and internal pallidum show coherent activity below 30 Hz that levodopa reduces (brown2001), and stimulation triggered by pathological activity in local field potentials beat continuous stimulation (little2013). Which afferents carry the therapeutic effect, and which features of the recorded activity should trigger stimulation?
approaches: Stimulate defined afferents to the subthalamic nucleus optogenetically in parkinsonian animals and compare their therapeutic effects.
In patients with sensing implants, compare adaptive stimulation triggered by different frequency bands of the local field potential.
Track subthalamic–pallidal synchrony and symptoms together across levodopa doses and stimulation settings.

questions.title: How does control pass from goal-directed actions to habits?
questions.text: In rats, lesions of the dorsolateral striatum keep actions sensitive to outcome devaluation after training that normally produces habits (yin2004), whereas prelimbic lesions abolish sensitivity to goal value even after limited training (killcross2003). In monkeys, striatonigrostriatal connections form an ascending spiral from the limbic to the motor striatum through midbrain dopamine cells (haber2000). Does this spiral carry the hand-off from goal-directed to habitual control?
approaches: Record dopamine release in dorsomedial and dorsolateral striatum across training, from goal-directed to habitual responding.
Silence the nigral dopamine cells that receive ventral striatal input and test whether habits still form.
Lesion the dorsolateral striatum after habits are established and test whether goal-directed control returns.

questions.title: Does the adult human hippocampus make new neurons?
questions.text: In adult mice, ablating dentate neurogenesis impairs fine spatial discrimination, increasing it improves discrimination of similar contexts, and disrupting it blocks behavioral responses to antidepressants (clelland2009, sahay2011, santarelli2003). In humans the evidence conflicts: new neurons were found in the dentate gyrus of adult patients labelled with BrdU (eriksson1998), young neurons declined sharply in childhood and were not detected in adults in one study (sorrells2018), and thousands of immature neurons were counted at ages 14 to 79 in another (boldrini2018). Do adult humans add dentate neurons, and if so, do they serve the functions seen in mice?
approaches: Apply the same markers and tissue handling to matched post-mortem and surgical samples across ages.
Birth-date neurons in human tissue with methods that do not rely on marker expression, such as retrospective isotope dating.
Relate dentate gyrus measures in living people to tasks that require telling similar experiences apart.

questions.title: A dorsal–ventral split, or a gradient?
questions.text: The dorsal (posterior in primates) hippocampus is linked mainly to cognitive functions and the ventral (anterior) to stress, emotion and affect (fanselow2010), and manipulations in mice fit this in the dentate gyrus and CA1 (kheirbek2013, jimenez2018). But gene expression shows discrete domains along the long axis while anatomy and recordings suggest gradients (strange2014), and ventral CA1 neurons in rats also carry goal-directed firing to the nucleus accumbens (ciocchi2015). Are long-axis functions discrete or graded, and how are they routed to different targets?
approaches: Record or image projection-identified neurons at many points along the long axis in the same animals during spatial and anxiety tasks.
Compare long-axis gene-expression boundaries with functional boundaries mapped by local manipulations.
In humans, relate anterior and posterior hippocampal activity to navigation and anxiety in the same participants.

questions.title: How do memories come to rely less on the hippocampus?
questions.text: The medial temporal lobe's role in declarative memory is thought to be temporary (squire1991, frankland2005): hippocampal lesions abolish contextual fear when made 1 day after training but not 7 to 28 days later (kim1992), and when a neocortical schema exists, new associations become hippocampal-independent rapidly (tse2007). Prefrontal engram cells form during learning but mature over time with hippocampal support, while hippocampal engram cells become silent (kitamura2017), and suppressing sharp wave-ripples after training impairs spatial memory (girardeau2009). What sets the pace of this transfer, and do silent hippocampal engrams still contribute to recall?
approaches: Suppress ripples at different delays after learning and test when retrieval stops depending on the hippocampus.
Reactivate silent hippocampal engram cells at remote time points while recording prefrontal engram cells.
Vary how well a schema is established and measure how fast new memories become hippocampal-independent.

questions.title: Does replay plan the future or consolidate the past?
questions.text: Place cells that fired together during behavior reactivate in later sleep (wilson1994), and disrupting sharp wave-ripples after training impairs spatial memory or slows learning (girardeau2009, egostengel2010). Before goal-directed navigation, hippocampal sequences depict paths from the current position to a remembered goal and predict immediate behavior (pfeiffer2013). Do the same events serve both consolidation and planning, and can the two be manipulated separately?
approaches: Disrupt ripples only during awake pauses before navigation, or only during sleep after learning, and compare route choice and next-day memory.
Decode, trial by trial, whether replay content predicts the next trajectory or repeats the last one.
Record ripples with intracranial electrodes in patients during memory and planning tasks.

questions.title: How does the amygdala keep good and bad apart?
questions.text: In monkeys, amygdala activity tracks the changing values of images rapidly enough to account for learning, and distinct populations encode positive and negative values (paton2006). In mice, basolateral neurons projecting to the nucleus accumbens or the centromedial amygdala undergo opposing synaptic changes after reward or fear conditioning and support positive or negative reinforcement (namburi2015), and two genetically distinct, spatially segregated basolateral populations take part in positive- or negative-valence behaviors and inhibit each other (kim2016). Are the projection-defined and the genetically defined populations the same cells, and do primates have a comparable division?
approaches: Map projection targets and molecular markers in the same basolateral neurons, for example with retrograde tracing and spatial transcriptomics.
Record genetically identified basolateral populations through reward and fear learning, including value reversals.
Look for marker- or projection-defined value-coding classes in the monkey amygdala.

questions.title: Is the amygdala needed to feel fear, or to detect threat?
questions.text: Patient SM, who has focal bilateral amygdala lesions, showed no fear with snakes, spiders or a haunted house and an impoverished experience of fear in daily life, although she showed other basic emotions; the authors conclude that the amygdala is pivotal for triggering a state of fear (feinstein2011). Yet her impaired recognition of fearful faces became normal when she was told to look at the eyes (adolphs2005), and a patient with selective bilateral amygdala damage learned which stimuli were paired with the unconditioned stimulus without acquiring conditioned autonomic responses (bechara1995). How much of the amygdala's role lies in detecting threat and directing attention to it, and how much in the feeling of fear itself?
approaches: Test people with focal amygdala lesions on threat detection, attention to threat cues, conditioning and reported feelings in the same sessions.
Relate intracranial amygdala recordings in neurosurgical patients to moment-by-moment reports of fear.
Ask whether guiding attention to threat cues restores conditioned responses, as instructions restored fear recognition.

questions.title: Where in the amygdala is a fear memory stored?
questions.text: Fear conditioning potentiates thalamic input to the lateral amygdala and drives AMPA receptors into its synapses (mckernan1997, rumpel2005), and the lateral amygdala is thought to engage the central nucleus, the principal output, during fear expression. Yet inactivating the central nucleus impairs acquisition as well as expression, and blocking protein synthesis there impairs consolidation (wilensky2006); activity in its lateral part is required for acquisition (ciocchi2010), and potentiation of lateral amygdala inputs onto its somatostatin neurons is needed for fear memory formation (li2013). Is the memory distributed across the lateral and central amygdala, and what does each part store?
approaches: Tag neurons active during learning in the lateral and central amygdala separately, and test which reactivation is sufficient for recall.
Block plasticity in each nucleus at different times after training to see when each is needed.
Record lateral and central amygdala neurons together across learning to see where conditioned responses first appear.

questions.title: Do separate amygdala outputs raise and lower anxiety?
questions.text: In mice, stimulating basolateral amygdala terminals in the central amygdala reduced anxiety-related behavior (tye2011), activating basolateral synapses in the ventral hippocampus increased it (felixortiz2013), and ventral CA1 neurons projecting to the lateral hypothalamus are enriched in anxiety cells (jimenez2018). In people with PTSD, social anxiety disorder or specific phobia, the amygdala is more active than in comparison subjects (etkin2007). How do these opposing projections combine in one animal, and which of them changes in anxiety disorders?
approaches: Manipulate two projections at once to see whether their effects on anxiety add up or cancel.
Record projection-identified basolateral neurons during anxiety tests.
Relate amygdala connectivity with the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex to symptoms in people with anxiety disorders.

questions.title: Can an old fear memory be rewritten?
questions.text: Consolidated fear memories return to a labile state when reactivated, and blocking protein synthesis in the lateral and basal amygdala shortly afterwards produces amnesia, whether the memory was 1 or 14 days old (nader2000). Deleting the lateral amygdala neurons that overexpressed CREB after learning blocked expression of the memory persistently, suggesting it was erased (han2009). Could weakening a reactivated memory, or targeting the neurons that hold it, reduce unwanted fear memories in people?
approaches: Test whether reconsolidation blockade also works for remote memories and for memories formed under strong stress.
Compare memory loss after blockade with the fate of the tagged neurons that hold the memory.
Run controlled trials of reactivation followed by a reconsolidation-blocking treatment in people with persistent fear memories.

questions.title: Does the cerebellum take part in seeing?
questions.text: Corticopontine input to the cerebellum appears to come from extrastriate areas concerned with spatial vision, visual motion and the peripheral field rather than object identification (schmahmann1993), and primary visual cortex sends only a few corticopontine cells (glickstein1985). Most of the human cerebellum is functionally coupled to cerebral association networks, in proportion to their cerebral extent, but primary visual cortex is the exception (buckner2011). Does the cerebellum use these visual signals only to guide movement, or does it also contribute to perception?
approaches: Record mossy fibre and Purkinje cell responses to visual motion in the lobules that receive these pontine inputs.
Test motion perception and visually guided reaching separately in people with cerebellar lesions.
Silence the visual corticopontine pathway and measure both perception and visually guided movement.

questions.title: Can the critical period be reopened to treat amblyopia?
questions.text: Ocular dominance plasticity in mouse V1 is confined to a critical period (gordon1996) whose onset may require a threshold level of inhibition (fagiolini2000), and degrading perineuronal-net proteoglycans reactivates it in adult rats (pizzorusso2002). In amblyopic monkeys, cortical binocularity is reduced, but the changes in V1 neurons do not explain the full deficit (kiorpes1998). Would reopening plasticity in adults restore vision through an amblyopic eye, and where beyond V1 does the deficit lie?
approaches: Combine treatments that reopen plasticity with patching of the good eye in animal models of amblyopia.
Record extrastriate areas in amblyopic monkeys.
Follow binocular responses and visual acuity together during treatment.

questions.title: Are seeing objects and acting on them separate?
questions.text: A patient who could not perceive the shape, orientation and size of objects grasped them accurately (goodale1991), which led to the proposal that a ventral stream identifies objects and a dorsal stream guides action (goodale1992). In healthy people, face and location matching engage separate occipitotemporal and parietal regions (haxby1991), and mouse higher visual areas may form motion- and pattern-related groups (marshel2011). How strictly are the streams separated, and do mice have the same division?
approaches: Test perception and grasping of the same objects after selective lesions of each stream.
Record parietal and inferotemporal neurons while animals both judge and grasp objects.
Silence groups of mouse higher visual areas during visually guided behaviour and during discrimination.

questions.title: What does V1 predict?
questions.text: In mice, running more than doubles V1 visual responses (niell2010) through VIP interneurons recruited by basal forebrain input (fu2014), layer 2/3 neurons signal mismatch between actual and expected visual flow (keller2012), and V1 neurons combine visual speed and run speed (saleem2013). Where do the motor-related predictions come from, and do primate V1 responses change in the same way?
approaches: Silence candidate sources of motor-related input to V1 and measure mismatch responses.
Record V1 in monkeys or humans during self-generated versus passively viewed visual flow.
Relate mismatch signals to learning of new visuomotor couplings.

questions.title: How do face cells relate to face areas?
questions.text: Inferotemporal cortex holds a population of face-selective neurons (desimone1984), almost all neurons in the largest face-selective fMRI region of macaques are face selective (tsao2006), and the human fusiform face area responds selectively to faces (kanwisher1997). The larger fusiform response to fearful faces depends on the amygdala (vuilleumier2004). How do face-selective neurons map onto the face areas seen with fMRI in each species, and how does the amygdala tune them?
approaches: Record single neurons in fMRI-defined face areas of neurosurgical patients.
Compare face-area responses to fearful faces before and after amygdala inactivation in monkeys.
Map face-selective neurons and face areas in the same animals.

questions.title: Does the anterior insula turn body signals into feelings?
questions.text: Right anterior insula activity and gray matter volume relate to how accurately people detect their own heartbeat and to visceral awareness (critchley2004), and the anterior insula is proposed to re-represent interoception as a basis for subjective feelings and awareness (craig2009). Smokers whose brain damage involved the insula were more likely to quit without a persisting urge to smoke (naqvi2007), and anxiety proneness is proposed to reflect an augmented interoceptive prediction signal (paulus2006). Is the anterior insula needed for feelings, or for awareness of them?
approaches: Test interoceptive accuracy and reported feelings in patients with focal anterior insula lesions.
Relate anterior insula responses to heartbeats to moment-by-moment ratings of urges and emotions.
Train interoceptive accuracy in anxious people and measure insula activity and anxiety.

questions.title: Where does a taste get its value?
questions.text: In mice each taste quality has its own field of gustatory cortex (chen2011), and manipulating the sweet or bitter field controls taste perception and behaviour (peng2015). Projections from those fields to the amygdala assign valence separately from identity (wang2018), and a projection to the lateral central amygdala is needed to learn taste-guided avoidance (schiff2018). Does the same split between identity in the insula and value in the amygdala hold in primates, and how does learning change it?
approaches: Record taste cortex and amygdala together while a taste is devalued by pairing it with illness.
Image the human taste cortex with high resolution for a gustotopic map.
Silence insula-to-amygdala projections in primates and measure taste preference and discrimination.

questions.title: How does the insula predict the body's needs?
questions.text: Insular neurons respond to food cues only when mice are hungry, a bias carried by AgRP neurons through the paraventricular thalamus and basolateral amygdala (livneh2017); insular activity tracks the return to homeostasis and cues shift it toward the predicted future state (livneh2020); and the posterior insula drives anxiety through the central amygdala and feeding through the accumbens (gehrlach2019). How do predicted and actual body states combine, and is the same circuit used for thirst, pain or fear?
approaches: Record insular neurons while feeding is delayed or the meal is infused directly into the stomach.
Manipulate amygdala input to the insula and measure prediction-related activity.
Compare insular coding of hunger, thirst and aversive bodily states in the same neurons.

questions.title: Is the anterior insula a switch between brain networks?
questions.text: The salience network is anchored by frontoinsular and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (seeley2007), the right fronto-insular cortex appears to drive switching between the central-executive and default-mode networks (sridharan2008), and the anterior insula is proposed as the network's hub (menon2010). Gray matter loss across psychiatric diagnoses converges on the same insula and cingulate regions (goodkind2015). Does the switch depend on the insula itself, and could its damage explain shared symptoms across disorders?
approaches: Test network switching in patients with focal anterior insula lesions.
Stimulate the anterior insula during intracranial recordings and measure network transitions.
Relate insula integrity to executive function across psychiatric diagnoses.

questions.title: Why is the bulb's map scattered in piriform cortex?
questions.text: Sensory neurons expressing one receptor converge on two fixed glomeruli (mombaerts1996), but each glomerulus projects diffusely across piriform cortex (sosulski2011) and piriform neurons sample the whole bulb (miyamichi2011); arbitrary piriform ensembles can acquire learned meaning (choi2011), and in humans posterior piriform patterns track perceived odour quality (howard2009). How does a scattered code support stable odour perception, and what does the stereotyped map in the cortical amygdala add?
approaches: Record the same piriform neurons across days while animals learn new odour meanings.
Compare odour responses of piriform and cortical amygdala neurons to innately and learned meaningful odours.
Test whether disrupting the stereotyped amygdala projection alters odour perception or only innate behaviour.

questions.title: Why does smell fail early in Parkinson's disease?
questions.text: Impaired smell can precede Parkinson's disease by at least 4 years (ross2008), 7% of people with idiopathic smell loss developed the disease within 4 years (haehner2007), and smell loss affects about 90% of early cases and correlates with neuron loss in the locus coeruleus, raphe and nucleus basalis (doty2012); Alzheimer's disease causes equally severe deficits (mesholam1998). Where in the olfactory pathway does the damage begin, and can smell tests pick out people at risk?
approaches: Follow people with idiopathic smell loss with dopamine-transporter imaging and repeated smell tests.
Map pathology along the olfactory pathway in people who died at prodromal stages.
Compare smell deficits across neurodegenerative diseases to separate shared from disease-specific damage.

questions.title: What does the cerebellum do for smell?
questions.text: Odours activate the posterior lateral cerebellar hemispheres, more strongly at higher concentrations, and sniffing activates the anterior cerebellum, and the authors propose that the cerebellum adjusts sniff volume to odour concentration (sobel1998cb). Sniffing alone drives piriform cortex (sobel1998), and rats discriminate odours within a single sniff (uchida2003). Does the cerebellum control sniffing, or does it take part in odour perception?
approaches: Measure sniff volume and odour discrimination in people with cerebellar lesions.
Record cerebellar activity in rodents while sniffing adapts to odour concentration.
Perturb the cerebellum during odour discrimination and measure sniffing and accuracy separately.

questions.title: Does breathing pace memory?
questions.text: Nasal breathing synchronizes oscillations in human piriform cortex, amygdala and hippocampus, and breathing phase enhanced fear discrimination and memory retrieval (zelano2016); respiration imposes a slow rhythm on piriform responses (poo2009), and lateral entorhinal-CA1 coupling develops as rats learn odour-guided navigation (igarashi2014). Is it the nasal airflow itself that times memory, and does the effect extend beyond smell?
approaches: Compare memory encoding during nasal and oral breathing with intracranial recordings.
Block nasal airflow signals in rodents and measure hippocampal oscillations and memory.
Time stimuli to inspiration or expiration in memory tasks without odours.

questions.title: Where does the noradrenaline for a new taste come from?
questions.text: New tastes are known to increase noradrenaline release in forebrain areas that process taste, yet locus coeruleus activity in mice is suppressed during licking and is not influenced by taste novelty, suggesting a possible role for other noradrenergic nuclei (fan2024). Phasic locus coeruleus activation does reshape taste coding in the gustatory cortex along a palatability axis (fan2026). Which noradrenergic nuclei signal taste novelty, and when does locus coeruleus release reshape taste coding during natural eating?
approaches: Record noradrenergic nuclei of the medulla (A1/A2) as mice first meet a new taste.
Measure noradrenaline release in the gustatory cortex with a genetically encoded sensor during novel and familiar tastes.
Activate the locus coeruleus at the end of a lick bout, when it naturally rises, and test taste preference later.

questions.title: How far did the vertical lobe converge on the hippocampus and the cerebellum?
questions.text: JZ Young likened the vertical lobe to the hippocampus, the cerebellum and the insect mushroom body (shomrat2015). Its input synapses show hippocampal-like LTP (hochner2003, sternmentch2022), and its cells resemble Drosophila Kenyon cells molecularly (styfhals2022). Yet octopus and cuttlefish place their plasticity at different layers while performing the same computation (shomrat2011), and its complex amacrine cells form part of a circuit the authors call unique (bidel2023). Which features does associative learning itself require, and which are accidents of each lineage?
approaches: Compare how sparsely single input axons drive simple amacrine cells with how mossy fibres drive cerebellar granule cells and perforant-path axons drive dentate granule cells.
Silence complex amacrine cells and test whether vertical lobe output loses stimulus specificity, as balancing inhibition predicts.
Locate the plastic synapses in the vertical lobes of other cephalopods, such as squid, to see how often the site changes.

questions.title: How does a brain without a body map steer one arm?
questions.text: Stimulating the basal lobes evokes movements without any site moving a single arm (zullo2009), and the higher motor centres work without body-part maps (hochner2023), yet octopuses guide a single arm to a visual goal (gutnick2011) and learn from one arm’s motion and touch (gutnick2020). The arms carry their own motor programs (sumbre2001), and nerve cords link arms outside the brain (kuuspalu2022). Where is the choice of arm made, and how does the command reach the right arm?
approaches: Record basal lobe neurons while an octopus reaches with one arm in a single-arm maze, and test whether activity predicts which arm is used.
Cut the nerve cords that link arms near the arm bases and test whether single-arm choices or multi-arm coordination change.
Stimulate the cerebrobrachial tract of one arm while recording from the others to compare central and peripheral routes.

questions.title: What does active sleep do for octopus memory?
questions.text: Active sleep bouts recur through quiet sleep in a cycle (medeiros2021). During them the superior frontal and vertical lobes, linked to learning and memory, show wake-like activity, and in quiet sleep they generate oscillations resembling sleep spindles (pophale2023). The vertical lobe acquires long-term memory through LTP (shomrat2008). Does active sleep replay or consolidate what the vertical lobe learned that day?
approaches: Prevent active sleep after a learning session and test recall the next day.
Record the vertical lobe during learning and look for the same activity patterns in the following active sleep.
Tetanize the vertical lobe pathway and test whether active sleep bouts change in number or length.

questions.title: Which optic gland signal ends an octopus mother’s life?
questions.text: Removing the optic glands abolishes maternal brooding and reverses the decline toward death (wangzy2018, wang2022). After reproduction the glands raise synthesis of pregnane steroids, 7-dehydrocholesterol and bile acid intermediates (wang2022), across reproductive stages they up- and downregulate catecholamine, insulin and feeding-peptide pathways (wangzy2018), and optic gland chemistry extends into neighbouring lobes of the peduncle complex (wangzy2024). Which of these signals drives fasting, self-injury and death, and what tells the gland that mating has happened?
approaches: Block each steroid pathway in brooding females and score fasting, self-injury and survival.
Give 7-dehydrocholesterol or bile acid intermediates to females without optic glands and test whether the decline returns.
Trace which brain lobes signal to the optic gland around mating.

questions.title: Where and why does the fly’s functional network depart from its wiring?
questions.text: Resting-state functional correlations across the central brain track direct region-to-region structural connectivity strongly, but in this comparison of published connectome and imaging data the fit varies, and the mushroom body depends more on indirect connections (turner2021). Spontaneous activity across the brain forms an intrinsic functional network (mann2017), yet much of whole-brain activity correlates with running and flailing (schaffer2023), and the connectome has a rich club of highly connected neurons (lin2024). Which features of the wiring, or of the fly’s behaviour during imaging, explain where structure and function diverge?
approaches: Image resting-state activity and then reconstruct the connectome of the same fly, so that structure and function come from one brain.
Regress behaviour-linked global activity (running, flailing) out of the imaging before computing functional connectivity, and test whether the mushroom body’s fit to direct connections improves.
Simulate activity on the whole-brain connectome, as connectome-based models do (shiu2024), and compare simulated with measured correlations region by region.

questions.title: How are innate and learned odour values combined?
questions.text: Projection neurons send each odour both to the mushroom body and to the lateral horn (jefferis2007). About 30% of lateral horn projections converge with mushroom body outputs (dolan2019), and MB-V2 output neurons, needed for retrieving aversive memory, project to the lateral horn (sejourne2011). Lateral horn cell types drive valence behaviour (dolan2019), as do mushroom body output neurons (aso2014b), and some output neurons contact descending neurons directly (lif2020). Where, and how, do the innate and the learned streams combine to choose an action?
approaches: Record the neurons where lateral horn and mushroom body outputs converge before and after conditioning an innately attractive odour.
Silence MB-V2 neurons and test whether retrieval of a learned odour avoidance still changes lateral horn activity.
List, from the whole-brain connectome, the neurons that receive both lateral horn and mushroom body output and reach descending neurons, and test them in valence assays.

questions.title: How does sleep help a memory become long-term?
questions.text: Inducing sleep after training that alone does not produce long-term memory lets flies form one, while activating the dorsal fan-shaped body without sleep does not (donlea2011). Sleep drive builds up through plasticity in a subset of ellipsoid body neurons (lius2016), and the mushroom bodies, where olfactory memories are localized (zars2000, pascual2001), also regulate sleep (joiner2006, pitman2006). Yet mushroom body α/β output is not needed during consolidation (mcguire2001). Which memory processes need sleep itself, and where in the mushroom body do they act?
approaches: Induce sleep after olfactory training and test whether long-term memory forms in flies lacking the mushroom body’s vertical lobes.
Record mushroom body output synapses during sleep induced by fan-shaped body activation and during matched wakefulness after training.
Trace in the connectome the paths from sleep-promoting fan-shaped body neurons to the mushroom body.

questions.title: How does the compass heading become a steering command?
questions.text: Neurons tiling the ellipsoid body hold a heading estimate (seelig2015), a heading representation in the central brain shows ring-attractor dynamics (kim2017), shifting neurons rotate it according to angular velocity (green2017), and fan-shaped body neurons turn body-centred velocity into world-centred coordinates (lu2022). Silencing E-PG compass neurons reverts sun navigation to frontal phototaxis (giraldo2018), and the central complex connectome shows motifs for vector-based navigation and many pathways for context-dependent action selection (hulse2021). How is a goal heading stored and compared with the current heading to steer?
approaches: Record central complex output neurons while flies hold a chosen heading to a simulated sun, and while that heading is perturbed.
Shift the heading representation optogenetically and measure which downstream neurons signal the resulting heading error and turning.
Use the paths from the central complex to descending neurons in the connectome to predict which descending neurons carry steering commands.

questions.title: How do sex differences in wiring produce sex-specific behaviour?
questions.text: Male-specific fruitless splicing specifies courtship (demir2005, manoli2005), a single class of olfactory neurons mediates responses to the pheromone cVA (kurtovic2007), and fruitless reroutes that pheromone signal by wiring different third-order neurons in males and females (kohl2013). The male CNS connectome finds 138 dimorphic, 289 male-specific and 71 female-specific neuron types, concentrated in higher brain centres while the sensory and motor periphery is largely isomorphic (berg2026). Do a few rerouting switches like the cVA one account for most behavioural differences, or do many distributed changes?
approaches: Compare male and female connectomes along the full path from Or67d neurons to descending neurons, to find where the pheromone pathways first diverge.
Masculinize single dimorphic cell types in females and score which elements of courtship each confers.
Count how many male-specific connection hotspots lie on paths from courtship-relevant sensory neurons, as a test of the few-switches view.

questions.title: How does the mushroom body read the order of odour and dopamine?
questions.text: Dopamine that follows Kenyon cell activity raises cAMP synergistically through rutabaga (tomchik2009), pairing an odour with dopamine neuron activation depresses its output synapses depending on the order of the two (hige2015), the timing of odour and dopamine writes or reverses an association through DopR1 and DopR2 (handler2019), and single dopamine neuron types follow different rules (aso2016). How do the two receptor pathways time-stamp a pairing, and do the same rules hold for natural rewards and punishments?
approaches: Image cAMP and the second messengers of both receptors in single Kenyon cell boutons while varying the interval between odour and dopamine.
Repeat backward pairing with sugar and shock, not only with optogenetic dopamine neuron activation, to test whether behaviour follows the same timing rule.
Model each compartment’s learning rule (aso2016) and test the predicted memory updates against behaviour.

questions.title: What can fly disease models tell us about human brain disorders?
questions.text: Human α-synuclein in flies causes loss of dopaminergic neurons, inclusions and locomotor dysfunction (feany2000); Aβ42 causes amyloid deposits, learning defects and neurodegeneration (iijima2004); dfmr1 mutants show courtship-memory and mushroom body defects that mGluR antagonists rescue (mcbride2005); and an expanded polyglutamine protein causes nuclear inclusions and degeneration (warrick1998). Which of these phenotypes arise in circuits the fly shares with mammals, and which treatments that work in flies also work in patients?
approaches: Map where each model’s neurons degenerate onto the whole-brain connectome and ask whether the vulnerable neurons share wiring features.
Express each disease gene in single identified cell types, such as Kenyon cells or dopamine neurons, with split-GAL4 lines to tie phenotypes to circuits.
Test in flies the drugs now in human trials and compare effects across species.

questions.title: Coordinated action of basal forebrain cell types
questions.text: How do divergent cholinergic, PV+ GABAergic, SOM+ GABAergic, and glutamatergic basal forebrain projection populations coordinate with one another to modulate cortical microcircuit states during attention and sleep?
approaches: Perform simultaneous multi-color fiber photometry or 2-photon imaging of ChAT+, PV+, and SOM+ basal forebrain axons in prefrontal cortex during attention tasks.
Optogenetically silence specific GABAergic or glutamatergic subsets while measuring local acetylcholine release using GRAB-ACh sensors.
Map reciprocal monosynaptic connections between BF SOM+ neurons and their cortical and subcortical partners using viral intersectional tracing.

questions.title: Transmitter specificity of human basal forebrain coupling
questions.text: Does human resting-state corticotopic coupling of Ch1-Ch3 and Ch4 territories reflect genuine acetylcholine transmission or mixed cholinergic-GABAergic and structural co-activation?
approaches: Combine 7T resting-state fMRI with PET imaging using [18F]FEOBV (VAChT ligand) to correlate functional coupling with cholinergic terminal density.
Perform high-resolution pharmacological fMRI before and after acetylcholinesterase inhibitor or muscarinic antagonist administration.
Compare cortical coupling changes in early-stage Alzheimer's and Lewy body dementia patients with verified Ch4 degeneration.

questions.title: Lateral septal gating of dopamine and memory replay
questions.text: How does hippocampal output routed through lateral septum modulate VTA dopaminergic neurons during sharp-wave ripple replay and reward-related spatial memory consolidation?
approaches: Record VTA dopamine neurons while selectively optogenetically inhibiting ventral lateral septal terminals in VTA during hippocampal sharp-wave ripples.
Use cell-type-specific tracing to identify whether LS projections to VTA synapse directly onto dopamine or GABAergic interneurons.
Test spatial memory retrieval and replay fidelity following pathway-specific chemogenetic silencing of the hippocampus-LS-VTA circuit.

questions.title: How do noncanonical gaseous messengers (NO and CO) interact with classical monoamines to set memory stability?
questions.text: While dopamine provides rapid reinforcement at Kenyon cell output synapses, a subset of dopamine neurons co-transmits nitric oxide (NO) to stimulate soluble guanylate cyclase in Kenyon cells, promoting memory updating and decay. Conversely, retrograde carbon monoxide (CO) produced by Kenyon cell heme oxygenase regulates presynaptic dopamine release. How are these gaseous signals compartmentalized, and what determines whether a memory is consolidated, updated, or erased?

questions.title: How does peptidergic volume transmission integrate with the synaptic connectome to select actions?
questions.text: Connectomic reconstructions map tens of thousands of chemical synapses, yet broad modulators such as SIFamide, sNPF, NPF, and Tachykinin act largely through extrasynaptic receptors and volume transmission across neuropil compartments. How do neuromodulatory states dynamically gate or reconfigure the rigid synaptic connectome during competing behavioral states like hunger versus courtship?

questions.title: How do distinct biogenic amines (tyramine vs octopamine vs histamine) segregate motor and sensory actions?
questions.text: Because Tdc2-positive driver lines label both tyraminergic and octopaminergic neurons, earlier studies often conflated tyramine and octopamine. Tyramine acts on TyrR receptors to regulate locomotor switching, whereas octopamine signals through OAMB and OctbetaRs. Concurrently, histamine acts as a fast inhibitory transmitter on photoreceptors and mechanosensory neurons via ort/HisCl channels. What are the specific non-overlapping target circuits of these distinct amines across the brain and ventral nerve cord?

questions.title: Which ADHD dimensions share a circuit mechanism?
questions.text: ADHD includes heterogeneous attention, inhibition, working-memory and reward-related dimensions, while group-level neural findings overlap and have limited individual specificity (posner2020; koirala2024). Which combinations of phenotype, state and developmental stage identify reproducible circuit patterns?
approaches: Measure attention stability, stopping, delay discounting and arousal repeatedly in the same participants rather than using one composite score.
Fit preregistered dimensional network models across development and test them in an independent cohort.
Compare ADHD-enriched patterns with clinical comparison groups to estimate disease specificity.

questions.title: How do catecholamines trade stability for flexibility?
questions.text: D1 stimulation and alpha2A signaling can strengthen or weaken prefrontal representations depending on dose and state in translational studies (gamo2010; arnsten2020). Which receptor, cell and state variables predict treatment benefit for different ADHD phenotypes?
approaches: Record prefrontal population activity during working-memory and effort tasks before and after selective D1- and alpha2A-directed perturbations.
Stratify participants by baseline arousal, delay sensitivity and working-memory phenotype, then test whether acute drug effects differ.
Use longitudinal pharmacodynamic measures to distinguish target engagement from durable symptom change.

questions.title: What changes across development and remission?
questions.text: Large imaging studies report age-dependent group differences, and longitudinal symptom data show fluctuating remission and recurrence rather than a simple outgrowth model (hoogman2017; hoogman2019; sibley2022). Which neural changes precede symptom change, and which reflect compensation, treatment or experience?
approaches: Follow the same participants with repeated imaging, phenotype and medication-state measurements from childhood into adulthood.
Test whether developmental trajectories predict recurrence better than a single endpoint diagnosis.
Integrate polygenic scores with longitudinal circuit measures without treating gene-set enrichment as localization.

vestib.label: Vestibular and oculomotor signs (not lesion-mapped here)

flatmap.note: Schematic flatmap in the style of SUIT (Diedrichsen & Zotow 2015). Scores (0–3) are qualitative summaries of the cited meta-analyses, connectivity maps and lesion studies, drafted with AI assistance; check them against the sources. King et al. (2019) found that functional boundaries do not follow lobular borders, so treat lobules as approximate addresses.

neuromodulation.desc: Which neuromodulators, neuropeptides and other slow messengers act on which parts of the cerebellar circuit. Each cell links to the evidence.
neuromodulation.note: Fast glutamate and GABA signaling is in the Microcircuit view. An empty cell means no direct evidence among the curated papers, not evidence of absence.

circuits.name: Cerebro-cerebellar loops
circuits.desc: Cortex → pons (crossing) → cerebellar cortex → nuclei → thalamus → back to the same cortical areas. Left cortex loops with the right cerebellum.

circuits.name: Olivo-cerebellar module
circuits.desc: Climbing fibers from the opposite inferior olive, Purkinje output to the nuclei, and inhibitory feedback from the nuclei to the olive.

circuits.name: Basal ganglia link
circuits.desc: Dentate → thalamus → striatum, cerebellar nuclei → substantia nigra dopamine neurons, and subthalamic nucleus → pons → cerebellar cortex.

circuits.name: Reward & social (VTA)
circuits.desc: Cerebellar nuclei excite VTA dopamine circuits and reach medial prefrontal cortex through thalamus.

circuits.name: Fear & anxiety
circuits.desc: Fastigial → ventrolateral PAG controls fear memory; fastigial → parafascicular thalamus modulates anxiety (relay to amygdala proposed); dentate → amygdala relieves anxiety after exercise.

circuits.name: Navigation (hippocampus)
circuits.desc: Restricted cerebellar regions reach dorsal hippocampus multisynaptically and synchronize at 6–12 Hz.

circuits.name: Satiation (gut → DCN)
circuits.desc: Gut nutrients activate anterior DCN neurons, which end meals by raising striatal dopamine. Dashed: routes unknown.

circuits.name: Eyes & balance
circuits.desc: Vestibulo-ocular reflex and its adaptation: labyrinth → vestibular nuclei → eye muscles, calibrated by the flocculus using retinal-slip errors.

circuits.name: Body: sensing & acting
circuits.desc: Spinocerebellar input and descending output through red nucleus and reticular formation.

circuits.name: Neuromodulators
circuits.desc: Where the cerebellum gets its neuromodulators: locus coeruleus (noradrenaline), brainstem serotonin neurons, VTA (dopamine), tuberomammillary nucleus (histamine), lateral hypothalamus (orexin), pedunculopontine and vestibular cholinergic inputs, and CRF-expressing olive neurons. Tags name the transmitter. Purkinje cells also project back to the locus coeruleus.

circuits.name: Descending output
circuits.desc: Pyramidal-tract neurons of layer 5B send axons to the spinal cord, brainstem motor centres and thalamus; the premotor areas also project to the spinal cord. Corticostriatal and corticopontine outputs reach the basal ganglia and, through the pons, the cerebellum.

circuits.name: Inputs to M1
circuits.desc: Motor thalamus (VA/VL), which relays cerebellar output, excites layers 2/3–5B; somatosensory cortex targets the upper layers; premotor input (rodent M2) reaches pyramidal-tract neurons directly.

circuits.name: Cerebellar & basal ganglia loops
circuits.desc: Motor cortex reaches the cerebellum through the pontine nuclei and the basal ganglia through the striatum. Cerebellar output returns through the motor thalamus, whose input drives feedforward inhibition in M1 (monkey).

circuits.name: Motor planning (ALM)
circuits.desc: In mice, preparatory activity in anterior lateral motor cortex depends on a loop with the thalamus: photoinhibiting the thalamus collapses it, and photoinhibiting ALM diminishes thalamic activity. Fastigial output reaches frontal cortex through the thalamus, and fastigial activity is needed to maintain cortical preparatory activity; silencing the dentate nucleus suppresses ALM preparatory activity. Pyramidal-tract neurons that project to the thalamus carry early preparatory activity; those that project to the medulla carry late preparatory activity and motor commands. Dashed: route not traced.

circuits.name: Go cue → movement
circuits.desc: In mice, ascending glutamatergic neurons of the midbrain reticular and pedunculopontine nuclei show short-latency, phasic changes in firing selective for an auditory Go cue. The signal reaches motor cortex via the thalamus and switches it from planning-related activity to a motor command; pyramidal-tract neurons that project to the medulla carry late preparatory activity and motor commands.

circuits.name: Learning signals
circuits.desc: Dopamine from the VTA and acetylcholine from the basal forebrain are needed for skill learning and the plasticity behind it (rat); after grasp training, thalamic input shifts toward corticospinal neurons of the distal forelimb (rat).

circuits.name: Working-memory network
circuits.desc: A loop between prefrontal cortex, mediodorsal thalamus, hippocampus, posterior parietal cortex, and basal forebrain, maintaining rule representations and delay activity (Obermayer et al., 2018; Parikh et al., 2007).

circuits.name: Fear, safety & mood
circuits.desc: Amygdala connections with orbital and cingulate cortex (monkey), the medial prefrontal theta input that marks safety and the proposed amygdala → prelimbic route for fear (rodents), and the medial prefrontal projection to the dorsal raphe.

circuits.name: Neuromodulator inputs
circuits.desc: Dopamine from the ventral tegmental area, noradrenaline from the locus coeruleus, acetylcholine from the basal forebrain (Ch4 / substantia innominata), and serotonin feedback to the dorsal raphe: tuning delay activity, attentional cue detection, and cognitive state (Parikh et al., 2007; Hangya et al., 2015; Sarter et al., 2005).

circuits.name: Cerebellar loop
circuits.desc: Prefrontal cortex → pontine nuclei → cerebellum, and dentate → thalamus → prefrontal cortex: the closed loop through Crus II (monkey).

circuits.name: Direct pathway
circuits.desc: Cortex → striatum → internal pallidum and substantia nigra → thalamus → cortex. Direct-pathway neurons, classically proposed to facilitate movement, project to the basal ganglia's output nuclei; activating them increases locomotion in mice.

circuits.name: Indirect pathway
circuits.desc: Cortex → striatum → external pallidum → subthalamic nucleus → internal pallidum → thalamus → cortex: the indirect pathway, classically proposed to inhibit movement.

circuits.name: Hyperdirect pathway
circuits.desc: Motor cortex excites the subthalamic nucleus directly, bypassing the striatum, and reaches the pallidum with a shorter conduction time than through the striatum.

circuits.name: Nigral dopamine and its inputs
circuits.desc: Nigral dopamine neurons receive input from the ventral striatum (monkey) and the cerebellar nuclei (mouse), and project to the striatum.

circuits.name: External pallidum: two cell types
circuits.desc: In rats, prototypic neurons of the external pallidum target the subthalamic nucleus, whereas arkypallidal neurons project back to the striatum and respond to Stop cues.

circuits.name: Saccade gate
circuits.desc: Striatonigral neurons → substantia nigra pars reticulata → superior colliculus. The pars reticulata tonically inhibits saccade-related collicular cells, and releasing them from this inhibition is suggested to start movements (monkey).

circuits.name: Basal ganglia–cerebellum loop
circuits.desc: Subthalamic nucleus → cerebellar cortex (via the pontine nuclei) → cerebellar nuclei → thalamus → striatum → external pallidum → subthalamic nucleus: disynaptic projections in both directions link the basal ganglia and cerebellum.

circuits.name: Trisynaptic pathway
circuits.desc: Entorhinal cortex → dentate gyrus → CA3 → CA1 → back to the entorhinal cortex, with a disynaptic route through CA2 alongside. In the mouse each field is its own structure; the human and macaque atlases do not separate the fields, so they sit in the hippocampus.

circuits.name: Ventral hippocampal outputs
circuits.desc: Ventral (anterior) hippocampal neurons reach the medial prefrontal cortex, nucleus accumbens, amygdala and lateral hypothalamus and route different information to each: anxiety-related firing to prefrontal cortex and goal-directed firing to the accumbens (rat), and anxiety signals through the lateral hypothalamus (mouse).

circuits.name: Hippocampus and prefrontal cortex
circuits.desc: Hippocampal-formation neurons project mostly to medial, then orbital prefrontal areas (monkey). In mice, direct hippocampal input supports the encoding of spatial cues in working memory, ventral hippocampal input supports anxiety-related prefrontal activity, and hippocampal–entorhinal input helps generate prefrontal engram cells for remote memory.

circuits.name: Cerebellum to hippocampus
circuits.desc: Restricted cerebellar regions reach dorsal hippocampus multisynaptically and synchronize at 6–12 Hz.

circuits.name: Fear conditioning pathway
circuits.desc: Tone information from the auditory thalamus reaches the lateral amygdala, which is thought to engage the central nucleus, the principal output for conditioned fear. Its projections to the periaqueductal gray and the lateral hypothalamus appear to mediate freezing and the conditioned arterial pressure response (rat), and an inhibitory pathway to the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray produces freezing (mouse). The human atlas does not separate the amygdala's nuclei, so the step from the lateral to the central nucleus lies inside the amygdala.

circuits.name: Intercalated cells and extinction
circuits.desc: Intercalated cells receive conditioned-stimulus information from the basolateral amygdala and send inhibitory projections to the central nucleus; after extinction training they could reduce the impact of basolateral input on the central nucleus, and partial lesions impair the expression of extinction (rat). In the human brain this circuit lies inside the amygdala, and in the macaque the intercalated cells are placed approximately.

circuits.name: Basolateral outputs
circuits.desc: Basolateral amygdala projections with distinct effects: terminals in the central amygdala reduce anxiety-related behavior and synapses in the ventral hippocampus increase it; neurons projecting to the nucleus accumbens support positive reinforcement and those projecting to the centromedial amygdala negative reinforcement (mouse); and the projection to prelimbic cortex increases freezing (rat).

circuits.name: Amygdala and prefrontal cortex
circuits.desc: Amygdala connections with orbital and cingulate cortex (monkey), the medial prefrontal theta input that marks safety (mouse), the proposed amygdala → prelimbic route for fear, and the basolateral projection to prelimbic cortex that increases freezing (rat).

circuits.name: Cerebellum and amygdala
circuits.desc: A fastigial → parafascicular thalamus pathway, which may relay to the amygdala, modulates anxiety, and glutamatergic dentate neurons drive PKCδ+ amygdala neurons to reduce anxiety during exercise (mouse).

circuits.name: From the eye to visual cortex
circuits.desc: Retinal input reaches V1 through the lateral geniculate nucleus, and in the monkey V1 and V2 feed areas V4 and MT (V5). In the human brain the geniculate is shown in the thalamus; V4 and MT are not placed in the mouse brain.

circuits.name: Ventral and dorsal streams
circuits.desc: The ventral stream runs from striate to inferotemporal cortex and is proposed to play the major role in identifying objects, and the dorsal stream runs to posterior parietal cortex and is proposed to mediate visually guided action (review). In the mouse, V1 projects to at least nine higher visual areas (mouse).

circuits.name: Attention, emotion and running
circuits.desc: Stimulating the frontal eye field enhances V4 responses at the corresponding location (monkey); amygdala damage abolishes the larger fusiform response to fearful faces (human); and basal forebrain input recruits VIP interneurons that raise V1 responses during running (mouse).

circuits.name: Visual cortex and cerebellum
circuits.desc: Extrastriate areas concerned mainly with spatial vision, motion and the peripheral field project to the pontine nuclei, whereas primary visual cortex sends only a few corticopontine cells (monkey); the pontine nuclei send crossed mossy fibers to the cerebellar cortex.

circuits.name: Taste: thalamus, insula and amygdala
circuits.desc: The thalamic taste area projects to insular-opercular cortex (review), and phasic locus coeruleus activation reshapes taste coding there along a palatability axis (mouse); sweet- and bitter-responsive taste cortex projects to distinct parts of the amygdala, whose inputs assign taste valence, and to the lateral central amygdala, needed to learn taste-guided avoidance (mouse). In primates the taste cortex is shown in the anterior insula.

circuits.name: Hunger reaches the insula
circuits.desc: Signals from hypothalamic AgRP hunger neurons reach insular cortex via the paraventricular thalamus and basolateral amygdala and bias insular neurons toward food cues (mouse).

circuits.name: Posterior insula outputs
circuits.desc: The posterior insula drives anxiety-related behaviour through the central amygdala and regulates feeding through the nucleus accumbens (mouse).

circuits.name: Anterior insula, cingulate and amygdala
circuits.desc: At rest the anterior insula is coupled with the anterior cingulate, and the two form a network activated by salient events (human); the insula connects with several amygdaloid nuclei (review).

circuits.name: From the nose to olfactory cortex
circuits.desc: Sensory neurons expressing one receptor converge on one or a few glomeruli of the olfactory bulb (rat, mouse); each glomerulus projects diffusely across piriform cortex and in stereotyped patches to the cortical amygdala (mouse). Sensory neurons are placed approximately in front of the bulb.

circuits.name: Beyond olfactory cortex
circuits.desc: Olfactory signals reach the lateroposterior orbitofrontal cortex through the anterior piriform cortex and the hypothalamus (monkey), and the lateral entorhinal cortex receives the predominant olfactory input to the hippocampal region (rat).

circuits.name: Vision to the vertical lobe
circuits.desc: Retinal photoreceptors project to the optic lobe, whose fibres reach the superior frontal lobe (HRP tracing); the median superior frontal lobe sends the glutamatergic input of the vertical lobe, the learning and memory centre (octopus).

circuits.name: Inside the vertical lobe
circuits.desc: Input axons from the median superior frontal lobe fan out onto millions of amacrine interneurons, which converge onto the large output neurons (fan-out fan-in); all three are shown in the vertical lobe (octopus).

circuits.name: Optic lobe connections
circuits.desc: The optic lobe receives the retina and input from the basal, subvertical and brachial lobes, and sends fibres to the superior frontal and lateral basal lobes (HRP tracing, octopus).

circuits.name: Brain and arms
circuits.desc: The basal lobes command movements without a body map, motor axons run along the cerebrobrachial tracts, the brain learns from one arm’s motion and touch, vision guides an arm, and each sucker’s ganglion sends fibres toward the arm’s nerve cord (octopus).

circuits.name: Neuromodulators
circuits.desc: Where the octopus brain gets its neuromodulators and chemical transmitters: nitric oxide (NO) in vertical lobe long-term potentiation; serotonin (5-HT) and dopamine (DA) in learning thresholds and motor reinforcement; octopamine (OA) in predatory arousal; tyramine (TA) in arm reflex tone; GnRH and FMRFamide in neuroendocrine reproduction; acetylcholine (ACh) in visual pathways; and glutamate (Glu) in MSFL-to-VL excitation. Each transmitter has its own colour; 3D arrows trace source clusters to their target lobes.

circuits.name: Smell: antennal lobe to mushroom body and lateral horn
circuits.desc: Olfactory receptor neurons expressing the same receptor converge on one or two antennal lobe glomeruli; projection neurons relay olfactory information to the mushroom body and the lateral horn (fly).

circuits.name: Mushroom body outputs
circuits.desc: Projection neurons bring odours to the mushroom body; MB-V2 output neurons project to the lateral horn, and some output neurons contact descending neurons directly (fly). Kenyon cells and output neurons are shown in the mushroom body.

circuits.name: Anterior visual pathway
circuits.desc: Medulla visual projection neurons feed neurons that connect the anterior optic tubercle with the ring neurons, whose axons largely form the ellipsoid body (fly). Ring neurons are shown in the ellipsoid body.

circuits.name: Motion vision to escape
circuits.desc: Photoreceptor signals split in the lamina; L1 and L2 start the ON and OFF pathways to T4 and T5 cells, which end in the lobula plate; LPLC2 looming detectors ramify in the T4/T5 layers and terminate on the giant fibre descending neuron (fly). T4/T5 are shown in the lobula plate, LPLC2 in the lobula and the giant fibre at the neck connective.

circuits.name: Brain to nerve cord
circuits.desc: Descending neurons traverse the neck and link sensory neuropils of the brain with motor neuropils of the nerve cord; some mushroom body output neurons contact them directly; sugar stimulation of taste neurons activates a pair of subesophageal motor neurons (fly).

circuits.name: Neuromodulators
circuits.desc: Where the fruit fly brain gets its neuromodulators: dopamine (DA), serotonin (5-HT), octopamine (OA), tyramine (TA), histamine (HA), nitric oxide (NO), carbon monoxide (CO), SIFamide (SIFa), pigment-dispersing factor (PDF), short neuropeptide F (sNPF), tachykinin (Tk), leucokinin (Lk), insulin-like peptides (DILP), allatostatin A (AstA), drosulfakinin (DSK), and adenosine (Ado). Each transmitter has its own colour; 3D arrows trace source clusters to their target neuropils across the brain and nerve cord.

circuits.name: Mesoscale tractography connectome (diffusion MRI)
circuits.desc: Mesoscale structural wiring reconstructed from high-resolution diffusion MRI tractography in Octopus bimaculoides (Jacobs et al., 2022).
