Illustrates the 3D scaffold linking optic lobes, optic tracts, supraesophageal cognitive centers (superior frontal, vertical, subvertical), subesophageal motor hubs (basal, pedal, palliovisceral, brachial), and peripheral arm cords.

circuits.name: Chemotactile sensory axis: suckers to brain
circuits.desc: Long-range chemotactile sensorimotor stream resolved in the Octo9 whole-body microCT atlas and functional studies (Sepela et al., 2025; van Giesen et al., 2020; Jung et al., 2018). Chemotactile receptors on suckers relay chemical and mechanical touch through axial arm cords into the brachial lobe, ascending to the inferior frontal lobe tactile memory matrix and basal motor control.

circuits.name: Vertical lobe synaptic connectome (serial EM)
circuits.desc: High-resolution synaptic wiring of the Octopus vulgaris vertical lobe acquisition network from serial electron microscopy (Bidel, Meirovitch et al., 2023). Median superior frontal axons fan out onto millions of amacrine interneurons, which converge onto large output neurons. Subvertical feedback and basal motor projections complete the learning loop.

circuits.name: Active sleep & dynamic skin patterning
circuits.desc: Synchronized multi-lobe oscillatory dynamics during two-stage octopus sleep recorded with Neuropixels probes (Pophale et al., Nature 2023). During active sleep, neural bursts sweep across the vertical, subvertical and basal lobes to drive rapid, awake-like chromatophore patterning via palliovisceral motor pathways.

circuits.name: Cholinergic corticopetal attention axis
circuits.desc: Basal forebrain cholinergic projections (Ch4 / substantia innominata / nucleus basalis) innervating prefrontal cortex (PL, IL, ACC, OFC), motor cortex, sensory cortices (V1, S1), and the amygdala, driving cue detection, cortical desynchronization, and attentional effort (Parikh et al., 2007; Hangya et al., 2015; Sarter et al., 2005).

circuits.name: Septohippocampal theta pacemaker & memory
circuits.desc: The canonical septohippocampal circuit: medial septum (Ch1/Ch2) cholinergic and GABAergic projections to CA1, CA3, dentate gyrus, subiculum, and entorhinal cortex pacing theta oscillations and memory encoding; with reciprocal CA1/subiculum projections to the lateral septum (Freund & Antal, 1988; Buzsáki, 2002; Hasselmo, 2006; Vandecasteele et al., 2014).

circuits.name: Ascending neuromodulatory arousal into basal forebrain
circuits.desc: Brainstem and midbrain neuromodulatory inputs to the basal forebrain: VTA dopamine, locus coeruleus noradrenaline, and dorsal raphe serotonin gating basal forebrain excitability and whole-brain state transitions (Gaykema & Zaborszky, 1996; Berridge & Waterhouse, 2003; Edlow et al., 2024).

circuits.name: Septohippocampal theta pacemaker
circuits.desc: Medial septal cholinergic and GABAergic pacemaker inputs to CA1, CA3, dentate gyrus, subiculum, and entorhinal cortex driving theta rhythms and memory encoding, balanced by reciprocal CA1/subiculum projections to the lateral septum (Freund & Antal, 1988; Buzsáki, 2002; Vandecasteele et al., 2014; Gu & Yakel, 2011).

circuits.name: Phenotypic dimensions → distributed systems
circuits.desc: Phenotypic dimensions are mapped first: response variability and attentional stability connect to distributed control, while stopping and delay sensitivity connect to frontostriatal and reward systems.

circuits.name: Control, reward and default-mode interactions
circuits.desc: A schematic ADHD network view linking frontoparietal control, default-mode/task-engaged interactions, salience monitoring and reward systems. Functional links are not monosynaptic projections.

circuits.name: Dopamine and noradrenaline modulation
circuits.desc: Translational catecholamine mechanisms: dopamine-related reward measures, D1 gain control and alpha2A prefrontal signaling. Acute drug mechanisms are not evidence of a universal transmitter deficit.

circuits.name: Genetics, development and measurement
circuits.desc: Polygenic risk and age-dependent morphology motivate longitudinal, dimensional measurement rather than a fixed brain-age explanation.

map.title: Functional map of the fly central brain
map.intro: How activity is organized across the central brain, set beside the wiring it is thought to come from. Functional connectivity is the correlation between brain regions’ spontaneous calcium signals, averaged over 20 flies; structural connectivity is the number of neurons in the hemibrain connectome with input in one region and output in the other. Both are recomputed here from the published data of Turner, Mann & Clandinin (2021). Click a region for its strongest partners.
map.note: Structural and functional connectivity come from different animals: activity from 20 flies imaged with a pan-neuronal calcium indicator, wiring from the hemibrain connectome of one fly, compared through a shared atlas. This is a cross-animal comparison of structure and function, not the two measured in the same brain, and the correlations come from spontaneous activity during imaging, not from tasks. Regions follow the insect brain nomenclature; the imaging covered the right side of the central brain and the midline, so most regions are right-hemisphere ones.

Virtual Fly Brain: neuron and neuropil anatomy on a standard brain

neuromodulation.desc: Which neuromodulators, neuropeptides, and diffusible gaseous messengers act on which cells of the fly brain. Each cell links to evidence grading, receptor identity, and functional sign.
neuromodulation.note: Fruit fly neuromodulation spans multiple organizational layers: synaptic and fast transmission (Histamine), presynaptic gain control (sNPF, Tachykinin), noncanonical gaseous cotransmission (NO, CO), and brain-wide state coordination (SIFamide, PDF, DILPs, AKH).
